                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S06
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Narrating the full path from a user typing a URL to bytes coming back is the backbone of a design round — every component you later discuss hangs off it, and it gives you a structure to think in when put on the spot.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The path: DNS resolution, TCP and TLS handshake, CDN (which may answer immediately), load balancer, API gateway, your service, cache, database — with the response returning through the same layers.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The useful habit is asking at each hop: can this answer without going further? Every layer that short-circuits removes everything downstream from both the latency budget and the load. That is what caching, CDNs and read replicas are all doing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The full path, and where you can stop
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1  DNS resolution         ~0-100 ms   cached in OS/browser; TTL matters
2  TCP handshake           1 RTT       0 with keep-alive
3  TLS handshake           1-2 RTT     0 with resumption / TLS 1.3
4  CDN / EDGE              <-- CAN ANSWER HERE. Everything below is skipped.
5  Load balancer           L4 or L7; health checks, connection draining
6  API gateway             authn, rate limiting, routing, validation
7  SERVICE                 your code
8  Cache                   <-- CAN ANSWER HERE
9  Database                the expensive, stateful bottom
10 (async) queue -> workers  anything not needed for the response

DESIGN RULE
  push work UP the stack (toward the edge) and OUT of the request
  (into async workers). Both remove load from the layer that is
  hardest to scale - the database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Where does authentication belong?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Coarse checks at the gateway — is the token valid, is this client rate-limited — so unauthenticated traffic never reaches your services. Fine-grained authorisation (may this user see this record) must be in the service, because only it knows the data model.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What is the biggest single win on this path?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Usually the CDN, because it removes both latency and origin load for anything cacheable. Then connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2), which eliminates handshake round trips entirely.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S07
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Vertical scaling is a bigger machine; horizontal scaling is more machines. Vertical is simpler, has a hard ceiling and a single failure domain; horizontal is effectively unbounded and forces you to solve coordination.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The honest position is that vertical scaling is underrated — one large modern machine handles a great deal, and it avoids distributed-systems complexity entirely. Reach for horizontal when you hit a ceiling, need redundancy, or need to be in multiple locations.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The real question is what must be true to add a second instance. Almost always: no local state. If the instance holds sessions in memory, writes uploads to local disk, or runs a scheduled job on a timer, a second copy breaks it — lost sessions, missing files, and the job running twice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The checklist before instance #2
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          MUST BE TRUE
  [ ] no session state in memory      -> Redis, or a signed cookie
  [ ] no local file writes            -> object storage
  [ ] no assumption that an in-memory cache is shared
  [ ] scheduled jobs are guarded      -> leader election or a distributed lock,
                                         or the job runs N times
  [ ] no in-memory rate-limit counters
  [ ] no dependence on a fixed hostname or instance identity
  [ ] graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests
  [ ] instances x pool size < database max_connections   <- easy to miss

VERTICAL FIRST, HONESTLY
  one machine today: 100+ cores, several TB RAM, millions of IOPS
  many "we need microservices" problems are "we never tried a bigger box"
  BUT: no redundancy, a hard ceiling, and a restart is full downtime
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          When is vertical scaling genuinely right?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          For a stateful component where distribution is hard — a relational primary, an in-memory index, a matching engine. Scaling those horizontally means sharding and cross-shard coordination, and a bigger machine may buy two years of simplicity. That is a legitimate engineering choice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What breaks first when you add instances?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Connection counts to shared dependencies. Twenty instances with fifty-connection pools is a thousand connections to a database configured for two hundred — which takes down every service on that database, not just yours.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S08
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A stateless service keeps no per-user data between requests, so any instance can serve any request. That is what makes horizontal scaling, rolling deploys and instance replacement trivial — the single most valuable property a service can have.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Session state has to live somewhere, so you externalise it: a shared store like Redis, or a signed token carried by the client. The trade is that a store is a new dependency and a new failure mode, while a token cannot be revoked easily and grows every request.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            sticky sessions look like an easy fix and hurt three ways: load becomes uneven and stays uneven, deploying an instance destroys its users' sessions, and autoscaling cannot rebalance existing traffic. They avoid the problem rather than solving it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Where session state can live
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            IN MEMORY + sticky sessions
  + zero latency, no extra dependency
  - uneven load; a deploy kills sessions; no rebalancing; scaling is fake

SHARED STORE (Redis)
  + any instance serves any request; revocation is instant
  - a dependency on the hot path; needs its own HA story
  -> the usual answer when revocation matters

SIGNED TOKEN (JWT in a cookie)
  + no server state at all; scales infinitely
  - REVOCATION IS HARD (valid until it expires)
  - carried on every request; size matters; key rotation must be planned

HYBRID - what most real systems do
  short-lived access token (5-15 min), no lookup
  + a refresh token whose validity IS checked against a store
  -> cheap request path, and revocation works within one token lifetime
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Is a stateless service really stateless?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            It has no session state. It still has caches, connection pools and circuit-breaker state, and those differ per instance — which is why a request can succeed on one instance and fail on another. Being precise about which state is per-instance is worth saying out loud.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you migrate off sticky sessions without logging everyone out?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Dual-read: write new sessions to the shared store while still reading local memory if not found, then let existing sessions expire. After the longest session lifetime, remove stickiness and the local path. The same expand-contract shape as a schema migration.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S09
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Availability is quoted in nines, and the useful skill is converting to time instantly — because four nines means nothing and 52 minutes a year means something.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Dependencies in series multiply, and this is what people get wrong. A service depending on five components that are each 99.9% available is 0.999⁵ = 99.5% — worse than any individual part. Every synchronous dependency lowers your ceiling.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Dependencies in parallel multiply their failure probabilities, which is why redundancy works so well: two independent 99% components give 99.99%. The catch is the word independent — two replicas in the same rack, on the same power, or behind the same load balancer are not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The arithmetic
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              NINES -> DOWNTIME
  99%      = 3.65 days/year   = 7.2 hours/month
  99.9%    = 8.8 hours/year   = 43 minutes/month
  99.95%   = 4.4 hours/year   = 22 minutes/month
  99.99%   = 52 minutes/year  = 4.4 minutes/month
  99.999%  = 5.3 minutes/year = 26 seconds/month

SERIES (all must work)      A x B x C
  5 dependencies at 99.9% = 0.999^5 = 99.50%   (43 hours/year)
  -> YOUR CEILING IS BELOW YOUR WORST DEPENDENCY

PARALLEL (any one suffices) 1 - (1-A)(1-B)
  2 components at 99% = 99.99%
  3 components at 99% = 99.9999%
  -> ONLY if failures are INDEPENDENT. Same rack, same power, same
     deploy, same bug = correlated, and the maths does not hold.

CONSEQUENCE
  removing a synchronous dependency raises availability more than
  making that dependency more reliable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you exceed your dependencies' availability?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              By not depending on them synchronously. Cache their responses so you serve stale data when they are down, make the call async, or design an explicit fallback. A circuit breaker plus a degraded response converts a hard dependency into a soft one — the only way the arithmetic works in your favour.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why is five nines almost never right?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Twenty-six seconds a month leaves no room for a deploy, a failover, or a human. It needs full redundancy, automation everywhere and rehearsed failure — an order of magnitude more cost than four nines. Most businesses find the last nine costs more than the downtime it prevents.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S10
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                An SLI is a measurement (the proportion of requests served successfully under 300ms). An SLO is your internal target for it. An SLA is a contract with financial penalties — and it should always be looser than your SLO, so you breach your own target long before you breach the contract.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The powerful idea is the error budget: 99.9% over 30 days permits about 43 minutes of failure. That is not a target to minimise, it is a budget to spend — and that reframing turns reliability from an argument into an engineering trade-off with a number.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Budget remaining means ship features and take risks. Budget exhausted means freeze and spend the sprint on reliability. It only works if that policy was agreed in advance, which is the point worth making in an interview.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Choosing an SLI that means something
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                GOOD SLI                            WHY
proportion of requests 2xx AND      measured AT THE LOAD BALANCER, so it
  under 300ms                       includes queueing and connection time
                                    your app metrics never see

BAD SLI
average latency                     the tail is what users feel
CPU utilisation                     a CAUSE, not a symptom
process uptime                      a process can be up and useless

BURN RATE ALERTING - alert on rate, not on a threshold
  14.4x burn = 2% of budget in 1 hour -> month gone in ~50h -> PAGE
  6x burn    = 10% in 6 hours                              -> TICKET
  Use a LONG and a SHORT window together, so it fires promptly
  and RESOLVES promptly.

  At low traffic, ratios are noisy - add a minimum-volume guard or you
  page on three failed health checks at 4am.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What happens when the budget is exhausted?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Whatever policy was agreed beforehand, usually a feature freeze until it recovers. The policy matters more than the number, and negotiating it mid-incident is how error budgets become decorative.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How do you pick the target?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                From what users need and what your dependencies allow. Measure current performance for a month first. An SLO tighter than the availability of the services you depend on is arithmetically unachievable — and promising it externally is worse than having no SLA.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S11
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A single point of failure is any component whose failure takes everything with it. Finding them is mechanical: walk the request path and ask at each box, what happens if this disappears right now?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  They hide in unglamorous places — a single NAT gateway, one Redis holding all sessions, a single-AZ database, one deploy pipeline, one person who knows how failover works, a certificate with one owner.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Redundancy comes in shapes with different costs. N+1 is one spare beyond need. Active-passive is a standby that takes over — cheaper, but the failover path is unexercised until you need it. Active-active means both serve, so the path is continuously proven, at the cost of solving state consistency.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Finding and removing them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  WALK THE PATH: "what if this vanishes?"
  DNS provider     -> a secondary provider? (a real, recurring outage cause)
  CDN              -> can the origin serve directly, at what load?
  load balancer    -> multi-AZ by default on managed LBs; VERIFY
  API gateway      -> same
  service          -> N+1 across zones
  CACHE            -> can the database survive a full miss storm?
                      Usually NO. That makes the cache load-bearing.
  database primary -> Multi-AZ standby, and TEST the failover
  NAT gateway      -> one per zone, or a zone failure kills all egress
  deploy pipeline  -> can you roll back if CI is down?
  the runbook      -> written down, or in one person's head?

REDUNDANCY SHAPES
  N+1              one spare. Cheapest real redundancy.
  active-passive   standby idle. Cheaper - but the failover path is
                   UNTESTED until the day you need it.
  active-active    both serve. Path continuously proven.
                   Cost: state consistency between them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Is a cache a single point of failure?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Almost always, and it is the one people miss. If the database cannot survive a full cache miss storm, losing the cache takes the system down — the cache is load-bearing, not an optimisation. Test it: shed load, warm gradually, or rate-limit cache-miss traffic to the database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  How do you find the ones you have not thought of?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Kill things deliberately in a game day. Every organisation doing it for the first time finds something — a hardcoded endpoint, a secret that exists in one region, a service that cannot start without one that depends on it. Reasoning finds the obvious ones; experiments find the rest.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S12
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    L4 balancers forward TCP connections without reading them — very fast, they preserve the client source IP, and they can offer static addresses. L7 balancers parse HTTP, so they route by host and path, rewrite headers, terminate TLS and integrate with a web application firewall.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Algorithms matter less than people expect. Round robin is fine when requests cost the same; least outstanding requests is better when they do not, because it naturally routes around a backend stuck on a slow query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The two settings that cause real incidents are the health check and the connection draining window. A health check that verifies a shared dependency fails every backend at once, turning a database blip into a total outage. A drain window shorter than your longest request cuts connections on every deploy.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The settings that cause incidents
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    HEALTH CHECK
  path: /health/readiness      SHALLOW - local only, no database
  WRONG: a check that verifies the database
    -> the DB blips -> ALL backends fail at once -> 503, no healthy targets
    -> a 20-second degradation becomes a full outage

DRAINING
  deregistration_delay > your longest request
    too low  -> a burst of 502s on EVERY deploy that nobody explains
    too high -> deploys crawl

SLOW START
  a fresh JVM is slow until JIT compiles - ramp traffic rather than
  sending a full share immediately

ALGORITHMS
  round robin                 equal-cost requests
  least outstanding requests  variable cost - routes around a stuck backend
  hash(key)                   stickiness without cookies; cache affinity
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When do you need L4 rather than L7?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When a partner must allowlist a fixed IP, when the protocol is not HTTP, when you need the true source IP without trusting a header, or at connection counts where parsing every request is too expensive. Otherwise L7 — routing and WAF integration are worth far more.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What causes 502s when all targets are healthy?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Usually the keep-alive race: the balancer pools connections to backends, and if the backend's idle timeout is shorter than or equal to the balancer's, it reuses a connection the backend is closing. Fix by making the application keep-alive timeout exceed the load balancer's.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S13
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A reverse proxy forwards requests to backends. An API gateway is a reverse proxy with product features: authentication, rate limiting, request validation, versioning, per-client keys and analytics.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Its job is everything true of every request, so services do not each reimplement it. The failure mode is business logic creeping in, at which point you have a distributed monolith with a shared deployment bottleneck.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A backend-for-frontend solves a different problem: a mobile client wants three screens of data in one call over a slow connection, a web client wants something else. Rather than making every service serve both shapes, you add a thin aggregation layer per client type — owned by the client team.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Who owns what
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      GATEWAY (cross-cutting, true of every request)
  TLS termination           authn: is this token valid?
  rate limiting             request size limits
  routing and versioning    logging
  WAF                       usage plans and API keys

SERVICE (needs the domain model)
  authorisation: MAY THIS USER see THIS record?
  business rule validation

BFF (per client type)
  aggregate several service calls into one response
  reshape for that client's screen

ANTI-PATTERN
  business logic in the gateway -> a shared deployment bottleneck,
  and every team waits on one config change
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Does a gateway add latency?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A hop, typically single-digit milliseconds, which is almost always worth centralised authentication and rate limiting. What is not worth it is chaining several gateways — teams accumulate an edge gateway, a mesh ingress and a per-team proxy on the same request without noticing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Is a BFF not just another service to maintain?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Yes, and that is the honest cost. It earns its place when client needs genuinely diverge. If every client wants the same shape, a BFF is pure overhead and you should serve that shape directly.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S14
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        DNS turns a name into an address and is the first hop of every request. It is also the layer where you have least control over caching — which makes it a poor failover mechanism and a common cause of long outages.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GeoDNS returns different answers by client location; anycast advertises one address from many places and lets routing choose. Anycast fails over faster because the change happens in the network, with no cache to expire.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        State the limitation plainly: you set a TTL, you do not control the cache. Resolvers may extend it, corporate resolvers frequently do, browsers cache separately, and the JVM caches DNS per a security property most applications never change. A 60-second TTL routinely means 5–15 minutes of real failover.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why DNS failover is slow
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        YOU SET      TTL 60s
RESOLVERS    may honour it, may extend it
BROWSERS     cache separately
THE JVM      caches per a security property most apps never touch
             + a connection pool holding open sockets
             -> a client stays pinned to a dead endpoint for MINUTES

-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=5
hikari.max-lifetime: 600000

FOR SECONDS-LEVEL FAILOVER, DNS IS THE WRONG TOOL
  anycast / Global Accelerator   failover happens IN THE NETWORK
  client-side retry across endpoints
  a load balancer in front, with health checks

POLICIES
  simple | weighted (migration, canary) | latency | geolocation (RESIDENCY)
  | failover | multi-value
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How would you test DNS failover properly?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        From a real client, not with dig. Fail the primary health check and measure until a JVM client makes a successful request. That number is your actual RTO and it is usually far worse than the TTL suggests — the most valuable measurement in a failover game day.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What is DNS good for, then?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Coarse planned routing: sending users to a nearby region, shifting weight during a migration, enforcing residency by geolocation, and disaster recovery where a ten-minute RTO is acceptable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S15
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A CDN caches content near users. Pull fetches from your origin on the first request and caches it; push means uploading in advance, which suits a small set of large, predictable files.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Beyond caching it terminates TLS close to the user and carries the rest over a private backbone — which helps even at a zero percent hit rate for a global audience, because a handshake is several round trips.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Two operational realities: origin shield prevents a stampede where every edge misses simultaneously and hammers your origin; and purging is slow and metered, so use versioned paths so a deploy produces new URLs and old objects age out.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The cache key decides everything
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          BAD (legacy default): forward all headers, cookies and query strings
  -> every request unique -> hit rate ~0% -> a hop for nothing

GOOD: include only what CHANGES THE RESPONSE
  cache key:  url + Accept-Encoding + [page, size]
  forwarded but NOT in the key:  Authorization, X-Request-Id

PERSONALISED CONTENT IS NEVER SHAREABLE
  Cache-Control: private, no-store
  caching per-user data at a shared edge is a LEAK

INVALIDATION
  versioned paths  /assets/app.9f2c4a.js   new deploy = new URL
  purge "/*"       emergency only - slow and metered
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Can you cache authenticated API responses?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Sometimes. If a response depends only on a coarse attribute — a tenant id, a role — put that in the key and share among users with the same value. Never key on the raw token. And be deliberate: a wrong key on authenticated content serves one user's data to another.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What if your audience is one region?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Then a CDN mostly adds a hop for uncacheable content and its value is limited to static assets. Saying that is a stronger signal than recommending it reflexively.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S16
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            HTTP caching is free performance most teams leave unused. Cache-Control carries the policy, and an ETag enables cheap revalidation — the client asks has this changed? and gets a 304 with no body when it has not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            max-age sets freshness; immutable tells the browser never to revalidate, which is correct for content-hashed assets. stale-while-revalidate is the most underused directive: serve stale instantly, refresh in the background, so revalidation never blocks a user.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The distinction that matters: no-cache means revalidate before using — it may still be stored. no-store means never write this down. People routinely use the first when they mean the second.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Directives that earn their place
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONTENT-HASHED ASSET
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
  -> never revalidated. A deploy changes the filename, so there is no
     invalidation problem to solve at all.

HTML / API RESPONSE THAT CAN BE SLIGHTLY STALE
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600
  -> fresh 60s; for the next 10 min served INSTANTLY from cache while
     refreshed in the background. Users never wait.

PER-USER CONTENT
  Cache-Control: private, no-store

REVALIDATION
  ETag: "9f2c4a"  ->  If-None-Match: "9f2c4a"  ->  304, no body

no-cache = store it, revalidate before use
no-store = do not write it down     <- what people usually mean
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why prefer ETag over Last-Modified?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Last-Modified has one-second granularity and breaks when a file is regenerated with identical content. An ETag is opaque and you control it, so you can derive it from a content hash and get correct behaviour regardless of timestamps.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Where does Vary fit?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            It tells caches which request headers change the response — Vary: Accept-Encoding keeps gzip and brotli variants separate. It is also a classic cause of a near-zero hit rate: Vary: User-Agent effectively gives every browser version its own entry.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S17
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Cache-aside is what most systems use: the application checks the cache and on a miss reads the database and populates it. The cache is a dumb store, the application owns the logic, and a cache outage degrades rather than breaks — provided the database can take the load.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Read-through and write-through move that logic into the cache layer, so the application only talks to the cache. Simpler code, but the cache becomes a hard dependency and must know how to reach your database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Write-behind acknowledges to the cache and persists asynchronously — fastest writes, with data loss if the cache dies before flushing. Refresh-ahead proactively refreshes entries about to expire, which helps predictable hot keys and wastes work on cold ones.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Choosing, and the invalidation question
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CACHE-ASIDE (lazy loading)         the default
  read:  miss -> DB -> populate -> return
  write: write DB, then INVALIDATE (do not update) the cache
  + a cache outage degrades, not breaks
  - first request per key is slow; a stale window exists

READ-THROUGH / WRITE-THROUGH
  + simpler app code; cache stays consistent with the DB
  - the cache is a HARD dependency; write latency includes both hops

WRITE-BEHIND
  + fastest writes, absorbs bursts
  - DATA LOSS if the cache dies before flushing

REFRESH-AHEAD
  + no stall on expiry for hot keys
  - wasted work on keys nobody asks for again

INVALIDATE, DO NOT UPDATE
  updating on write races with concurrent readers and can leave a
  PERMANENTLY stale value. Deleting is idempotent and safe.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why invalidate rather than update on a write?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because two concurrent writers can interleave so the older value lands last and stays until the TTL expires. Deleting has no such race — the next reader repopulates from the database. Update-on-write is only safe with a version check or a lock.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you handle the stale window between the DB write and the invalidation?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Bound it with a short TTL, or delete the key before the write and again after (double delete) to catch readers who repopulated mid-write. Where staleness is unacceptable, do not cache — read from the primary.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S18
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                LRU evicts the least recently used entry and is the sensible default. LFU evicts the least frequently used, which is better for stable popularity and worse when popularity shifts, since an old hot key resists eviction long after it cools.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A TTL is not really an eviction policy, it is a correctness bound — it caps how stale any value can be. Most systems want both: a TTL for correctness, LRU for memory pressure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The detail that matters operationally is TTL jitter. Populate a thousand keys in one batch with an identical TTL and they all expire simultaneously, giving you a synchronised stampede against the database exactly one hour later.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Jitter, and Redis policies
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                WITHOUT JITTER
  1,000 keys cached at 12:00:00 with ttl=3600
  -> ALL expire at 13:00:00 -> 1,000 simultaneous misses
  -> a spike the database was never sized for
  -> and the refill RE-SYNCHRONISES them for the next hour

WITH JITTER
  ttl = base + random(0, base * 0.1)
  -> expiry spreads over six minutes; the database sees a trickle

REDIS EVICTION POLICIES
  noeviction     writes FAIL when full   <- the default; usually wrong
                 for a cache, and presents as application errors
  allkeys-lru    evict any key, LRU      <- usual choice
  volatile-lru   only keys with a TTL
  allkeys-lfu    stable popularity
  volatile-ttl   shortest remaining TTL first
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                When is LFU actually better than LRU?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                When popularity is stable and there is a long tail of one-off requests — a catalogue where the same hundred items dominate and a scan of rare items would flush them under LRU. Redis decays LFU counters over time, which addresses the complaint that old hot keys never leave.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What eviction policy should a session store use?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                None — noeviction, with correct capacity planning. Evicting a session logs a user out arbitrarily, which is a correctness failure rather than a performance one. Sessions expire by TTL; running out of memory is a sizing problem to fix.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S19
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A cache stampede is the classic one: a hot key expires, and every concurrent request misses simultaneously and hits the database at once. The fix is a lock or single-flight — one request repopulates while the others wait briefly or serve stale.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A hot key is a single key taking disproportionate traffic, which saturates one cache node however well the rest is balanced. Fixes are local in-process caching in front of the shared cache, or replicating that key across several nodes with a suffix.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  cache penetration is requests for keys that do not exist anywhere — often a scraper or an attack enumerating identifiers. Every request misses the cache and misses the database. Cache the negative result with a short TTL, or put a Bloom filter in front.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Four failure modes, four fixes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  STAMPEDE - hot key expires, everyone misses at once
  single-flight: one request repopulates, others wait on the same future
  or: serve stale while one refreshes in the background
  or: probabilistic early expiry (refresh before the TTL, at random)

THUNDERING HERD - everything expires together (see TTL jitter)
  jitter every TTL

HOT KEY - one key saturates one node
  in-process cache in front of the shared cache (short TTL)
  or replicate: key -> key#0..key#9, read a random one

PENETRATION - keys that exist NOWHERE
  cache the negative: SET key "NULL" EX 60
  or a Bloom filter of existing ids in front

// SINGLE-FLIGHT, the most useful one
private final ConcurrentMap<String, CompletableFuture<V>> inflight
        = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

V get(String key) {
    V hit = cache.get(key);
    if (hit != null) return hit;
    return inflight.computeIfAbsent(key, k ->
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            V v = db.load(k);
            cache.put(k, v);
            return v;
        }).whenComplete((v, e) -> inflight.remove(k))
    ).join();
}   // 1,000 concurrent misses -> ONE database query
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What is the difference between a stampede and a thundering herd?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A stampede is many requests for one expired key; a thundering herd is many keys expiring together, or many waiters woken at once. The first is fixed by single-flight, the second by TTL jitter. People use the terms interchangeably, and distinguishing them shows you have debugged one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Is caching negative results dangerous?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  It can be, if a key is created shortly after you cached its absence — the creation must invalidate the negative entry, or the new record is invisible until the TTL expires. Keep negative TTLs short (30–60 seconds) and invalidate on write, which is why a Bloom filter is often cleaner for large id spaces.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S20
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Redis is not just a string cache — its value is the data structures, because they let you push logic into the store and avoid read-modify-write round trips. Sorted sets for leaderboards and rate limiters, hashes for objects, sets for membership, lists for simple queues, streams for a real log, HyperLogLog for cardinality.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Persistence has two modes. RDB snapshots periodically — compact, fast to restore, and you lose everything since the last snapshot. AOF appends every write and replays on restart — far less loss, larger files, needs periodic rewriting. Most production setups run both.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Cluster mode shards the key space into 16,384 hash slots spread across nodes. The constraint that shapes your data model is that a multi-key operation must have all its keys in the same slot — which you force with a {hashtag} in the key.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Structures, and the cluster constraint
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    STRUCTURE     USE
string        cache, counters (INCR is atomic)
hash          an object, field-addressable without fetching the whole thing
list          simple queue (LPUSH/BRPOP), capped log (LTRIM)
set           membership, unique visitors, tags
SORTED SET    leaderboards, rate limiters, delayed jobs, time-ordered feeds
stream        a real append-only log with consumer groups
HyperLogLog   approximate cardinality in 12 KB regardless of volume
bitmap        per-user daily flags at one bit each

CLUSTER: multi-key ops must be in ONE slot
  MGET user:1:name user:1:email        -> CROSSSLOT error, maybe
  MGET user:{1}:name user:{1}:email    -> same slot, works
  the {braces} are the part that is hashed

PERSISTENCE
  RDB   snapshot; lose everything since the last one
  AOF   appendfsync everysec is the usual compromise (lose <= 1s)
  both  RDB for fast restore, AOF for durability
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Is Redis single-threaded, and does that matter?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Command execution is single-threaded, which is why every command is effectively atomic and why you never need a lock for a single operation. It matters because one slow command (KEYS *, a large ZRANGE, a big Lua script) blocks everything. Use SCAN rather than KEYS, and keep scripts short.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When would you not use Redis?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When the data must not be lost — Redis persistence is good but it is a cache-shaped tool with an asynchronous durability story. And when the working set exceeds memory economics: at some point a disk-backed store with a good cache is cheaper than holding everything in RAM.
