                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S21
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A distributed lock coordinates exclusive access across processes. The naive Redis version is SET key value NX PX 30000 — set if absent, with an expiry — and the value must be a unique token so only the holder can release it, using a small Lua script to make check-and-delete atomic.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Redlock extends this across several independent Redis nodes, requiring a majority. Martin Kleppmann's critique is the important part to know: it relies on bounded clock drift and bounded pauses, and a process can be stopped by a GC pause for longer than the lock TTL — after which it believes it still holds a lock that has expired and been granted elsewhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The robust answer is a fencing token. The lock service issues an increasing number; the protected resource remembers the highest it has seen and rejects anything older. Then a paused holder waking up late is harmlessly rejected — which is a property of the resource, not of the lock.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Why fencing is the real answer
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      THE FAILURE WITHOUT FENCING
  t=0   client A acquires the lock, TTL 30s
  t=1   client A begins a long GC pause
  t=31  lock EXPIRES. Client B acquires it and writes.
  t=32  client A wakes, believes it holds the lock, and WRITES.
        -> two writers. The lock did not protect anything.

WITH FENCING
  A acquires -> token 33
  B acquires -> token 34
  storage remembers the highest token it has accepted
  A wakes and writes with token 33 -> REJECTED (33 < 34)

  The safety property lives in the RESOURCE, not the lock.

SAFE RELEASE (atomic check-and-delete)
  if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1]
    then return redis.call("del", KEYS[1]) else return 0 end

BETTER STILL: DO NOT NEED THE LOCK
  a conditional write / unique constraint / optimistic version check
  gives you the same guarantee with no lock at all
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      When do you actually need a distributed lock?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Less often than people reach for one. If the goal is correctness, prefer a conditional write, a unique constraint or an optimistic version check — those are enforced by the resource and cannot be defeated by a pause. A lock is reasonable for efficiency (avoid duplicate expensive work) where a rare double-execution is merely wasteful.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Is Redlock wrong, then?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      It is fine for efficiency and contested for correctness. The honest framing is: if a double-execution would corrupt data, you need fencing at the resource regardless of which lock you use — so the lock algorithm stops being the interesting question.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S22
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A queue distributes work: a message is consumed by one worker and then gone. A pub/sub topic fans out: every subscriber gets a copy, and if a subscriber is down it misses the message entirely. A distributed log retains an ordered sequence that many independent consumer groups read at their own pace, each tracking its own position.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The distinguishing question is: will anyone ever want to read this history again? Queues consume; logs retain. If a consumer with a bug needs to re-read last week after a fix, only a log gives you that without a bespoke backfill.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The second question is ordering. A queue gives you at best per-group ordering; a log gives strict ordering within a partition, which is what lets you rebuild per-key state deterministically.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Choosing between the three
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        QUEUE (SQS, RabbitMQ work queue)
  one logical consumer; per-message retry; DLQ; simple
  message is GONE once acknowledged
  -> task distribution, background jobs

PUB/SUB (SNS, Redis pub/sub)
  every subscriber gets a copy; NO retention
  a subscriber that is down MISSES the message
  -> notifications where loss is acceptable

DISTRIBUTED LOG (Kafka, Kinesis)
  retained, ordered per partition
  many INDEPENDENT consumer groups, each with its own offset
  replay from any offset
  -> event streaming, CDC, rebuilding projections

THE TELL
  "will anyone ever want to re-read this?"  -> log
  "is this a unit of work?"                 -> queue
  "is loss acceptable?"                     -> pub/sub

COMMON HYBRID
  a log (or an event bus) fanning out to ONE QUEUE PER CONSUMER
  -> the queue is the failure-isolation boundary: a slow consumer
     accumulates depth in its own queue and affects nobody else
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Can you get replay with a queue?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Not natively — a consumed message is gone. Workarounds are archiving every message to object storage as it is published, or using an event bus with an archive that supports replaying a time range. Both work and both are less convenient than an offset. If replay is a first-class requirement, use a log.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why put a queue in front of each consumer rather than delivering directly?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Isolation. A slow or broken consumer accumulates depth in its own queue and affects nobody — not the producer, not the other consumers. Each gets its own retry policy and dead-letter queue. Delivering straight to a function turns a downstream outage into retries, then loss, and a spike into a concurrency storm.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S23
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A Kafka topic is split into partitions, and a partition is the unit of ordering and parallelism. Messages with the same key always land in the same partition, which is what gives you per-key ordering — and choosing that key is the main design decision.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A consumer group divides partitions among its members, so parallelism within a group is capped by partition count: you cannot have more active consumers than partitions. Different groups read the same topic independently, each tracking its own offset.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Two operational realities dominate. rebalancing pauses consumption whenever membership changes — and a slow consumer can trigger a rebalance that slows everyone and triggers another. And consumer lag must be monitored and alerted, because a lagging consumer is invisible until the retention window expires and the data is genuinely gone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Partitions, keys and the metrics that matter
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          PARTITION = the unit of ORDERING and of PARALLELISM
  key -> hash -> partition          same key, same partition, ordered
  no key -> round robin             no ordering guarantee at all

CHOOSING THE KEY
  accountId    order per account, parallel across accounts   <- usually right
  a constant   TOTAL order, ONE consumer, no parallelism     <- almost never
  random       maximum parallelism, no ordering

PARTITION COUNT
  size from your PEAK consumer count, with headroom
  increasing later BREAKS key-to-partition mapping -> breaks ordering
  over-provisioning is cheap; under-provisioning is a migration

THE ALERT THAT MATTERS
  consumer lag measured in TIME, alerting well before the retention window
  -> past that point the data is GONE and scaling the consumer cannot recover it

OFFSET COMMITS
  commit AFTER processing -> at-least-once (redelivery on crash)
  commit BEFORE           -> at-most-once (loss on crash)
  there is no third option
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you reduce rebalancing pain?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Cooperative incremental rebalancing (the default in modern clients) reassigns only the moving partitions rather than stopping everything. Beyond that: tune max.poll.interval.ms above your worst-case processing time so a slow batch is not mistaken for a dead consumer, and keep processing per poll bounded.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Does Kafka guarantee exactly-once?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          It offers exactly-once semantics within Kafka — transactional writes across topics and offset commits atomically. It does not extend to your database or an external API, so a consumer writing elsewhere still needs idempotency. Presenting Kafka EOS as end-to-end exactly-once is a common overstatement.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S24
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            At-most-once means acknowledge before processing: no duplicates, and you lose messages on a crash. At-least-once means acknowledge after: no loss, and duplicates on a crash. Every practical system chooses at-least-once, because losing data is worse than doing work twice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Exactly-once delivery does not exist across a network — it is provably impossible in the general case, because the acknowledgement itself can be lost. What people mean when they say it is exactly-once effect: the message may arrive many times, and the outcome is as if it arrived once.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            That is achieved in the consumer, with idempotency: derive a deterministic key from the content, claim it with a conditional write, and skip if the claim fails. The queue never gives you this; your handler does.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The only design that works
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            AT-MOST-ONCE    ack, then process     -> loss on crash. Rarely acceptable.
AT-LEAST-ONCE   process, then ack     -> duplicates on crash. The default.
EXACTLY-ONCE    does not exist at the DELIVERY layer.

EXACTLY-ONCE EFFECT, in the consumer:
  String key = "SETTLE#" + msg.fileId() + "#" + msg.rowRange();
  //  ^ derived from CONTENT. Never from the broker's message id,
  //    which changes on redelivery.
  try {
      ddb.putItem(r -> r.item(Map.of("pk", s(key), "ttl", n(ttl30d())))
          .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"));   // ATOMIC claim
  } catch (ConditionalCheckFailedException dup) {
      ack(); return;                      // already done - safe no-op
  }
  process(msg);
  ack();

CLAIM BEFORE THE WORK, NOT AFTER
  claim after  -> a crash between work and claim does the work TWICE
  claim before -> a crash leaves work UNDONE, which a reconciliation job
                  can find. The safer failure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why can exactly-once delivery not exist?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Because the sender cannot distinguish the message was lost from the acknowledgement was lost. It must either resend (risking a duplicate) or not (risking loss). No protocol removes that choice — you can only make the duplicate harmless.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Where should the idempotency record live?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Ideally in the same store as the effect, so the claim and the work commit together. If they are in different systems you are back to a dual write, and you need the claim to be the durable one so a crash leaves work undone rather than duplicated. A TTL on the record keeps it from growing forever.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S25
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A poison message is one that always fails — malformed, or referring to something deleted. Without protection it is redelivered forever, consuming capacity, filling logs, and on an ordered queue blocking every message behind it in its group.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A dead-letter queue is the answer: after a configured number of receive attempts, the message is moved aside instead of retried. Alarm on any non-zero depth, because a message there is by definition something automation could not handle.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A retry topic is the tiered variant used with logs: failed messages go to a retry topic with a delay, then a longer one, then the DLQ. It keeps transient failures out of the DLQ while still bounding attempts, and it avoids blocking the main partition while a downstream recovers.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Configuration, and the redrive path
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SQS
  VisibilityTimeout: 180        > your p99 processing time (measure it)
  RedrivePolicy:
    maxReceiveCount: 4          4 tries, then park it for a human
    deadLetterTargetArn: ...
  ALARM on DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0

KAFKA (no built-in DLQ - you build the tiers)
  main topic -> fails -> retry-5s -> retry-1m -> retry-10m -> dlq
  each retry topic has its own consumer that waits then republishes
  -> transient failures never reach the DLQ
  -> and a slow downstream does not block the main partition

TWO KINDS OF DLQ ARRIVAL - distinguish them
  a BURST during an incident   the messages are fine, the world was broken
                               -> redrive them back when it recovers
  a steady TRICKLE             a real poison-message bug
                               -> fix the code, then redrive

THE REDRIVE PATH MUST BE ROUTINE
  rehearse it in staging, or it gets written during an incident
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What should the consumer do with a message it cannot parse?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Fail it immediately rather than retrying — a malformed message will never parse, so retries are pure waste. Distinguish terminal failures (send straight to the DLQ) from transient ones (retry with backoff). Conflating them means a bad payload burns four attempts and a downstream blip gets no second chance.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you stop the DLQ becoming a graveyard?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Give it an owner and an alarm, and treat non-zero depth as a ticket rather than a dashboard number. The healthy pattern is that DLQ arrivals are investigated within a day and redriven or explicitly discarded with a reason. A DLQ with ten thousand messages nobody has looked at is worse than no DLQ, because it hides the ones that matter.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S26
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Fixed window counts requests per clock interval. It is trivial and has a real flaw: a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, achieving double the rate across the boundary.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sliding log stores a timestamp per request and counts those inside the window — exact, and memory grows with traffic. Sliding counter approximates it by weighting the previous window, which is what most production limiters use: nearly exact, constant memory.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size while bounding the sustained rate, which is usually what you want for an API — a client should be able to send ten requests at once without being throttled. leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate instead, which suits protecting a fragile downstream.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sliding counter and token bucket in Redis
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                FIXED WINDOW - the boundary flaw
  limit 100/min: 100 requests at 11:59:59 + 100 at 12:00:00
  -> 200 requests in one second, within the rules

SLIDING COUNTER - what most systems use
  count = current_window_count
        + previous_window_count * (overlap_fraction)
  nearly exact, O(1) memory

-- TOKEN BUCKET, atomic in one Lua script
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call("hget", KEYS[1], "tokens") or ARGV[1])
local last   = tonumber(redis.call("hget", KEYS[1], "ts") or ARGV[4])
local delta  = math.max(0, ARGV[4] - last)
tokens = math.min(ARGV[1], tokens + delta * ARGV[2])   -- refill
if tokens < 1 then return 0 end                        -- reject
redis.call("hset", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens - 1, "ts", ARGV[4])
return 1

WHERE TO LIMIT - layer it, each catches something different
  edge/WAF        crude per-IP volumetric abuse, before it costs you
  gateway         per-client quotas - a contract concern
  application     per USER or TENANT - the only layer that can see
                  "this user is requesting other people's records"
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What do you return when rate limited?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                429 with a Retry-After header, and ideally X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset so a well-behaved client can pace itself rather than retrying blindly. Silently dropping or returning 500 makes clients retry harder, which is the opposite of what you want.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why is IP-based limiting insufficient?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A distributed attacker defeats it trivially, and it unfairly penalises shared corporate NAT where hundreds of legitimate users share one address. IP limits are a blunt edge control; the meaningful limit is per authenticated user or tenant, which requires knowing who they are — so it belongs in the application.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S27
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Plain hash(key) % N works until N changes — and then almost every key maps somewhere new. For a cache that means a total miss storm; for a data store it means moving nearly all your data. consistent hashing solves this by mapping keys and nodes onto a ring and assigning each key to the next node clockwise.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Adding a node then only steals keys from its immediate successor, so roughly 1/N of keys move rather than all of them. That is the whole idea, and it is what makes elastic scaling of a cache or a partitioned store practical.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  virtual nodes fix the two remaining problems: with few nodes the ring is uneven, and removing a node dumps all its keys onto a single neighbour. Giving each physical node a few hundred ring positions makes distribution even and spreads a departure across many nodes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Why modulo fails, and what replaces it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  hash(key) % 4  ->  hash(key) % 5
  key "user:1234"  was node 2, now node 4
  ~80% of keys move. For a cache: total miss storm. For storage: a migration.

CONSISTENT HASHING
  place nodes on a ring at hash(nodeId)
  key belongs to the FIRST node clockwise from hash(key)
  add a node -> only keys between it and its predecessor move  (~1/N)

VIRTUAL NODES
  each physical node placed at ~150-300 ring positions
  -> even distribution with few nodes
  -> removing a node spreads its keys across MANY successors, not one

BOUNDED LOAD variant
  cap any node at (1 + eps) x average; overflow spills to the next node
  -> prevents one hot range from overwhelming a single node

WHO USES IT
  Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak (partitioning)
  memcached clients, Envoy ring-hash (routing)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Does consistent hashing solve hot keys?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  No — it solves hot ranges and rebalancing. A single key that is disproportionately popular still lands on one node however you hash it. That needs a different fix: replicate the key across several nodes with a suffix, or cache it locally in front of the shared tier.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What is rendezvous hashing and why mention it?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  An alternative that computes hash(key, node) for every node and picks the highest — same minimal-movement property, no ring or virtual nodes to manage, and naturally even. It is O(N) per lookup, which is fine for tens of nodes. Worth knowing as the simpler option when N is small.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S28
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Object storage is the right home for anything large and immutable — uploads, media, backups, exports. It is cheap, effectively unbounded, durable across zones, and it is not a filesystem: no rename, no partial update, no directory semantics. You overwrite whole objects.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The architectural move is presigned URL: your service authorises and signs, and the client transfers directly to storage. Bandwidth and memory never touch your instances, which is what makes a 200MB upload a non-event rather than a capacity problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Constrain the signature narrowly, because a presigned URL is a bearer token: short expiry, an exact key chosen server-side, a content-length range, a pinned content type. And for large files use multipart upload so a network blip costs one part rather than the whole transfer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Direct upload, and the cost trap
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    var key = "uploads/%s/%s".formatted(tenantId, UUID.randomUUID());  // SERVER chooses

s3Presigner.presignPutObject(b -> b
    .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(10))     // short
    .putObjectRequest(r -> r
        .bucket("uploads-prod")
        .key(key)                                  // exact object
        .contentType("application/pdf")            // pinned
        .contentLength(declaredSize)));            // client cannot exceed

// then: S3 event -> QUEUE -> workers   (never straight to a function:
//       the queue gives you buffering, retry, a DLQ and bounded concurrency)

MULTIPART
  parts uploaded in PARALLEL, each retried independently
  a blip costs one 8MB part, not a 200MB transfer
  COST TRAP: incomplete uploads are billed INDEFINITELY and do not appear
             in a normal listing
  -> a lifecycle rule aborting them after 7 days is MANDATORY

NEVER TRUST THE CLIENT'S KEY
  the key is chosen server-side and recorded in your database.
  The client is told where to put bytes; it does not decide.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How does the client know when processing finished?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Do not hold the HTTP connection. Record the upload as PENDING at signing time, have the worker update it, and let the client poll a status endpoint or receive a push over WebSocket or SSE. That is the standard async shape — accept, return 202, report completion separately.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What stops someone reusing the presigned URL?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Only time and scope — it is a bearer credential with no notion of who uses it. Hence the short expiry and the exact key: a replay overwrites the same object, which your version check and processing state make detectable. If replay must be impossible, enable versioning and reject writes to a key already marked complete.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S29
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      normalization means each fact lives in exactly one place, which makes writes cheap and correct — you update one row and every reader sees it. Third normal form is the practical target; the higher forms are academic for most systems.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      denormalization is the deliberate reverse: duplicate data so a read needs no join. It is a read optimisation paid for with write complexity, because now every copy must be updated together, and any bug leaves them disagreeing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Normalise first and denormalise with evidence. The right trigger is a measured query that cannot be fixed with an index — not a hunch that joins are slow. And when you do it, be explicit about how the copies stay in sync: in the same transaction, by a trigger, or asynchronously with an accepted staleness window.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      When denormalising is right
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      NORMALISED                          DENORMALISED
one fact, one place                 duplicated for read shape
writes are cheap and correct        writes must update every copy
reads may need joins                reads are a single lookup
schema changes are local            schema changes touch every copy

DENORMALISE WHEN
  a measured query is slow AND an index cannot fix it
  the read:write ratio is extreme (100:1+)
  the duplicated field rarely changes (a display name, not a balance)
  you can state HOW copies stay in sync

DO NOT DENORMALISE
  because "joins are slow" - a join on an indexed key is fast
  before measuring
  a field that changes often - you have created a consistency problem

THE MIDDLE GROUND, usually better
  a materialised view or a read model updated asynchronously
  -> the write path stays normalised and correct
  -> the read path is a projection you can rebuild
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What is the safest way to denormalise?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Keep the normalised tables as the source of truth and build a separate read model, updated from a change stream or in the same transaction via an outbox. Then a bug means a stale projection you can rebuild, rather than corrupted source data you cannot recover.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Is a JSON column denormalisation?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      It is a related trade. A JSON column avoids a join and a schema migration, at the cost of weaker validation, harder indexing and queries the optimiser understands less well. It is reasonable for genuinely schemaless attributes and a poor substitute for modelling something you query on.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S30
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A B-tree index keeps keys sorted with every leaf at the same depth, so a lookup costs a handful of page reads whether the table has a thousand rows or a billion. That logarithmic behaviour is the entire reason indexes work.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        For a composite index, column order is the design decision, because of the leftmost-prefix rule. An index on (merchant_id, created_at) serves queries filtering on merchant alone, or merchant plus a date range — but nothing filtering only on date.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The ordering heuristic: equality columns first, then the range column, then columns you only need for sorting or covering. Getting it backwards produces an index the optimiser ignores, which looks like the index did not help rather than the index is in the wrong order.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Column order, worked
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        QUERY
  WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?
  ORDER BY created_at DESC

INDEX (merchant_id, created_at)          <- CORRECT
  equality first, then the range
  -> seeks straight to the merchant, then scans a contiguous date range
  -> and the range is already in order, so no sort is needed

INDEX (created_at, merchant_id)          <- WRONG
  -> scans every merchant within the date range, filtering as it goes

LEFTMOST PREFIX - index on (a, b, c) serves:
  WHERE a = ?                      YES
  WHERE a = ? AND b = ?            YES
  WHERE a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ?  YES
  WHERE b = ?                      NO   <- needs its own index
  WHERE a = ? AND c = ?            partially - a only, then filter

RULE
  equality columns, then ONE range column, then covering columns.
  A second range column after the first gains you nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why does only one range column benefit?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Because once you scan a range on column b, the values of c within that range are not globally sorted — they are only sorted within each b. So the index can seek to the start of the b range but must filter on c row by row. That is why (a, b_range, c_range) is effectively (a, b_range).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How many indexes is too many?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Every index is maintained on every write, so they trade write throughput and storage for read speed. A table with fifteen indexes has slow writes and probably several unused ones. Check usage statistics — most databases track index scans — and drop the ones nobody uses. Unused indexes are pure cost.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S31
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A covering index contains every column the query touches, so the database never reads the table itself. That turns two lookups into one and can be an order of magnitude faster on a wide table, because the index is far smaller and better cached.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          In PostgreSQL that is an index-only scan, and it has a caveat worth knowing: it still needs the visibility map to confirm rows are visible, so a table that has not been vacuumed recently will fall back to heap reads and the benefit disappears.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          selectivity decides whether an index is used at all. An index on a boolean column matching half the table is worse than a sequential scan — random reads for half the rows cost more than reading everything in order. This is why the optimiser sometimes ignores an index you were sure it would use, and it is usually right.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Covering, and when an index is useless
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          COVERING
  SELECT merchant_id, created_at, amount
  FROM settlement WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at > ?

  INDEX (merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount)
  -> everything the query needs is IN the index
  -> no table reads at all

SELECTIVITY - the optimiser's actual decision
  matches 0.1% of rows   -> index, definitely
  matches 5%             -> index, probably
  matches 20%            -> borderline
  matches 50%            -> SEQUENTIAL SCAN IS FASTER
     because random reads for half the rows cost more than reading
     everything in order

CARDINALITY
  high (user_id, email)     -> a great index
  low (status, is_active)   -> a poor index ALONE
                            -> useful as the SECOND column of a composite,
                               or as a PARTIAL index:
     CREATE INDEX ON settlement (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';
     -> tiny index, only the rows you actually query
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why would the optimiser ignore my index?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Usually selectivity — it estimates the condition matches too many rows. Sometimes stale statistics make that estimate wrong, which ANALYZE fixes. Sometimes a type mismatch or a function on the column makes the index unusable: WHERE lower(email) = ? cannot use an index on email, but can use one on lower(email).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What is a partial index good for?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Indexing only the rows you query. A work queue where you always filter status = 'PENDING' and pending rows are 0.1% of the table gets an index a thousand times smaller, which stays cached and is far cheaper to maintain. It is one of the highest-value and least-used index features.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S32
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the single most useful debugging tool for a slow query, and the skill is not reading every node — it is finding where estimated rows diverge from actual rows. That divergence is almost always the root cause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            When the estimate is wrong, the optimiser picks the wrong strategy: a nested loop that would be fine for 10 rows becomes catastrophic for 100,000. So the fix is often not rewriting the query but fixing the statistics that produced the bad estimate.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Read it inside-out: the deepest node runs first. Look for a sequential scan on a large table, a nested loop with a large outer row count, a sort spilling to disk, and any node where actual rows exceed the estimate by an order of magnitude.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What to look for
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...

Nested Loop  (cost=0.43..8.47 rows=1 width=64)
             (actual time=0.02..2841.19 rows=124,503 loops=1)
                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  ESTIMATED 1 row, GOT 124,503.
  The optimiser chose a nested loop because it expected one row.
  That is the bug - not the join itself.

CHECKLIST
  estimated vs actual rows      an order of magnitude out -> statistics
  Seq Scan on a large table     missing index, or low selectivity
  Nested Loop with a big outer  should probably be a hash join
  Sort ... Disk: 48000kB        work_mem too small; it spilled
  Rows Removed by Filter        the index found rows the WHERE discarded
                                -> the index is missing a column
  BUFFERS: shared read=...      actual I/O, not cache hits

FIXES, IN ORDER
  1. ANALYZE the table          stale statistics are the commonest cause
  2. add or reorder an index
  3. increase the statistics target on a skewed column
  4. rewrite the query          LAST, not first
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What causes bad row estimates?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Stale statistics after a bulk load, correlated columns the planner assumes are independent (city and postcode), a skewed distribution where the average is meaningless, and expressions the planner cannot reason about. PostgreSQL's extended statistics can capture column correlation explicitly, which fixes a whole class of these.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than EXPLAIN?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Because EXPLAIN shows only what the planner expects. The divergence between expected and actual is the diagnosis, and you cannot see it without running the query. Just be careful: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement, so wrap a write in a transaction you roll back.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S33
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 makes the database produce 100,020 rows and discard 100,000 of them. The cost grows linearly with the page number, so page one is instant and page five thousand times out — and no index fixes it, because the work is inherent to counting past rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              keyset pagination instead remembers the last row and asks for rows after it. That is an index seek to a position and then a scan of twenty rows, so every page costs the same regardless of depth.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              It also fixes a correctness problem people miss: with offset, a row inserted or deleted while the user pages shifts everything, so they see a duplicate or skip an item. Keyset pagination is stable under concurrent writes because the cursor is anchored to data, not to a position.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Offset versus keyset
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              OFFSET - cost grows with depth, and it is UNSTABLE
  SELECT * FROM settlement ORDER BY created_at DESC
  OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20;
  -> produces 100,020 rows, throws away 100,000
  -> and a new row inserted between requests shifts every subsequent page

KEYSET / CURSOR - constant cost, stable
  SELECT * FROM settlement
  WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)   -- row comparison
  ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 20;
  -> index seek + 20 rows. Page 5,000 costs the same as page 1.

WHY THE COMPOSITE (created_at, id)
  created_at alone is not unique - ties would skip or repeat rows.
  Adding a unique tiebreaker makes the cursor total.
  INDEX (created_at DESC, id DESC) to match.

WHAT YOU GIVE UP
  no "jump to page 500" - only next and previous
  no total count without a separate (expensive) query
  -> usually acceptable: infinite scroll and "load more" need neither
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What if the UI genuinely needs page numbers?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Then bound it — offer keyset paging for deep navigation and a total count only for small result sets, or cap the offset at a few thousand and require filtering beyond that. An approximate count from table statistics is often enough for about 12,000 results, and it costs nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you encode the cursor?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Base64 the sort key values and any filter state, so the client treats it as opaque and you can change the encoding later. Include the sort direction and filters so a cursor cannot be reused against a different query. Signing it prevents clients from crafting cursors that scan arbitrary ranges.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S34
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The N+1 problem is one query for a list, then one per item — 101 queries for a page of 100. Each is fast, so nothing looks wrong in a slow-query log; the damage is 101 round trips, and it is the most common performance bug in application code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                In an ORM it comes from lazy loading a relation inside a loop. The fixes are a join fetch, an IN query batching the ids, or an explicit batch size — and the durable fix is a test that counts queries and fails when the count scales with the result size.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The same shape appears across service boundaries and in GraphQL, where it is worse: a nested query can fan out into thousands of downstream calls, and the client controls the shape. That is what DataLoader-style batching exists for — collect the ids requested within one tick and issue a single batched call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The same bug in three places
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                ORM
  for (var order : orderRepo.findAll())     // 1 query
      total += order.getCustomer().name();  // N queries (lazy load)
  FIX  join fetch / entity graph / @BatchSize
       and a TEST that counts queries

SERVICE BOUNDARY
  var orders = orderService.list();                    // 1 call
  for (var o : orders) custService.get(o.customerId()); // N calls
  FIX  a batch endpoint: custService.getMany(ids)
       -> and design APIs to accept collections from the start

GRAPHQL - worst case, because the CLIENT controls the shape
  query { orders(first:100) { customer { organisation { name } } } }
  -> 1 + 100 + 100 = 201 resolver calls, and nesting multiplies it
  FIX  DataLoader: collect ids requested in one tick, issue ONE batched
       call, distribute results
       AND a query depth/complexity limit, or a client can craft a query
       that takes your service down

THE DURABLE FIX
  assert query count in tests:
    assertThat(queryCounter.count()).isEqualTo(2);
  -> the bug cannot come back silently
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Is eager loading the answer?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Not globally. Eager-loading everything means every query drags relations nobody asked for, which is a different performance problem. The right default is lazy with explicit fetch plans per use case — the query decides what it needs, rather than the mapping deciding for every query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How do you find N+1 in production?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Distributed tracing shows it immediately as a wide fan of identical spans under one parent — visually obvious in a trace waterfall in a way it never is in a log. Failing that, group your slow-query log by normalised statement and look for one executed thousands of times per minute with a tiny individual duration.
