                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S35
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  ACID: Atomicity — all or nothing. Consistency — constraints hold before and after. Isolation — concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other. Durability — a committed write survives a crash.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Isolation is the one with dials. Each isolation level permits a specific set of anomalies, and the useful way to remember them is by which anomaly each level prevents rather than by name.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The practical point: most databases do not default to serializable, and most developers do not know what their default is. PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed; MySQL InnoDB to Repeatable Read. Knowing your default, and which anomaly it still permits, is what separates a real answer from a recited list.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Levels by the anomaly they prevent
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  LEVEL              PREVENTS                       STILL ALLOWS
Read Uncommitted   nothing                        dirty reads
Read Committed     dirty read                     non-repeatable read, phantom
  <- PostgreSQL default                             lost update, write skew
Repeatable Read    + non-repeatable read          phantom (in the standard)
  <- MySQL InnoDB default                           write skew
                   InnoDB also prevents phantoms via next-key locking
                   PostgreSQL "Repeatable Read" is actually snapshot
                   isolation and prevents phantoms too
Serializable       everything                     nothing - but retries and
                                                  contention

THE PRACTICAL DEFAULT
  Read Committed for most work
  Serializable (or explicit locking) for the few operations where a
  concurrency anomaly is a correctness bug - money movement, inventory,
  anything with a check-then-act shape

AND: Serializable means TRANSACTIONS CAN FAIL AND MUST BE RETRIED.
  If your code does not retry serialisation failures, you have not
  actually enabled it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Does ACID guarantee correctness?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  No — it guarantees the database will not corrupt itself. Application-level correctness still requires you to choose the right isolation level and to express your invariants as constraints. A transaction that reads a balance, decides, and writes at Read Committed is atomic and still wrong under concurrency.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What does the C in ACID actually mean?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Less than people assume. It means declared constraints (foreign keys, uniqueness, checks) hold at commit — it is the database enforcing what you declared, not a guarantee about your business logic. Several database researchers argue it does not belong in the acronym at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Dirty read: you read a value another transaction wrote but has not committed, and it then rolls back — you acted on data that never existed. Prevented at Read Committed and above.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Non-repeatable read: you read a row twice in one transaction and get different values, because another transaction committed in between. Phantom: you run the same range query twice and the second returns new rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The two that matter most in practice are the ones weak isolation still allows. Lost update: two transactions read a value, both compute a new one, and the second overwrites the first — the classic balance = balance - 100 bug. Write skew: two transactions each check a condition that holds, each write different rows, and jointly break the rule neither broke alone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The two that bite in production
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    LOST UPDATE
  T1: SELECT balance -> 100
  T2: SELECT balance -> 100
  T1: UPDATE balance = 100 - 30  -> 70
  T2: UPDATE balance = 100 - 50  -> 50      T1's deduction is GONE

  FIXES
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30   -- atomic, no read first
    SELECT ... FOR UPDATE                        -- pessimistic lock
    WHERE version = :v  (optimistic, retry on 0 rows)

WRITE SKEW - the one Repeatable Read does NOT prevent
  RULE: at least one doctor must be on call.
  T1: count on-call = 2, so Alice may go off call  -> UPDATE alice
  T2: count on-call = 2, so Bob may go off call    -> UPDATE bob
  both commit. ZERO doctors on call.
  Neither transaction wrote a row the other read, so snapshot isolation
  sees no conflict.

  FIXES
    SERIALIZABLE (PostgreSQL SSI detects and aborts one)
    materialise the conflict: lock a row representing the invariant
    SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the rows you counted
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Why is write skew the interesting one?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Because snapshot isolation — which most people believe is basically serializable — does not prevent it, and the failure is silent. It appears wherever there is a check-then-act on an aggregate: seat booking, inventory, on-call rotas, spending limits. Naming it and giving that example is a strong signal.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What is the cheapest fix for lost update?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Do the arithmetic in the database: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 rather than reading, computing and writing. It is atomic under any isolation level and needs no lock or retry. Most lost updates exist because someone read the value into application code first.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S37
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      MVCC is why readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers in PostgreSQL, Oracle and InnoDB. Each update writes a new row version; each transaction sees the versions that were committed when it started.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      That gives you snapshot isolation almost for free, and it moves the cost somewhere else: old versions accumulate and must be cleaned up. In PostgreSQL that is VACUUM; in InnoDB it is the purge thread and the undo log.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The operational failure is a long-running transaction. vacuum cannot remove any version still visible to any open transaction — so one forgotten session with an open transaction, or an idle-in-transaction connection, prevents cleanup across the whole database. Tables bloat, indexes bloat, and performance degrades in a way that looks unrelated to the culprit.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Why one open transaction hurts everything
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      MVCC
  UPDATE does not overwrite - it writes a NEW VERSION and marks the old
  one dead. Readers see the version valid at their snapshot.
  -> no read locks, no blocking

THE COST: dead versions must be reclaimed
  VACUUM can only remove a version invisible to EVERY open transaction.
  One transaction open for hours pins the horizon for the WHOLE database.

  SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS age, query
  FROM pg_stat_activity
  WHERE state IN ('idle in transaction','active')
    AND now() - xact_start > interval '5 minutes'
  ORDER BY age DESC;

SYMPTOMS OF BLOAT
  table size grows while row count does not
  sequential scans get slower over time
  autovacuum runs constantly and never catches up
  n_dead_tup climbing in pg_stat_user_tables

PREVENT
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout   (kill forgotten transactions)
  statement_timeout
  keep transactions SHORT - never hold one open across a network call
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Why does an idle-in-transaction connection matter so much?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Because the transaction is open even though nothing is running, so it still pins the vacuum horizon. It is usually an application bug — a transaction opened before an HTTP call, or a connection returned to the pool without commit or rollback. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and the database kills them for you.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Does MVCC mean no locks at all?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      No — writes still take row locks, so two transactions updating the same row serialise. What MVCC removes is read locking. It also means a long read never blocks writes, which is why an analytical query against a transactional database is safe from a locking perspective, even if it is a bad idea for other reasons.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S38
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pessimistic locking assumes conflict and takes a lock up front — SELECT FOR UPDATE. It is correct and simple, and it serialises access, so it costs throughput and can deadlock. Use it where conflict is likely and correctness is non-negotiable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Optimistic locking assumes conflict is rare: read a version number, and include it in the update's WHERE. If zero rows change, someone else won and you retry. No locks are held, so throughput is high — and under real contention you burn CPU on retries.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Deadlocks come from inconsistent lock ordering: two transactions taking the same locks in different orders. The fix is a convention — always lock in a deterministic order, such as ascending primary key — and it prevents an entire class of production incident.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Choosing, and avoiding deadlock
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        PESSIMISTIC
  BEGIN;
  SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE;   -- blocks others
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 42;
  COMMIT;
  + always correct     - serialises, can deadlock, holds locks across
                         whatever you do in between (NEVER a network call)

  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED   -- the work-queue pattern
    grab the next unlocked row instead of waiting - perfect for pulling
    jobs from a table with several workers

OPTIMISTIC
  UPDATE settlement SET status='PAID', version=version+1
  WHERE id=? AND version=?;
  if (rowsAffected == 0) retry;
  + no locks held      - wasted work under high contention

DEADLOCK
  T1: lock A then B        T2: lock B then A     -> deadlock
  FIX: always lock in a deterministic order (ascending id)
  Databases detect and kill one victim - so your code MUST retry
  deadlock errors, not just log them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Which should you default to?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Optimistic for typical CRUD, where two users rarely edit the same row — it is cheaper and has no deadlock risk. Pessimistic where contention is genuinely high or the operation is expensive to redo, such as decrementing shared inventory. The tell is the retry rate: if optimistic retries are frequent, you have chosen wrong.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Pulling work from a queue table. Each worker takes the next row nobody has locked instead of blocking behind another worker, so N workers process N distinct rows with no coordination. It is how you build a reliable job queue on a relational database without a message broker.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S39
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A connection pool exists because connections are expensive to create and databases cap how many they will accept. The pool is almost always much smaller than your thread count, which means threads wait for a connection — and that waiting is invisible in database metrics.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          That is why pool exhaustion presents as a latency problem with a perfectly healthy-looking database. Queries are fast, the database is bored, and requests take seconds — because they spent that time waiting to borrow a connection.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Sizing is counter-intuitive: smaller is usually faster. A pool larger than the database can service concurrently just moves the queue from your application into the database, where it competes for CPU and locks. A common formula is roughly cores × 2 + effective spindles, and for most services a pool of 10–20 outperforms 100.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Diagnosing exhaustion
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          THE SYMPTOM
  p99 latency 4s | database CPU 20% | slow query log EMPTY
  -> the time is spent WAITING FOR A CONNECTION

THE METRIC THAT SHOWS IT
  hikaricp_connections_pending > 0      <- requests queued for a connection
  hikaricp_connections_active == max    <- pool saturated

CONFIGURATION THAT MATTERS
  maximum-pool-size: 15          smaller than you think
  connection-timeout: 3000       FAIL FAST - do not block a request thread
                                 for 30 seconds waiting for a connection
  max-lifetime: 600000           recycle below any infra idle timeout
  leak-detection-threshold: 20000  logs a stack trace for a connection
                                   held too long - finds the actual bug

THE ARITHMETIC THAT BITES
  20 instances x 15 connections = 300
  database max_connections = 200
  -> connection refused, for EVERY service on that database, not just yours

  And with Lambda: concurrency x pool size, unbounded -> use RDS Proxy
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why is a bigger pool usually slower?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Because the database can only do so much concurrent work. Beyond that point, extra connections queue inside the database competing for CPU, locks and memory, and context switching increases. Moving the queue from your pool into the database makes it worse, not better — and it removes your ability to shed load early.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What is the most common cause of a leak?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A connection borrowed outside a try-with-resources, or a transaction opened before a long network call and left open. Leak detection with a threshold prints the stack trace of whoever holds it, which turns a mysterious exhaustion into a one-line fix. Enable it in non-production permanently.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S40
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Leader-follower replication has one node accepting writes and streaming them to followers that serve reads. Synchronous means the leader waits for a follower to acknowledge before committing — no data loss on failover, higher write latency, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Asynchronous means the leader commits immediately and streams afterwards — fast writes, and on an unplanned failover you lose whatever had not replicated. Semi-synchronous waits for one follower out of several, which is the usual compromise: bounded loss without depending on any specific replica.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            replication lag is the thing to monitor and to design around. It is normally milliseconds, and it grows under write bursts, long-running queries on the replica, and single-threaded replay. Any read path that must see a just-written value has to account for it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The three modes, and their real cost
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SYNCHRONOUS       leader waits for follower ack before commit
  RPO = 0
  write latency includes a network round trip
  a SLOW FOLLOWER STALLS THE LEADER  <- the failure people forget

ASYNCHRONOUS      leader commits, streams after
  fast writes
  UNPLANNED FAILOVER LOSES unreplicated writes (RPO = lag)

SEMI-SYNCHRONOUS  wait for ANY ONE of N followers
  bounded loss, no dependence on a specific replica
  -> the usual production compromise

MONITOR
  pg_stat_replication: sent_lsn - replay_lsn      (bytes behind)
  now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()         (time behind)
  ALARM on the TIME measure - bytes mean nothing to an on-call engineer

CAUSES OF SUDDEN LAG
  a bulk write or backfill        <- throttle it, check lag between batches
  a long query on the replica blocking replay
  single-threaded replay hitting its ceiling
  a schema change rewriting a large table
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Should you read from replicas by default?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Only for reads that tolerate staleness — reporting, dashboards, exports, search. Route anything in a read-your-own-writes path to the primary. Making replica reads the default and adding exceptions is the wrong way round; the exceptions are silent bugs that appear as I saved it and it did not save.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What happens on failover with async replication?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Whatever had not replicated is lost, and if the old leader comes back it may hold writes the new leader never saw — which is why it must be fenced and rebuilt rather than rejoined. Design so replay is safe: idempotency keys on every write, and reconciliation against an external record where one exists.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            My notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S41
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              read-your-writes is the one users notice immediately: you save your profile, the page reloads from a lagging replica, and your change appears to have vanished. Preserve it by routing reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or by pinning that user to the primary for the session.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              monotonic reads means you never see time run backwards. It breaks when consecutive requests hit different replicas with different lag — refresh twice and an item appears, disappears, reappears. Fix by pinning a user to one replica, usually by hashing the user id.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Consistent prefix means you see writes in the order they happened, never a reply before the message it answers. It breaks with partitioned or multi-leader systems where related writes take different paths, and the fix is to keep causally related data in the same partition.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three guarantees, three mechanisms
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              READ-YOUR-WRITES
  symptom  "I saved it and it did not save"
  fix      after a write, read from the PRIMARY for N seconds
           (store lastWriteAt in the session, compare against replica lag)
           or: track the write's LSN and require a replica at or past it

MONOTONIC READS
  symptom  refresh twice, the item appears then disappears
  cause    two requests, two replicas, different lag
  fix      pin a user to ONE replica: hash(userId) % replicas

CONSISTENT PREFIX
  symptom  a reply is visible before the message it answers
  cause    related writes travelled through different partitions
  fix      keep causally related data in the SAME partition
           (partition a conversation by conversationId, not by messageId)

THE HONEST FRAMING
  these are not exotic distributed-systems concerns - they are the
  three ways "eventually consistent" becomes a visible bug, and each
  has a cheap, well-known fix.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How long should the read-from-primary window be?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Long enough to exceed typical replication lag with margin — often a few seconds — and it should be derived from measured lag rather than guessed. The more precise version tracks the log position of the write and only uses a replica that has replayed past it, which gives correctness without a fixed timer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Does session stickiness solve all three?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              It solves monotonic reads and, if pinned to the primary, read-your-writes. It does not solve consistent prefix, which is about partitioning rather than routing. And stickiness has its own costs — uneven load, and a replica failure disrupting the users pinned to it.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S42
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Failover promotes a replica when the leader is unreachable, and the hard part is that unreachable and dead are indistinguishable from the outside. Promote too eagerly and you get split-brain; promote too slowly and you extend the outage.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                quorum is the standard defence: require a majority to agree on promotion. Two disjoint partitions cannot both hold a majority, so only one side can act. This is why cluster sizes are odd — three tolerates one failure, five tolerates two.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Fencing closes the remaining gap. A partitioned old leader may still be running and accepting writes. So you fence it: revoke its access, kill the instance, or use a fencing token that the storage layer checks — the shared resource rejects anything from an epoch older than the current one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why quorum plus fencing
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                THE PROBLEM
  the leader is unreachable. Is it DEAD, or is the NETWORK broken?
  You cannot tell. If you promote and it was alive -> two leaders.

QUORUM
  3 nodes, majority = 2      tolerates 1 failure
  5 nodes, majority = 3      tolerates 2 failures
  a 2-node cluster has NO useful majority - which is why witnesses exist

  a partition of 3 into {2} and {1}: only the side of 2 can act.

FENCING - because the old leader may still be RUNNING
  1  STONITH        kill the old node outright
  2  revoke access  remove its credentials / detach its storage
  3  FENCING TOKEN  each leadership term gets an increasing number;
                    storage rejects writes from an older epoch
                    -> the safety property lives in the RESOURCE

WITHOUT FENCING
  old leader in a GC pause wakes up after promotion and writes.
  Two writers. Quorum did not prevent it - quorum decided WHO SHOULD
  lead, not who can WRITE.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why do managed databases still take 60–120 seconds to fail over?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Because most of it is detection, not promotion. You must wait long enough to be confident the leader is genuinely gone rather than briefly slow — too aggressive and a GC pause triggers a needless failover. Then promotion, DNS or endpoint update, and client reconnection. The promotion itself is often the fastest part.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What is a witness or arbiter node?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A node that participates in voting but holds no data, used to make an even-sized cluster odd. Two data centres with two nodes each cannot form a majority when the link between them fails; adding a witness in a third location breaks the tie. It is cheap and it is the standard answer to two-site deployments.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S43
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  sharding splits one dataset across independent databases. Range partitioning keeps keys ordered, so range scans are cheap and sequential keys create a hotspot — every new write lands on the last shard.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Hash partitioning spreads evenly by hashing the key, which kills hotspots and also kills range queries — adjacent keys land on different shards, so all orders in March becomes a scatter-gather across every shard.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Directory-based keeps an explicit lookup table from key to shard. Maximum flexibility — you can move individual tenants — at the cost of a lookup on every request and a directory that is itself a single point of failure and a bottleneck.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Three strategies and their failure mode
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  RANGE          shard by key ranges: A-F, G-M, N-Z
  + range scans are cheap; ordered iteration works
  - SEQUENTIAL KEYS = HOTSPOT. Timestamps or auto-increment ids mean
    every write goes to the last shard while the rest idle.

HASH           shard = hash(key) % N  (or consistent hashing)
  + even distribution, no hotspot from key ordering
  - NO RANGE QUERIES. "all orders in March" hits every shard.
  - resizing with plain modulo moves nearly everything

DIRECTORY      an explicit key -> shard lookup table
  + move individual tenants; uneven shard sizes are fine
  - a lookup on every request; the directory is a SPOF and a bottleneck
  -> good for multi-tenant where tenants differ enormously in size

HOTSPOTS PERSIST EVEN WITH HASHING
  one key that is 40% of traffic lands on ONE shard however you hash.
  fixes: a shard suffix (key#0..key#9, read fanned out), a time bucket,
         or caching that key locally in front of the shard
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  When should you shard at all?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Later than people think. A single modern instance handles a great deal, and sharding costs you cross-shard joins, distributed transactions, and a key you cannot easily change. Exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, archiving cold data and partitioning within one instance first — those buy years and none of them are irreversible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What is the difference between partitioning and sharding?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Partitioning usually means splitting a table within one database — the engine handles routing and you keep transactions and joins. Sharding means splitting across independent databases, so the application routes and cross-shard operations become your problem. Native partitioning gives much of the benefit with none of the distributed cost.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  My notes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Saved links
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    1↗
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    2↗

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S44
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The shard key is the most consequential and least reversible decision in a sharded system. Choose it so that the overwhelming majority of queries can be answered from one shard — because anything else becomes a scatter-gather.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Three properties to check: it must be high cardinality (many distinct values), evenly distributed (no tenant is 40% of traffic), and present in your dominant queries (or you cannot route without a lookup).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Then state the hidden costs out loud, because they are what the interviewer is testing. Cross-shard joins do not exist — you fetch from each shard and join in the application. Cross-shard transactions do not exist either, so multi-shard writes become a saga with compensation. Both are why the key should keep related data together.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Choosing, and what it costs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    CHECK THREE PROPERTIES
  high cardinality      millions of values, not five
  even distribution     no single value is a large share of traffic
  in your queries       present in the WHERE of your dominant reads

WORKED: a payments system
  shard by merchant_id
    + a merchant's settlements, disputes and reports are CO-LOCATED
    + almost every query filters by merchant
    - one enormous merchant is a hotspot -> sub-shard them by a suffix
  shard by transaction_id (hash)
    + perfectly even
    - "all transactions for merchant X" hits EVERY shard. Unusable.
  shard by created_at (range)
    - all writes on the newest shard. The worst option.

THE HIDDEN COSTS
  CROSS-SHARD JOIN         does not exist. Fetch from each shard, join
                           in the application, paginate in memory.
  CROSS-SHARD TRANSACTION  does not exist. Becomes a saga with
                           compensating actions.
  GLOBAL UNIQUENESS        an auto-increment id is not unique across
                           shards -> UUID, Snowflake, or a central allocator
  GLOBAL SECONDARY QUERY   "find by email" when sharded by merchant needs
                           a separate lookup table or a search index
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What if a query genuinely needs data from every shard?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Accept a scatter-gather for the rare case, and bound it: fan out in parallel, cap the per-shard result size, and set a strict timeout so one slow shard does not hold the request. If it becomes common, build a separate read model — a search index or a denormalised aggregate — rather than making every query pay for it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Can you change the shard key later?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Effectively it is a full data migration: dual-write to a new cluster keyed differently, backfill, verify, cut over. That is weeks of work with real risk, which is why the choice deserves real time up front. Prefer a key tied to a stable business entity over one tied to a current access pattern.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S45
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Resharding without downtime is the same expand-contract shape as a schema migration, and the same discipline makes it safe: every step must be individually reversible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Dual-write first — the application writes to both old and new topology while reading only from the old. Then backfill historical data in bounded batches, watching replication lag. Then verify by comparing counts and checksums, ideally on a sample of live reads.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Only then shift reads, gradually and by percentage, keeping the old topology intact until you are confident. Cut writes over last, and keep the ability to roll back until the old data is genuinely stale.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The sequence, and why each step
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1  DUAL-WRITE      app writes BOTH old and new. Reads stay on old.
                    -> the new topology starts receiving current data
                    -> rollback is free: stop writing to new

2  BACKFILL        copy history in BOUNDED batches
                    -> throttle; check replication lag between batches
                    -> resumable from a checkpoint, and IDEMPOTENT
                       (it will be interrupted)

3  VERIFY          row counts per shard, checksums over key ranges,
                    and a SHADOW READ: serve from old, compare with new,
                    log differences without affecting the user
                    -> do not proceed on a mismatch

4  SHIFT READS     5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%, watching error rate
                    -> rollback is a percentage change, seconds

5  CUT WRITES      stop dual-writing; new topology is authoritative
                    -> keep the old data readable for a quiet period

6  DECOMMISSION    and actually do it - a half-migrated estate is the
                    worst outcome

THE INVARIANT: at every step, you can go back without data loss.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      How do you handle writes during the backfill?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Dual-writing handles new writes; the backfill handles history. The subtlety is ordering — a backfill must not overwrite a newer value written by the dual-write path. Use a version or timestamp check so the backfill only writes when the target is absent or older, which also makes it safe to re-run.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What if verification finds a mismatch?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Stop and investigate rather than proceeding and fixing later — a mismatch during migration usually means a bug in the dual-write path that will keep producing them. Common causes are writes that bypass the dual-write layer (a batch job, an admin tool) and a shard-routing function that disagrees between paths.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S46
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Key-value stores do one thing extremely fast: get and put by key. Document stores add querying inside a nested structure, so you can fetch a whole aggregate in one read and index its fields.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Wide-column (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable) is built for enormous write throughput with a partition key plus a clustering key — a good fit for time-series and event data, and a poor fit for anything needing ad-hoc queries or joins.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Graph stores make traversal cheap, which relational databases do badly beyond a couple of hops. Time-series stores exploit the fact that data is append-only and ordered, giving huge compression and fast range aggregation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Which, and what you give up
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        KEY-VALUE      Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached
  get/put by key, microseconds
  give up: querying by anything but the key

DOCUMENT       MongoDB, Couchbase, DynamoDB
  fetch a whole aggregate in one read; index nested fields
  give up: joins, and multi-document transactional guarantees are limited
  good when the aggregate boundary matches your access pattern

WIDE-COLUMN    Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable
  partition key + clustering key; enormous write throughput; linear scale
  give up: ad-hoc queries, joins, and read-modify-write patterns
  QUERY-FIRST design - you model tables per query, duplicating data

GRAPH          Neo4j, Neptune
  traversal is cheap; "friends of friends who bought X" is one query
  give up: throughput at scale, and operational familiarity

TIME-SERIES    TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus
  append-only, ordered; huge compression; fast range aggregation
  give up: updates and deletes, which are awkward by design

THE QUESTION THAT PICKS ONE
  not "which is fastest" but "what does my ACCESS PATTERN look like,
  and what QUERIES will someone ask in a year that I have not thought of?"
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        When is 'NoSQL' the wrong answer?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        When you need ad-hoc queries nobody designed for, multi-row transactions, or strong referential integrity — which is most business systems. The classic failure is choosing a document store for a domain with real relationships, then reimplementing joins in application code, badly, without transactions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Is Postgres a reasonable answer to all of these?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Increasingly, yes, and saying so is a defensible position. JSONB covers document use cases, extensions cover time-series and vector search, and you keep transactions, joins and one operational story. The honest limit is write throughput beyond a single leader, and genuine graph traversal at depth.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S47
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A B-tree updates data in place: find the page, modify it, write it back. Reads are predictable — a handful of page reads — and writes are random I/O, with write amplification from page splits and write-ahead logging.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          An LSM tree never updates in place. Writes go to an in-memory table, which is flushed as an immutable sorted file, and background compaction merges those files. Writes are sequential and therefore very fast; reads may have to check several files, which is why LSM stores rely heavily on Bloom filters.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The trade in one line: B-tree favours reads, LSM favours writes. And LSM's cost is not free — compaction consumes I/O and CPU continuously, and a compaction backlog causes latency spikes that look mysterious if you do not know to look for them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The trade, and what to watch
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          B-TREE                              LSM TREE
in-place updates                    append-only, never in place
random writes                       SEQUENTIAL writes  <- much faster
predictable read: ~log(n) pages     read may check memtable + N SSTables
                                      -> Bloom filters make misses cheap
write amp from page splits + WAL    write amp from COMPACTION
space: fragmentation                space amp: old versions until compacted
                                    -> can be 2x logical size temporarily

Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, most RDBMS  Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, ScyllaDB

WHAT TO WATCH ON LSM
  compaction backlog -> read latency climbs as more files must be checked
  compaction I/O competing with foreground writes -> latency spikes
  tombstones: a DELETE writes a MARKER, and until compaction the data
    is still there and still read. Delete-heavy workloads on LSM are a
    known trap - the reads get slower after you delete things.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why do Bloom filters matter so much for LSM?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Because a read may need to check many files. A Bloom filter per file answers definitely not here in constant time, so most files are skipped without any I/O. Without them, a point lookup on a store with twenty files would cost twenty reads, and LSM read performance would be unusable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Which would you choose for a payments ledger?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A B-tree engine — a relational database. The workload is not write-dominant enough to need LSM, and you need transactions, joins and ad-hoc queries for reconciliation. Reach for LSM when write throughput is the binding constraint and the access pattern is narrow and known.
