                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S48
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            These trade exactness for space, and each has a one-sided error you must know. A Bloom filter answers set membership: definitely not present or possibly present. It never gives a false negative, which is what makes it safe as a pre-filter — you only pay for a real lookup when it says maybe.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts in about 12 KB with roughly 2% error, whether you feed it a thousand items or a billion. Counting unique visitors exactly needs memory proportional to the visitors; HyperLogLog does not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Count-Min Sketch estimates item frequency in fixed memory and may overestimate but never underestimate — which makes it right for finding heavy hitters (the hot keys, the top talkers) where a small overcount is harmless and missing one is not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Three structures, three one-sided errors
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            BLOOM FILTER          "is X in the set?"
  false POSITIVE possible, false NEGATIVE impossible
  ~10 bits per item for ~1% error rate
  USE: skip a disk read (LSM), skip a cache lookup for keys that
       cannot exist (cache penetration), dedup with a tolerable miss
  CANNOT delete (a counting Bloom filter can, at more space)

HYPERLOGLOG           "how many DISTINCT items?"
  ~2% error, ~12 KB REGARDLESS of input size
  mergeable: union two sketches to combine two days or two shards
  USE: unique visitors, distinct IPs, cardinality on a dashboard

COUNT-MIN SKETCH      "how often did X occur?"
  OVERestimates, never underestimates
  USE: heavy hitters - hot keys, top talkers, abuse detection

THE DECIDING QUESTION
  "is an approximate answer acceptable, and which direction of error
   is safe?" If neither direction is safe, use the exact structure and
   pay for the memory.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Where would you use a Bloom filter in a system you designed?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            In front of a cache to stop penetration attacks — requests for ids that exist nowhere miss the cache and hit the database. A Bloom filter of existing ids answers definitely not in memory. Also inside any LSM store, and for dedup where an occasional false positive means skipping a duplicate you would have skipped anyway.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What if you need exact counts?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Then you pay for them: a set in Redis, or a counter table, with memory or write cost proportional to cardinality. The point of these structures is not that approximate is better — it is that for dashboards, monitoring and routing decisions, 2% error is invisible and the memory saving is three orders of magnitude.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S49
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it. That inversion is the whole trick: finding documents containing refund is a single lookup rather than a scan of every document.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Tokenisation decides what a term is, and it is where search quality is actually won or lost — lowercasing, stemming (running → run), stop-word handling, and language-specific analysers. Query and index must use the same analyser, or the terms will not match.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              BM25 ranks results by term frequency and inverse document frequency, with two refinements over naive TF-IDF: saturation (the twentieth occurrence of a word adds little over the tenth) and length normalisation (a short document matching once is more relevant than a long one matching once).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The index, and the sharding constraint
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              INVERTED INDEX
  "refund"  -> [doc3, doc7, doc12, ...]  with positions and frequencies
  "chargeback" -> [doc7, doc19, ...]
  a phrase query intersects the lists AND checks positions

TOKENISATION decides quality
  "Refunds aren't processed" ->  [refund, not, process]
  lowercase | stem | stop words | language analyser
  THE INDEX AND THE QUERY MUST USE THE SAME ANALYSER

BM25 over naive TF-IDF
  SATURATION        the 20th occurrence adds little over the 10th
  LENGTH NORM       a short doc matching once beats a long doc matching once

ELASTICSEARCH SHARDING - the constraint that bites
  shard count is FIXED AT INDEX CREATION and cannot be changed
  -> too few: cannot scale out
  -> too many: overhead per shard, slow queries (each is a Lucene index)
  every query hits EVERY shard and results are merged
  RESHARDING = reindex into a new index behind an ALIAS, then swap
  -> use aliases from day one, or you cannot reindex without downtime
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why is deep pagination so bad in a distributed search index?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because to return results 10,000–10,020 ranked globally, every shard must return its top 10,020 and the coordinator merges them. Cost grows with the offset multiplied by the shard count. Use search_after — the same keyset idea — which is constant cost per page.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Should search be a separate system from your database?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Usually yes, because the workloads conflict: search wants an inverted index and denormalised documents, your transactional store wants normalised rows and ACID. Keep the database authoritative and feed the search index asynchronously from a change stream, accepting a small lag. Trying to serve both from one engine compromises both.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S50
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                OLTP is many small transactions touching few rows, optimised for latency and concurrency. OLAP is few enormous queries scanning many rows, optimised for throughput. They want opposite things — row storage versus columnar, indexes versus scans, small transactions versus long ones.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Running analytics against your transactional primary is therefore a recurring source of incidents: a report holds a long transaction that blocks vacuum, saturates I/O, and competes for the buffer cache with the workload paying your bills.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The standard separation is change data capture — read the transaction log and stream changes to an analytical store. No application code, no dual-write problem, and complete ordering per key. The trade is that CDC events are row changes, not business intent, which couples consumers to your schema.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Keeping analytics off the primary
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                OLTP                                OLAP
many small transactions             few large scans
row storage                         COLUMNAR storage
indexes for point lookups           compression, partition pruning
latency-sensitive                   throughput-sensitive
minutes of retention in cache       years of history

WHY NOT JUST USE A READ REPLICA?
  it helps, and it is not enough:
    a long analytical query on a replica BLOCKS REPLAY -> lag grows
    the replica has the same row-oriented layout - scans are still slow
    you still cannot keep years of history there

THE PIPELINE
  primary --(WAL / binlog)--> CDC (Debezium, DMS)
         --> stream (Kafka/Kinesis)
         --> columnar store (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse)

  no application changes | no dual-write problem | ordered per key

THE TRADE
  CDC emits ROW CHANGES, not business intent:
    {"op":"U","before":{"status":"PENDING"},"after":{"status":"SETTLED"}}
  consumers are coupled to your SCHEMA - a column rename breaks them.
  -> an outbox with designed events avoids that, at the cost of app code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                When is a read replica sufficient for reporting?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                When the reports are small, bounded and infrequent — an operations dashboard, a support lookup. It stops being sufficient when queries scan large ranges, run for minutes, or need history the primary no longer holds. The tell is replication lag spiking whenever someone opens the reporting tool.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Outbox or CDC?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                CDC when you want zero application change and the consumer is a data platform that can tolerate schema coupling. An outbox when other teams build against the events, because then the event is a public contract and it should be designed rather than derived from your table structure.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S51
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  CAP says that during a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability. The precise version matters: it is not a menu of three where you pick two. Partitions are not optional — they happen — so the real statement is when partitioned, choose C or A.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That makes CAP a claim about a rare condition, which is why PACELC is more useful day to day. It adds: else, when there is no partition, you still trade latency against consistency — and that trade is happening on every single request, not just during a failure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  So the useful framing in an interview is: during a partition we do X, and in normal operation we accept Y milliseconds of coordination or Z seconds of staleness. That describes a real system; we chose AP does not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  CAP precisely, and why PACELC is better
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  CAP - only meaningful DURING A PARTITION
  CP   refuse writes on the minority side; stay consistent, lose availability
       (etcd, ZooKeeper, a quorum database)
  AP   accept writes on both sides; stay available, reconcile later
       (Cassandra with low consistency, DynamoDB global tables, DNS)
  CA   NOT AN OPTION. You cannot choose to not have partitions.

PACELC - describes NORMAL operation too
  if (P) then A or C
  ELSE       then L or C          <- this is every request, every day

  PostgreSQL sync replication     PC / EC   consistent, slower writes
  PostgreSQL async replication    PC / EL   consistent-ish, fast, lag
  Cassandra QUORUM                PC / EC
  Cassandra ONE                   PA / EL   fastest, weakest
  DynamoDB (default read)         PA / EL   eventually consistent

SAY THIS INSTEAD OF "WE CHOSE AP"
  "During a partition the minority side serves reads but rejects writes.
   Normally we take one extra round trip for a quorum write, which is
   about 2ms, and that is worth it because this is a ledger."

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Is a single-node database CP or AP?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Neither meaningfully — CAP is about partitioned systems. A single node is consistent and unavailable when it is down, which is not the same trade. The question only becomes interesting once state is replicated, which is worth saying if an interviewer tries to apply CAP to something that has no partitions to survive.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Can different parts of one system make different choices?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Yes, and good designs do. A payments platform might run the ledger CP (refuse writes rather than risk divergence) while the notification service runs AP (send twice rather than not at all). Making that choice per component, with a reason, is a much stronger answer than picking one label for the whole system.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S52
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    linearizable is the strongest practical model: every operation appears to happen instantaneously at a single point, and every client agrees on the order. It behaves like a single copy of the data — and it requires coordination, so it costs a round trip and is unavailable during a partition.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    causal consistency is the sweet spot most people should aim for. If A could have influenced B, everyone sees A before B; genuinely concurrent operations may be seen in either order. That is enough to prevent the anomalies users actually notice — a reply appearing before its message — without global coordination.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Eventual consistency promises only that replicas converge if writes stop. On its own that is a very weak guarantee, which is why the session guarantees from earlier — read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix — matter: they are the cheap additions that make eventual consistency usable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The models, strongest to weakest
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    LINEARIZABLE       one copy, one global order, real-time respected
  cost: coordination on every operation; unavailable when partitioned
  use: leader election, locks, unique constraints, account balances

SEQUENTIAL         all clients see the same order, but not necessarily
                   real-time order
  cheaper; rarely the thing you specifically want

CAUSAL             causally related ops are ordered for everyone;
                   concurrent ops may differ
  cost: track causality (vector clocks / dependencies)
  THE SWEET SPOT - prevents what users notice, needs no global agreement

EVENTUAL           replicas converge IF writes stop. That is all.
  add the SESSION GUARANTEES to make it usable:
    read-your-writes | monotonic reads | consistent prefix

THE PRACTICAL QUESTION
  not "which model" but "which ANOMALY would a user notice, and what is
  the cheapest thing that prevents it?"
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Is strong consistency always better?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    No — it costs a round trip on every operation and availability during a partition, and most operations do not need it. A like count that is two seconds stale harms nobody; a balance that is two seconds stale allows a double spend. Apply the strong model to the few operations that need it rather than to the whole system.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What does 'strong consistency' mean when a vendor says it?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Ask, because it is used loosely. It may mean linearizable, or serializable (a transaction property, different thing), or merely read-after-write on a single key. DynamoDB's strongly consistent read is per-item linearizability, not transactional isolation. Pinning down which guarantee is meant is a good question to ask in an interview.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S53
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Every distributed system delivers at least once, so the question is never how do I avoid duplicates — it is how do I make a duplicate harmless. The mechanism is an idempotency key plus an atomic claim.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Derive the key from content, deterministically: a client-supplied header, an event id from the producer, or a hash of the meaningful fields. Never from something that changes on redelivery — a broker message id, a timestamp, or a UUID generated by the consumer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Then claim it with a conditional write: a unique constraint in a relational database, or attribute_not_exists in a key-value store. Both are atomic. A read-then-write has a race and will eventually lose it, which is the bug that produces double refunds under load.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The complete pattern
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      // CLAIM BEFORE THE WORK, not after
String key = idempotencyKeyFromRequest();      // client-supplied header

try {
    ddb.putItem(r -> r.tableName("processed")
        .item(Map.of("pk", s(key), "status", s("IN_PROGRESS"),
                     "ttl", n(ttl30d())))                 // bounded growth
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"));
} catch (ConditionalCheckFailedException dup) {
    return existingResult(key);       // return the ORIGINAL response
}
var result = process(request);
store(key, result);
return result;

WHY CLAIM FIRST
  claim AFTER  -> a crash between work and claim does the work TWICE
  claim BEFORE -> a crash leaves work UNDONE, which a reconciliation job
                  finds. The safer failure.

THE DEDUP WINDOW
  a TTL bounds the table's growth, and it also bounds the guarantee:
  a retry after the TTL expires will be processed again.
  30 days is generous and cheap. State the window explicitly.

RETURN THE ORIGINAL RESPONSE
  a repeated key should return what the first call returned, not a
  conflict error - otherwise a client retrying a timed-out request
  cannot tell success from failure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Where should the idempotency record live?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Ideally in the same store as the effect, so the claim and the work commit in one transaction. If they are in different systems you are back to a dual write — and then the claim should be the durable one, so a crash leaves work undone rather than duplicated.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What makes an operation naturally idempotent?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Setting an absolute value rather than applying a delta. SET status = 'PAID' is idempotent; balance = balance - 100 is not. Where you can express the operation as make the world look like this rather than apply this change, you get idempotency for free and need no key at all.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S54
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The dual-write problem: you must change your database and publish an event, and there is no atomic commit across the two. Crash between them and you get either a state change nobody heard about, or an event for a change that rolled back.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Ordering does not fix it. Publish first and the transaction may roll back, leaving a phantom event. Commit first and the publish may fail, losing the event. Wrapping the publish inside the transaction achieves nothing, because a broker acknowledgement cannot be rolled back.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The transactional outbox resolves it by making the intent to publish part of the same local transaction: insert a row into an outbox table alongside the business write. One database, one commit, fully testable. A separate relay then publishes those rows and marks them sent.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        One transaction, then a relay
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        @Transactional
void settle(Settlement s) {
    repo.save(s);
    outbox.insert(new OutboxRow(
        UUID.randomUUID(),      // eventId -> the consumer's idempotency key
        "PaymentSettled",
        s.getAccountId(),       // ordering key
        json(s),                // FULL PAYLOAD, snapshotted at write time
        Instant.now(), null));  // sentAt
}   // ONE database, ONE commit. Atomic and unit-testable.

// RELAY - poller. SKIP LOCKED stops two instances double-publishing.
SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
  -> publish -> UPDATE sent_at = now()
  (may publish then crash -> republishes. Fine.)

// or CDC: read the transaction log, no polling, lower latency

WHY THE FULL PAYLOAD, NOT AN ID
  store only an id and the relay must RE-READ the entity - and may see
  a LATER state, publishing an event that does not match the transaction
  it came from.

THE GUARANTEE, precisely
  AT-LEAST-ONCE publication corresponding EXACTLY to committed state.
  NOT exactly-once -> consumers must be idempotent. That is the contract,
  not a footnote.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you stop the outbox table growing forever?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Delete sent rows on a schedule, keeping a few days for debugging and replay. Do not delete immediately on publish — a short history lets you re-drive events after a consumer bug, which is one of the pattern's practical benefits. Monitor the age of the oldest unsent row; a rising value means the relay has stopped.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Does the outbox preserve ordering?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Per key, if you make it so. Put an ordering key in the row and publish with it as the partition key or message group, so events for one entity stay ordered. Global ordering across all events is neither achievable at scale nor usually needed — and consumers should be order-tolerant across keys.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S55
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          two-phase commit makes a transaction span several systems: a coordinator asks everyone to prepare, and if all agree, tells everyone to commit. It is correct, and it is why nobody uses it at scale.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The problems are structural. Participants hold locks between the phases, so throughput collapses under contention. The coordinator is a single point of failure at the worst possible moment — if it dies after prepare, participants are blocked, holding locks, unable to decide alone. And availability is the product of every participant's, so adding systems makes it worse.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          So the practical answer in modern architecture is: do not span a transaction across services. Redesign so the transaction is local, or accept eventual consistency and use a saga with compensation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why it does not scale
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          PHASE 1  coordinator -> "PREPARE"     participants lock and vote yes/no
PHASE 2  coordinator -> "COMMIT"      participants commit and release

THE FAILURES
  locks held ACROSS a network round trip
     -> throughput collapses; one slow participant blocks everyone
  coordinator dies after prepare
     -> participants are BLOCKED. They cannot commit (maybe someone
        voted no) and cannot abort (maybe everyone voted yes).
        They hold locks until it returns. This is the blocking problem.
  availability multiplies
     -> 5 participants at 99.9% = 99.5% for the transaction

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD
  1  REDESIGN so the transaction is LOCAL
     -> put the data that must change together in ONE service
     -> this is what "aggregate boundary" means in DDD, and it is the
        real answer most of the time
  2  SAGA with compensating actions, and accept eventual consistency
  3  outbox + idempotent consumers for the propagation

WHERE 2PC STILL LIVES
  inside one database across shards (Spanner, CockroachDB - with
  bounded clocks and a Paxos-replicated coordinator, which removes
  the blocking problem)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Is XA ever acceptable?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          In a small, stable set of participants inside one datacentre with low contention — a legacy integration between a database and a message broker, for instance. It is a legitimate tool with a narrow window. What is not acceptable is reaching for it as the default answer to cross-service consistency.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How does Spanner avoid the blocking problem?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          By making the coordinator itself fault-tolerant — it is a Paxos group, not a single node, so it cannot simply disappear. Combined with bounded clock uncertainty from TrueTime, that makes distributed transactions practical at the cost of infrastructure most organisations do not have.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S56
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A saga replaces a distributed transaction with a sequence of local ones, each with a compensating transaction. There is no rollback — the earlier steps really happened and were visible — so you undo them with new actions: refund the payment, release the reservation, cancel the booking.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Choreography means each service listens for events and reacts. It is decoupled and it has no central place where the process is visible, so understanding what happens when an order is placed means reading five services. Debugging is genuinely hard.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Orchestration means a coordinator drives the steps explicitly. The flow is visible in one place, testable, and easy to change — at the cost of a component that knows about everyone. For anything with more than about three steps, orchestration is usually the better trade.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The two shapes, and the limits
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CHOREOGRAPHY - services react to events
  OrderPlaced -> Payment listens -> PaymentTaken -> Inventory listens -> ...
  + decoupled, no central component
  - the process exists NOWHERE. Reading it means reading every service.
  - cyclic dependencies creep in; debugging is hard
  -> fine for 2-3 steps

ORCHESTRATION - a coordinator drives
  Orchestrator: takePayment -> reserveStock -> ship
                on failure at step N, run compensations N-1 .. 1
  + the flow is VISIBLE, testable, and changeable in one place
  + retries and timeouts per step
  - the orchestrator knows about everyone
  -> the right default beyond three steps

THE LIMITS - state these, they are what interviewers probe
  NO ISOLATION. Intermediate states are VISIBLE to other transactions.
    another request can see the reservation before the payment settles.
    -> use semantic locks (a PENDING status) if that matters
  COMPENSATION CAN FAIL. Then you need retries, and eventually a human.
  SOME THINGS CANNOT BE COMPENSATED. An email is sent. A physical
    package shipped. -> order the steps so irreversible ones are LAST.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What if a compensating action fails?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Retry it with backoff, because it must eventually succeed — then, if it still fails, escalate to a human with the full context. That is why sagas need durable state and a dead-letter path: an un-compensated saga is money or inventory stuck in limbo, and it needs to be visible rather than silently retried forever.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you handle steps that cannot be undone?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Order them last, so everything reversible happens first and the irreversible step is the commit point. Where that is impossible, insert a confirmation gate before it — reserve everything, verify, then perform the irreversible action. Designing the step order around reversibility is the main structural decision in a saga.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S57
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Consensus is getting a group of nodes to agree on a value despite failures. Raft is the one to be able to explain, because it was explicitly designed to be understandable and it is what etcd, Consul and many others run.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three pieces. Leader election: time is divided into terms, and a candidate wins a term by getting votes from a majority. Log replication: all writes go to the leader, which appends to its log and replicates to followers. Commit: an entry is committed once a majority have stored it, and only then applied.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The majority requirement is what makes it safe under partition: two disjoint groups cannot both hold a majority, so at most one side can elect a leader and make progress. Paxos solves the same problem and is famously harder to reason about; the intuition is the same — a majority quorum, and any two majorities must overlap.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Raft, and what to say about it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              TERMS       time divided into numbered terms; at most one leader per term
ELECTION    a follower whose election timeout fires becomes a candidate,
            increments the term, and requests votes.
            A node votes ONCE per term -> at most one winner.
            Randomised timeouts prevent repeated split votes.
LOG         all writes go to the LEADER, appended and replicated
COMMIT      once a MAJORITY have stored an entry, it is committed
            and can be applied to the state machine

WHY MAJORITY IS THE WHOLE TRICK
  any two majorities of the same set OVERLAP in at least one node
  -> that node's vote prevents two conflicting decisions
  -> a partition of 5 into {3} and {2}: only the 3 can make progress

CLUSTER SIZE
  3 nodes -> tolerates 1 failure
  5 nodes -> tolerates 2
  EVEN sizes gain nothing: 4 also tolerates only 1, and costs more.
  This is why you always see 3 or 5.

WHERE YOU MEET IT
  etcd (Kubernetes control plane), Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV,
  Kafka KRaft mode
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why is consensus slow, and where does that matter?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Every write needs a round trip to a majority, so latency is bounded by the slowest node in the quorum — and across regions that is tens or hundreds of milliseconds. That is why you use consensus for metadata (who is the leader, what is the cluster membership, configuration) and not for high-volume application data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What does 'the cluster lost quorum' mean operationally?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              More than half the nodes are unavailable, so no majority exists and the cluster cannot elect a leader or commit anything. It stops accepting writes entirely — which for etcd means the Kubernetes control plane freezes. Recovery is restoring enough nodes, or in the worst case restoring from a backup and forcing a new cluster.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S58
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Leader election answers a common need: exactly one instance should run a scheduled job, own a partition, or coordinate a process. With three replicas of a service and a cron trigger, the job runs three times unless something elects a leader.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The mechanism is usually a lease in a strongly consistent store — etcd, ZooKeeper, or a database row with a conditional update. One instance acquires it, renews it periodically, and if it dies the lease simply expires and someone else takes over. No failure detection is needed; expiry is the detection.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The critical caveat is the same one as with distributed locks: a leader can be paused. It may still believe it holds a lease that expired while it was stopped, so the protected resource must reject writes from a stale term — fencing again. Leadership tells you who should act; fencing enforces who can.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A lease in a database, and the caveat
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                -- leader election with nothing but a table
UPDATE leader_lease
SET owner = :me, expires_at = now() + interval '15 seconds', term = term + 1
WHERE lease_name = 'settlement-job'
  AND (owner = :me OR expires_at < now());
-- 1 row updated -> I am the leader for this term
-- 0 rows        -> someone else holds it; do nothing

-- renew every 5s. Miss two renewals and it expires - no detection needed.

WHERE THIS IS USED
  a scheduled job that must run ONCE across N replicas
  ownership of a Kafka partition or a shard
  a singleton coordinator for a saga

THE CAVEAT - same as distributed locking
  a GC pause longer than the lease means a node wakes up believing it
  still leads, after someone else took over.
  -> the RESOURCE must reject writes from an older term (fencing token)
  -> leadership decides who SHOULD act; fencing decides who CAN

ZOOKEEPER / ETCD give you this properly
  ephemeral nodes / leases tied to a session, watches for change
  -> use them when you already run one, rather than adding one for this
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Do you need ZooKeeper or etcd for leader election?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Rarely, if you already have a strongly consistent database — the conditional-update lease above is a few lines and has the same properties for job coordination. Adding a coordination service is justified when you need watches, ephemeral membership, or election across many resources. Adding one just to run a cron job once is disproportionate.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What is the simplest correct alternative?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Make the job idempotent and let it run N times. If the work is a conditional write or an upsert keyed deterministically, three replicas racing produce one outcome and no coordination is needed at all. That is often cheaper and more robust than electing a leader — worth proposing before reaching for election.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S59
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  heartbeat and leases are how distributed systems decide a node is gone — and the uncomfortable truth is that you cannot distinguish a dead node from a slow network. Every failure detector is a guess with a timeout attached.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That forces a trade. A short timeout detects failure quickly and produces false positives, so healthy nodes get evicted during a brief network blip — which can cascade. A long timeout avoids that and extends every outage.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  phi accrual detectors, used by Cassandra and Akka, improve on a fixed threshold by tracking the recent distribution of heartbeat intervals and emitting a suspicion level. A node that normally responds in 1ms and has been silent for 50ms is far more suspicious than one that is always erratic.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Detection, and why fencing is still required
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  FIXED TIMEOUT
  short  -> fast detection, FALSE POSITIVES during a network blip
            (and evicting healthy nodes under load can cascade)
  long   -> fewer false positives, longer outages

PHI ACCRUAL (Cassandra, Akka)
  track the distribution of recent inter-arrival times
  output a suspicion LEVEL rather than a boolean
  -> adapts to a node that is normally fast vs normally erratic

LEASE - detection for free
  the holder must RENEW before expiry.
  A crashed holder simply stops renewing. Nothing needs to notice.
  -> this is why leases beat heartbeat-plus-timeout for ownership

AND STILL: FENCING IS REQUIRED
  t=0   A holds the lease, TTL 15s
  t=1   A begins a 30-second GC pause
  t=16  lease expires. B takes over and writes.
  t=31  A wakes, believes it holds the lease, and WRITES.

  The detector was CORRECT. The lease expired CORRECTLY. And there were
  still two writers - because A did not know time had passed.
  -> the RESOURCE must reject an older term. Detection cannot fix this.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Why can a paused process not just check the clock when it wakes?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  It can, and that helps — but the check and the subsequent write are not atomic. It can verify the lease is valid, then be paused again between the check and the write. Only the resource, rejecting an older fencing token at the moment of the write, closes the gap completely.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What timeout would you choose in practice?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Derive it from the observed distribution, not from a round number: a timeout around ten times the p99 heartbeat interval is a common starting point. Then ask what a false positive costs — if evicting a healthy node triggers a rebalance that hurts, bias long; if failover is cheap and fast, bias short.
