                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S60
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Wall-clock timestamps are unreliable for ordering across machines, because of clock skew. NTP usually keeps clocks within milliseconds, and usually is doing a lot of work — a clock can jump backwards after a correction, and a leap second can make it stand still.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    So last write wins by timestamp is a coin flip when writes are close together, and it silently discards data. That is the practical consequence to state: a system resolving conflicts by wall clock can lose a write because one server's clock was 40ms fast.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Lamport clock give a consistent total order without physical clocks — a counter incremented on each event and carried on each message — but they cannot tell you whether two events were concurrent. vector clock can: one counter per node, and comparing two vectors tells you whether one causally precedes the other or they are genuinely concurrent, which is exactly what conflict detection needs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Why timestamps lie, and what replaces them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    WALL CLOCK
  skew of a few ms is normal; NTP corrections can move it BACKWARDS
  -> "last write wins" discards a write when clocks disagree
  -> and you never find out. It is silent.

LAMPORT CLOCK          a single counter
  on local event:   c = c + 1
  on send:          send (msg, c)
  on receive:       c = max(c, received) + 1
  gives:  if A -> B then C(A) < C(B)
  CANNOT tell you: whether two events were concurrent

VECTOR CLOCK           one counter PER NODE
  A = [2,1,0]   B = [1,2,0]
  neither dominates -> CONCURRENT -> a real conflict to resolve
  A = [2,1,0]   B = [3,1,0]
  B dominates   -> B happened after A -> no conflict

  cost: size grows with node count; needs pruning in large clusters

HYBRID LOGICAL CLOCKS (HLC)
  physical time + a logical counter
  -> close to wall clock (so it is human-readable and sortable)
  -> but monotonic and causally correct. Used by CockroachDB, MongoDB.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When is 'last write wins' acceptable?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    When a lost write is genuinely harmless — a user preference, a cached projection, a presence indicator. It is not acceptable for anything cumulative or financial, because the discarded write is real data and nothing records that it vanished. If you use LWW, say explicitly which data it applies to and why loss is tolerable there.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What does Spanner do differently?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    It bounds clock uncertainty with TrueTime — GPS and atomic clocks giving an interval rather than a point — and then deliberately waits out the uncertainty before committing. That converts clock skew from an unknown into a known bound, which is what makes externally consistent distributed transactions possible. It is also why it needs special hardware.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S61
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      total order means everyone agrees on the sequence of all operations. It is what a single database gives you for free and what a distributed system pays dearly for, because it requires global coordination on every write.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Per-partition ordering is the practical compromise and it is what Kafka, Kinesis and most sharded stores give you: strict order within a partition, no guarantee across partitions. Since the partition key is yours to choose, you get to decide what is ordered.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      That makes the key the design decision. Partition by account and you get order per account with parallelism across accounts — almost always what you want. Partition by a constant and you get total order with no parallelism and a single consumer. Partition randomly and you get maximum parallelism and no ordering at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Choosing what is ordered
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      TOTAL ORDER          everyone agrees on everything
  requires consensus on every write -> expensive, and it does not scale
  you rarely need it

PER-PARTITION ORDER  the practical answer
  key -> partition -> strict order within that partition
  YOU CHOOSE THE KEY, so you choose what is ordered

  accountId    order per account, parallel across accounts   <- usually right
  a constant   TOTAL order, ONE consumer, no parallelism     <- almost never
  random       maximum parallelism, NO ordering

CAUSAL ORDER         only causally related events are ordered
  cheaper than total; enough to prevent what users notice

DESIGN CONSEQUENCES
  a consumer rebuilding per-account state from an ordered partition is SAFE
  a consumer assuming global chronological order across accounts is WRONG
  -> make consumers idempotent AND order-tolerant across keys

AND: ORDERING IS LOST ON RETRY
  if message 5 fails and is retried while 6 succeeds, order is broken.
  -> either block the partition on failure (slow), or accept reordering
     and design handlers that do not care.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Do you actually need ordering, or idempotency?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Usually idempotency, and people reach for ordering when the real requirement is that the final state is correct regardless of arrival order. If each event carries the full resulting state, or a version you can compare, out-of-order delivery becomes harmless — which is far cheaper than enforcing order end to end.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What breaks ordering in a system that nominally has it?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Retries (a failed message reprocessed after a later one), consumer parallelism within a partition, a rebalance mid-batch, and any point where you fan out to workers. Each is easy to introduce accidentally, which is why we have ordering is worth verifying rather than assuming.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S62
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        backpressure is what a system does when it cannot keep up. Without it, work accumulates in an unbounded queue: memory grows, latency grows, and eventually the process dies — having accepted work it was never going to complete.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The choices are: block the producer (natural in a synchronous call, and it propagates the stall upstream), buffer with a bounded queue (absorbs bursts, and must decide what to do when full), shed load by rejecting early, or sample and drop some work deliberately.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The important principle is fail fast rather than queue deep. A request that will miss its deadline should be rejected immediately, so the caller can fall back now rather than timing out in twenty seconds. Accepting work you cannot complete converts your capacity problem into everyone's latency problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Four responses, and where each fits
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        BLOCK      the producer waits
  natural in synchronous calls; propagates the stall upstream
  dangerous if the caller has no timeout - the stall spreads

BUFFER     a BOUNDED queue absorbs bursts
  unbounded queues are the classic bug: memory grows, latency grows,
  and you crash having accepted work you could not do
  -> ALWAYS bound the queue, and decide the full policy explicitly

SHED       reject early with 429 / 503 + Retry-After
  the CALLER can fall back NOW instead of timing out later
  -> shed the LOWEST-PRIORITY traffic first (background before interactive)

SAMPLE     drop a percentage deliberately
  right for telemetry and metrics, wrong for transactions

DEADLINE PROPAGATION - the underrated one
  the caller sends "I will give up in 800ms"
  every hop passes the REMAINING budget down
  a service with 50ms left does not start a 200ms query - it fails fast
  -> stops the whole chain doing work whose result nobody will read

REACTIVE STREAMS
  the consumer REQUESTS n items; the producer sends at most n
  -> backpressure built into the protocol rather than bolted on
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What is wrong with an unbounded queue?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It converts a throughput problem into a memory problem and then into an outage, while hiding the symptom. Latency climbs steadily, nothing errors, monitoring looks fine, and then the process dies. A bounded queue makes the problem visible immediately as rejections, which is a signal you can alarm on and scale against.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How does backpressure interact with retries?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Badly, if you are not careful — a shed request that the client immediately retries adds load rather than removing it. That is why a 429 should carry Retry-After and clients should honour it with jitter. Shedding without a retry policy on the other side just moves the queue into the client.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S63
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A gossip protocol spreads information without a coordinator: each node periodically picks a few random peers and exchanges state. Information reaches everyone in roughly logarithmic rounds, and the protocol degrades gracefully — no node is special, so no node's failure stops it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          That makes it the standard mechanism for cluster membership and failure detection in systems like Cassandra, Consul and Riak. It is eventually consistent by nature, which is fine for who is in the cluster and unsuitable for anything needing agreement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Anti-entropy is the repair counterpart: replicas periodically compare and reconcile. Doing that by comparing every row would be prohibitive, so replicas exchange a Merkle tree — comparing a handful of hashes narrows the difference to specific ranges, and only those are transferred.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Gossip and Merkle repair
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          GOSSIP
  every T seconds, each node picks k random peers and exchanges state
  -> information reaches N nodes in O(log N) rounds
  -> no coordinator, no single point of failure, scales to thousands
  -> EVENTUALLY consistent: fine for membership, useless for agreement

  used for: cluster membership, failure detection, config propagation
  NOT used for: leader election, locks, anything needing consensus

ANTI-ENTROPY with MERKLE TREES
  comparing 10 million rows between replicas: prohibitive
  comparing hashes:
     root hash equal?        -> replicas agree, done. One comparison.
     differ                  -> compare children, recurse
     -> O(log n) comparisons to find the differing RANGES
     -> transfer only those

  Cassandra: nodetool repair
  Dynamo-style stores: read repair (fix on read) + periodic full repair

WHY BOTH EXIST
  gossip spreads MEMBERSHIP cheaply
  anti-entropy fixes DATA that diverged during a partition or a
  dropped write
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why not use gossip for everything?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Because it gives you no agreement — two nodes can hold different views for a while, and there is no moment where the cluster has decided. That is acceptable for membership and unacceptable for leadership or locks. Systems typically use gossip for membership and a consensus group for the decisions that must be singular.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What is read repair?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          When a read touches several replicas and finds them disagreeing, the coordinator returns the newest value and writes it back to the stale replicas. It repairs the data people actually read, cheaply and continuously — but it never touches data nobody reads, which is why a periodic full anti-entropy repair is still needed.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S64
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Active-passive across regions means one region takes writes and the other is a warm standby — simple, with a data-loss window equal to the replication lag on unplanned failover. Active-active means both take writes, which requires you to answer: what happens when the same record is written in both places?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            There are only three real answers. Last write wins, which silently discards data and is only safe where loss is meaningless. CRDT, whose merge is designed to be order-independent so replicas converge automatically. Or regional partitioning, where each record has a home region and conflicts cannot arise.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            For anything financial, partitioning is the answer. Give each account a home region, route writes there, and serve reads locally from a replica. You get single-writer consistency with multi-region presence — and it aligns naturally with data residency requirements.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Three ways to resolve, one that is safe
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            LAST WRITE WINS
  compare timestamps, keep the newer
  SILENTLY DISCARDS a write - and clock skew decides which
  safe ONLY where loss is meaningless (presence, a cached view)

CRDTs - merge is commutative, associative, idempotent
  G-Counter      grow-only counter: merge = max per node, sum the parts
  PN-Counter     two G-Counters (increments, decrements)
  OR-Set         add/remove with unique tags, so a re-add survives
  LWW-Register   still LWW, but with explicit causality
  -> replicas converge regardless of order or duplication
  -> used by Riak, Redis CRDTs, collaborative editors
  -> cost: metadata grows; not every data type has a useful CRDT

REGIONAL PARTITIONING - the answer for anything consistent
  each account has a HOME REGION; writes route there
  reads served locally from a replica
  -> single-writer consistency WITH multi-region presence
  -> and it aligns with data residency requirements
  -> cost: a cross-region hop for the minority of misrouted writes

FOR A LEDGER: active-passive or partitioning. Never LWW.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why are CRDTs not used more widely?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Because the merge semantics have to genuinely match your business rule, and for most domains they do not. Converge to some value is not the same as converge to the correct value — a counter that merges correctly still cannot express reject this if the balance would go negative. They shine for collaborative text and presence, and rarely for transactions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What is the honest cost of active-active?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Roughly double the infrastructure plus a permanent complexity tax on every deploy, migration and incident. And complexity has its own failure rate, so a poorly-run active-active system is often less available than a well-run single-region one. Recommend it when a regulator, a contract, or genuine global latency demands it — not by default.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S65
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              data residency is a constraint that partitions the architecture before anything else does. If EU personal data must stay in the EU, you do not build one global system with a filter — you build separate regional stacks with no cross-border data flow.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Getting that order wrong is the classic mistake: design globally, then try to constrain it, and discover that logs, metrics, backups, caches, search indexes and the analytics pipeline all quietly carry personal data across the boundary.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              So the architecture becomes: route by geolocation to a regional stack, each holding its own data end to end, with a shared control plane that holds no regulated data — code, infrastructure definitions, dashboards and alert rules, but never records.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Where residency leaks
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              THE SHAPE
  Route 53 geolocation
    -> stack-EU (eu-west-1)   all EU data, end to end
    -> stack-UK (eu-west-2)   all UK data, end to end
  shared control plane: CI, IaC, container images, alert definitions
    -> holds NO regulated data

WHERE IT LEAKS - check every one
  LOGS            a log line with a customer id is regulated data
                  -> aggregate in-region; only non-identifying metrics leave
  metrics         usually fine IF labels carry no identifiers
  BACKUPS         cross-region backup copies move the data
  caches / CDN    a cached personalised response is the data
  search index    a second full copy, often forgotten
  analytics       the pipeline is the biggest leak of all
  SUPPORT TOOLS   an admin console that queries across regions
  error tracking  stack traces and request payloads

GDPR BEYOND LOCATION
  right to erasure    -> you must be able to DELETE across every copy,
                         including derived stores and logs
  data minimisation   -> short log retention is a compliance feature,
                         not just a cost saving
  purpose limitation  -> the analytics copy may not be usable for
                         everything the operational copy is
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Can you have a global user directory?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Only if it holds no regulated personal data — an opaque user id and a home-region pointer is usually acceptable, while names and emails are not. The common design is a global routing table mapping id to region, with all personal attributes stored only in that region. Getting legal to confirm what counts is part of the work.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How does erasure work across regional stacks?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Each region deletes independently, and the request must reach the right one — which the routing table gives you. The hard part is derived copies: search indexes, caches, analytics, backups, and logs. Design for it by recording where every copy lives, or an erasure request becomes a manual investigation each time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S66
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                RTO and RPO are independent numbers and they are the inputs to a disaster recovery design, not outputs of it. Fix them first and the architecture follows almost mechanically.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                An RPO of five seconds rules out backup-and-restore and any batched replication — it demands continuous, near-synchronous replication. An RTO of two minutes rules out provisioning compute on demand, because capacity must already exist. Together those two numbers select the pattern.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                And they must come from the business in money and obligation: what an hour of downtime costs, what a regulator requires, what the contract commits to. Engineers choosing these unilaterally is how you end up over-engineering a reporting tool and under-protecting a ledger.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The four patterns, selected by the numbers
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                PATTERN            RTO         RPO        COST     PROVEN BY
backup + restore   hours       backup     lowest   a restore TEST
                               interval
pilot light        10-45 min   seconds    low      partly - the COMPUTE
                                                   path is UNPROVEN until
                                                   the day you need it
warm standby       minutes     seconds    moderate CONTINUOUSLY - it runs
active-active      ~0          ~0         ~2x +    continuously
                                          complexity

FOR A PAYMENTS API: warm standby
  the argument is PROOF, not speed - a scaled-down but functioning copy
  is continuously exercised, so you know it works

  data     cross-region replica, lag < 1s -> RPO ~5s (MEASURE it, alarm on it)
  compute  same IaC both regions, standby at 20-30%, WARM
  routing  health-checked failover + client-side retry
  KEYS     multi-region encryption keys, or the standby decrypts NOTHING
           - and that is not fixable during the incident

AND STATE WHAT IS LOST
  on unplanned failover, writes committed but not replicated are GONE.
  -> the design must make REPLAY SAFE: idempotency keys, a re-drivable
     outbox, and reconciliation against an external record.

THE PART EVERYONE SKIPS
  REHEARSE IT. An untested plan has an UNKNOWN RTO - you have an
  aspiration, not a capability.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What does not fail over automatically?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Queues (messages in the dead region are stranded), caches (you fail over into a cold cache, and the miss storm can overwhelm the newly promoted database), scheduled jobs (both regions firing is double execution, neither is a silent gap), in-flight workflows, and every open connection. Naming these unprompted is a strong signal.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why is warm standby usually the right answer?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Because pilot light's compute path is a hypothesis until the incident, and active-active costs double plus a permanent complexity tax on every change. Warm standby is continuously exercised, so the RTO you quote is a measurement rather than an estimate — which is the property that actually matters at 3am.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Done whenFor any dependency you add to a design, you can immediately state its timeout, retry policy, failure mode, and degraded behaviour.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S67
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Every network call needs a timeout, and the default in most libraries is infinite — which is how one slow dependency exhausts your thread pool and takes down a service that was otherwise healthy.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The subtler requirement is that timeouts must nest. If your caller gives up after 10 seconds and you wait 30 for a downstream, you spend 20 seconds producing a response nobody will read, holding a thread the whole time. Every timeout must be shorter than its caller's.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The robust version is a timeout budget: the original caller states a deadline, and each hop passes the remaining time down. A service with 50ms left does not start a 200ms query — it fails immediately. That stops the entire chain doing work whose result is already worthless.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Nesting, and deadline propagation
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  WRONG - every service picks its own timeout
  client   30s
  gateway  30s
  service  30s
  database 30s
  -> the client gave up at 30s while four layers keep working

RIGHT - budgets shrink down the chain
  client   10.0s
  gateway   9.0s   (1s reserved for its own overhead + retry)
  service   7.5s
  database  5.0s
  -> every layer gives up before the one above it

BETTER - propagate the DEADLINE, not a fixed timeout
  caller sends:  X-Deadline: 2026-08-30T10:00:00.800Z
  each hop computes remaining = deadline - now
  if remaining < estimated cost of this call -> FAIL FAST, do not start

  gRPC has this built in (context deadlines). Over HTTP, pass a header.

TIMEOUTS THAT NEED SETTING EXPLICITLY (defaults are often infinite)
  connect | read/socket | overall request | connection pool acquire
  and: the pool ACQUIRE timeout is the one people forget - a request
  can wait forever for a connection before the call even starts
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  How do you choose a timeout value?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  From the measured p99 of that dependency, plus margin — not from a round number. A timeout at the p99 means 1% of healthy requests are killed and retried, which adds load at exactly the wrong moment. Set it above p99 and below your caller's budget; if those two constraints conflict, the dependency is too slow and that is the real finding.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What about long-running operations that legitimately exceed any budget?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  They should not be synchronous. Accept the request, return 202 with a status URL, and do the work asynchronously. A timeout is a statement that a synchronous response is expected — if none is, the design is wrong rather than the timeout.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S68
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A retry is only safe if the operation is idempotent. Retrying a non-idempotent write after a timeout can charge a card twice — and a timeout is precisely the case where you cannot tell whether the first attempt succeeded.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Exponential backoff spreads attempts out, and jitter is the part people omit. Without it, a thousand clients that failed at the same instant retry at the same instant, then again together — you have built a synchronised herd that keeps the dependency down.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    And cap the attempts. Two or three is usually right. Unbounded retries under a sustained failure multiply load and latency while achieving nothing, and they turn a brief degradation into a sustained outage.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Full jitter, and what not to retry
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    FULL JITTER - the version AWS recommends
  delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))

  attempt 1  random(0, 100ms)
  attempt 2  random(0, 200ms)
  attempt 3  random(0, 400ms)
  -> retries spread across a window instead of clustering

WITHOUT JITTER
  1,000 clients fail at t=0, all retry at t=100ms, all fail, all retry
  at t=300ms... a synchronised herd that keeps the dependency down

RETRY ONLY
  connection errors and timeouts on IDEMPOTENT operations
  429 and 503 - and HONOUR Retry-After if present
  explicitly retryable application errors

NEVER RETRY
  4xx other than 429    the request is wrong; retrying will not fix it
  non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key
  anything already past its deadline

THE RETRY BUDGET
  cap retries as a FRACTION of total requests (say 10%), not per-request.
  -> under a broad failure, retries cannot exceed 10% extra load,
     however many individual requests would like to retry.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What makes a write safely retryable?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    An idempotency key the server honours — the retry is recognised and returns the original response rather than performing the work again. Without that, a timeout leaves you genuinely unable to know whether to retry, and the only safe options are to query for the result or to fail the request to the user.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Should the client or the server retry?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Both, at different scopes. The client retries transient network failures with backoff; the server may retry an internal dependency. What you must avoid is retries at every layer multiplying — three layers each retrying three times is 27 requests from one user action. Budget retries at one layer and pass failures through the others.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S69
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Retries at multiple layers multiply. A client retrying three times, calling a gateway that retries three times, calling a service that retries three times, produces 27 requests from one user action — arriving precisely when the system is already struggling.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      That is the retry storm: the load increase caused by retries prevents recovery, which causes more failures, which causes more retries. The system cannot climb out on its own even after the original trigger is gone, which is why these incidents last far longer than their cause.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The defences are a retry budget (cap retries as a fraction of total traffic rather than per request), retrying at one layer only, and a circuit breaker that stops calls entirely once failure is established — the only mechanism that actually reduces load rather than reshaping it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The amplification, and how to stop it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      AMPLIFICATION
  client   3 attempts
  gateway  3 attempts   -> 9
  service  3 attempts   -> 27 requests to the database
  from ONE user action, arriving while the database is already struggling

THE FEEDBACK LOOP
  failures -> retries -> more load -> more failures -> more retries
  -> the system cannot recover EVEN AFTER the original cause is gone
  -> this is why these incidents outlast their trigger by hours

DEFENCES, in order of effectiveness
  1  CIRCUIT BREAKER - stop calling entirely once failure is established.
     The only one that actually REDUCES load.
  2  RETRY AT ONE LAYER ONLY - usually the outermost that can be
     idempotent. Others pass failures through.
  3  RETRY BUDGET - cap retries at ~10% of total requests, globally.
     Under a broad failure, retries add at most 10%, not 900%.
  4  FULL JITTER - spreads what remains
  5  LOAD SHEDDING at the target - reject early rather than queueing

THE TELL IN AN INCIDENT
  request rate to a dependency RISES while its success rate FALLS
  -> that is retry amplification, and adding capacity will not fix it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      How do you recover from a retry storm in progress?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Shed load at the entry point rather than trying to serve it — reject a percentage of traffic so the dependency can recover, then ramp back up. Adding capacity mid-storm often fails, because the retry load scales with the failure rate rather than with user demand. Circuit breakers opening is the automated version of the same move.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Does a service mesh solve this?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      It gives you the controls in one place — retry budgets, circuit breaking and timeouts as configuration rather than per-language library code — which makes them consistent and auditable. It does not decide the policy for you, and a mesh with retries enabled at every hop by default is an excellent way to build amplification without noticing.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S70
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A circuit breaker has three states. Closed is normal: calls pass through and failures are counted. Open means the failure threshold was crossed, so calls fail immediately without being attempted. Half-open is the probe: after a cooldown, a limited number of calls are allowed through to test recovery.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It protects you as much as the dependency. Without one, calls to a dead service still consume a thread and a connection for the full timeout — so an upstream outage becomes thread-pool exhaustion in your service, and then your other endpoints fail too.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What trips it should be genuine unavailability: connection failures, timeouts, 5xx. A 4xx is the caller's fault and should not open the breaker — otherwise a client sending malformed requests can trip the breaker for everyone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The three states, and what trips it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        CLOSED     normal. Calls pass, failures counted in a sliding window.
           failure rate > threshold -> OPEN

OPEN       calls FAIL IMMEDIATELY without being attempted.
           no thread held, no connection consumed, no waiting.
           after waitDuration -> HALF-OPEN

HALF-OPEN  allow N probe calls.
           all succeed -> CLOSED.   any fail -> OPEN again.

resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.partner:
  slidingWindowSize: 50
  failureRateThreshold: 50          # 50% of the last 50 calls
  slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s     # slow counts as failure
  slowCallRateThreshold: 50
  waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3
  recordExceptions: [IOException, TimeoutException]
  ignoreExceptions: [BadRequestException]   # 4xx must NOT trip it

WHAT IT PROTECTS
  the DEPENDENCY  - stops hammering something already down
  YOU             - stops burning threads waiting on it   <- the bigger win

AND ALWAYS PAIR IT WITH A FALLBACK
  an open breaker that just throws has converted a slow failure into a
  fast one. Useful, but a cached value or a degraded response is better.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What should happen when the breaker is open?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Something better than an error, if you can: a cached value, a default, a reduced feature set, or a queued request for later. An open breaker with no fallback turns a slow failure into a fast failure, which helps your threads and not your users. Designing the fallback per dependency is the actual work.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you pick the threshold and cooldown?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        From the dependency's normal behaviour. A threshold below its usual error rate opens constantly; a cooldown shorter than its typical recovery causes flapping between open and half-open. Start around a 50% failure rate over a window of several dozen calls, and a cooldown of tens of seconds — then tune from observed behaviour rather than theory.
