                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S71
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A bulkhead isolates resources so one failure cannot consume everything. Named after ship compartments: a breach floods one section rather than sinking the vessel.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The concrete version is separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency. Without it, one slow downstream consumes every thread in a shared pool, and endpoints that do not even touch that dependency start failing — including your health check, which then gets you restarted.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Load shedding is the complement: rejecting work you cannot complete, rather than accepting it and failing slowly. Shed the lowest-priority traffic first, and reject early — a fast 429 lets the caller fall back now, where a slow timeout wastes both sides' capacity.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Isolation, and priority shedding
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          WITHOUT BULKHEADS - one shared pool of 200 threads
  the partner API slows to 30s
  -> all 200 threads block on it
  -> /health, /orders, /login all fail. Kubernetes restarts healthy pods.
  -> one dependency took down the whole service

WITH BULKHEADS
  partner API   pool of 20    <- saturates, and ONLY partner calls fail
  database      pool of 50
  cache         pool of 20
  everything else keeps working, including the health check

resilience4j.bulkhead.instances.partner:
  maxConcurrentCalls: 20
  maxWaitDuration: 100ms       # fail fast rather than queue

LOAD SHEDDING - reject what you cannot complete
  priority tiers:
    interactive user traffic   shed LAST
    background / batch         shed FIRST
    health checks              NEVER shed
  reject with 429 + Retry-After, EARLY
  -> a fast rejection lets the caller fall back now
  -> a slow timeout wastes capacity on both sides

AND: keep the health endpoint on a SEPARATE connector/port with its own
threads, so saturation cannot make a healthy service look dead.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Thread-pool bulkhead or semaphore bulkhead?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A semaphore just caps concurrency on the calling thread — cheap, and it does not isolate you from a call that blocks forever. A separate thread pool genuinely isolates, at the cost of context switching and more threads. For a blocking client with an unreliable dependency, the thread pool is worth it; for a non-blocking client, a semaphore is enough.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you decide what to shed?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          By business value, decided in advance and encoded as a priority on the request. Background reindexing before a checkout; an analytics write before a payment. The decision must exist before the incident, because choosing under pressure means shedding whatever is easiest to identify rather than whatever matters least.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S72
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Graceful degradation means deciding, per dependency, what the system does when that dependency is unavailable — and deciding it before the incident rather than during it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The useful exercise is to list every dependency and write the fallback next to it. Recommendations down means show popular items. Search down means show a browsable category tree. The fraud service down is different: you must decide explicitly whether to fail open (accept the risk) or fail closed (decline the transaction), and that is a business decision, not an engineering one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The two rules that make it work: make degradation visible to the user rather than silently serving worse results, and exercise the fallback regularly, because a path that is never taken is a path that is broken.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A fallback per dependency
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            DEPENDENCY        DOWN -> WHAT HAPPENS                    FAIL OPEN/CLOSED
recommendations   show popular items                     open
search            browsable category tree                open
user avatars      initials placeholder                   open
pricing service   last known price + a notice            open, with a TTL
                                                         beyond which: closed
FRAUD CHECK       *** a business decision ***            usually CLOSED
                  accept the risk, or decline?           above a value threshold
payment gateway   queue and retry; tell the user         closed
auth service      NO fallback. Fail closed. Always.      closed

THE RULES
  1  MAKE IT VISIBLE. "Recommendations are temporarily unavailable"
     beats silently showing worse results - users forgive a stated
     degradation and lose trust in unexplained bad output.
  2  EXERCISE THE FALLBACK. A path never taken is a path that is broken.
     Force it for a small percentage of traffic, weekly.
  3  BOUND STALENESS. Serving a cached price is fine for minutes and
     not for days - past the bound, fail closed.
  4  DO NOT LET A DEGRADED DEPENDENCY FAIL YOUR HEALTH CHECK.
     Readiness should reflect "can I serve", not "is everything perfect".
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Should you fail open or fail closed?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            It depends entirely on the cost asymmetry. For fraud checking, failing open accepts fraudulent transactions and failing closed rejects legitimate ones — and which is worse depends on transaction value, so a threshold is often the right answer. The important part is that it is decided deliberately and written down, not left to whatever the code happens to do.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you test a fallback path?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Force it deliberately: a feature flag that disables a dependency for a percentage of traffic, run on a schedule. Fault injection in staging is a start, and production is where the path actually needs to work. Every organisation that first tests a fallback finds it broken — usually a missing configuration or a code path that throws.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S73
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Three signals, three jobs. Metrics are cheap aggregates you alarm on, with no per-request detail. Logs are events with arbitrary context, expensive at volume and searchable. A distributed trace is the only one that answers where did the time go across service boundaries.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              context propagation is the hard part, and where tracing usually breaks. The trace id must survive every hop — HTTP headers, message queue attributes, thread pool handoffs, async boundaries, scheduled jobs. Miss one and the trace fragments into two disconnected trees, which is worse than no tracing because it looks complete.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The multiplier is putting the trace id in every log line. Then a slow span leads to exactly the log output produced during it, and an error log leads to the full request tree. That one field costs nothing and is worth more than any of the three signals alone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Where context is lost
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              METRIC   an aggregate       cheap, alarmable, no detail
LOG      one event          expensive, searchable, high cardinality is fine
SPAN     one timed op       has a PARENT - the only signal that crosses
                            service boundaries coherently

WHERE PROPAGATION BREAKS
  thread pools        context is a thread-local and is LOST
                      -> wrap the executor
  CompletableFuture / reactive schedulers
  MESSAGE QUEUES      no HTTP headers - inject into message attributes,
                      extract on the consumer. Without this, every async
                      workflow is a set of ORPHAN traces.
  scheduled jobs      no incoming context - create a root span explicitly
  third-party clients that do not propagate

SAMPLING
  head sampling at 1% is cheap and throws away exactly the traces you want
  TAIL sampling decides AFTER the trace completes:
    keep 100% of errors, 100% over a latency threshold, 1% baseline

THE CORRELATION THAT MAKES IT WORK
  put trace.id in EVERY log line (MDC)
  -> slow span -> the exact log lines from that request
  -> error log -> the full trace
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Should every method be a span?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              No — span-per-method produces enormous traces that are harder to read than a stack trace and expensive to store. Instrument boundaries: incoming requests, outgoing calls, database queries, message publish and consume, cache operations. The goal is to see which component owns the latency, not to profile.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why do traces show gaps with no span?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Usually uninstrumented work — a thread pool that lost context, a library with no instrumentation, a queue hop never wired up. Occasionally it is real: GC pauses, CPU throttling and scheduler delay produce no span at all. Check throttling metrics alongside the trace; unexplained gaps under load are very often that.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S74
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                RED method covers request-driven services: Rate (requests per second), Errors (how many failed), Duration (how long they took, as percentiles). Three metrics per service, and they answer most questions about whether users are having a good time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                USE method covers resources: Utilisation (how busy), Saturation (how much queued work), Errors. Saturation is the one people omit and the one that predicts trouble — a queue growing is a leading indicator, where utilisation at 100% is already too late.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Together they give you the four graphs that matter: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, and saturation of your scarcest resource. If a dashboard has forty graphs and none of these, it will not help you at 3am.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The four graphs that matter
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                RED - per SERVICE (request-driven)
  Rate       requests/sec, split by endpoint
  Errors     failures/sec, and as a RATIO of rate
  Duration   p50, p95, p99 - never the average

USE - per RESOURCE (CPU, memory, disk, pool, queue)
  Utilisation  % of time busy
  SATURATION   queued work - the LEADING indicator
               (run queue, pending connections, queue depth, lag)
  Errors       disk errors, dropped packets, rejected connections

THE FOUR GRAPHS ON ONE SCREEN
  1  request rate            is the load what I expect?
  2  error RATIO             are users failing?
  3  p99 latency             are users suffering?
  4  saturation of the
     scarcest resource       am I about to fall over?

WHY SATURATION MATTERS MOST
  utilisation at 100% -> you are already in trouble
  saturation rising    -> you have minutes of warning
  e.g. hikaricp_connections_pending > 0 is a problem LONG before
       CPU or latency shows anything

GOOGLE'S FOUR GOLDEN SIGNALS
  latency, traffic, errors, saturation - the same idea, and the
  version to name if asked.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why split errors by ratio rather than count?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Because a raw count moves with traffic — 100 errors is fine at a million requests and catastrophic at two hundred. The ratio is comparable across time of day and across services, and it is what an SLO is expressed in. Keep the count for capacity reasoning and alarm on the ratio.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What saturation metric matters most for a typical JVM service?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Connection pool pending count, then thread pool queue depth. Both fill long before CPU shows anything, and both produce the classic high latency, healthy database symptom. For a consumer, queue depth or consumer lag replaces them as the primary signal.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S75
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  cardinality is the number of distinct time series a metric produces, and it is multiplicative across labels. A metric with 10 endpoints × 5 status codes × 3 regions is 150 series — fine. Add a user id and it is millions.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That is the classic monitoring outage: someone adds a useful-looking label, the metrics backend's memory grows until it dies, and you lose observability at exactly the moment you need it. The irony is that the monitoring system fails because someone tried to monitor more carefully.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The rule is that metric labels must be bounded and low-cardinality. Anything unbounded — user id, request id, full URL path, error message, customer name — belongs in logs or traces, which are designed for high cardinality.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What kills a metrics backend
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  CARDINALITY MULTIPLIES
  http_requests{endpoint, status, region}
    10 x 5 x 3 = 150 series          fine

  http_requests{endpoint, status, region, user_id}
    150 x 500,000 users = 75,000,000 series
    -> the backend dies, and you lose observability during the incident

NEVER A LABEL           PUT IT HERE INSTEAD
  user_id                 logs, traces
  request_id              logs, traces
  full URL path           templated route: /orders/{id}
  error message           logs (label with an error CLASS, not the text)
  customer name           logs
  timestamp               it is already the time axis

TEMPLATE YOUR PATHS
  /orders/12345  /orders/12346  ...      -> 1 series per order. Fatal.
  /orders/{id}                            -> 1 series

GUARDRAILS
  alert on your own series count and ingestion rate
  a shared instrumentation library with an APPROVED label set
  review new metrics in code review - it is easier than recovering

HIGH CARDINALITY BELONGS IN TRACES
  Embedded Metric Format / exemplars link a low-cardinality metric to a
  representative high-cardinality trace - the best of both.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  How do you find the metric that is killing you?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Most backends expose per-metric series counts — in Prometheus, topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})). Look for the metric with orders of magnitude more series than its neighbours; it is almost always one label added recently. Then drop the label at the scrape config to recover before fixing the code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Is high cardinality always wrong?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  In metrics, effectively yes. In traces and logs it is the point — you want per-request detail there. Purpose-built columnar observability stores handle high-cardinality events well, which is a different architecture from a time-series database. Knowing which system you are feeding is what determines the answer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S76
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Alert on symptoms, not causes. High CPU with healthy latency needs no human — the service is working and using capacity you paid for. Meanwhile a deadlocked connection pool takes you down at 5% CPU and never trips a CPU alarm. So CPU alerts produce false positives and false negatives, which is the worst combination available.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The better mechanism is burn rate against your error budget. A threshold alert on error rate above 1% fires at 3am for a two-minute blip and flaps as the metric oscillates. A burn-rate alert asks at this rate, how fast am I consuming the month? — which scales urgency to consequence.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate: a long window and a short one, ANDed. The long window establishes that it is real; the short one makes the alert fire promptly and, crucially, resolve promptly once it stops.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Burn rate alerting
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    SLO 99.9% over 30 days -> budget = 0.1% = ~43 minutes

BURN RATE = how fast you are spending it
  1x     exactly on budget, exhausted at day 30
  14.4x  2% of the budget in 1 hour -> whole month gone in ~50h  -> PAGE
  6x     10% in 6 hours                                         -> TICKET

MULTI-WINDOW (the short window makes it RESOLVE quickly too)
- alert: FastBurn
  expr: (error_ratio_1h > 14.4 * 0.001) and (error_ratio_5m > 14.4 * 0.001)
  for: 2m
  severity: page

- alert: SlowBurn
  expr: (error_ratio_6h > 6 * 0.001) and (error_ratio_30m > 6 * 0.001)
  for: 15m
  severity: ticket

CAUSE METRICS BELONG ON THE DASHBOARD, NOT IN ALERTS
  CPU, memory, queue depth, connection counts, GC time
  -> they tell you WHY once you are paged. They should not page you.

THE TEST FOR AN ALERT
  "is a human needed, RIGHT NOW, and is there a bounded action?"
  if no -> it is a ticket or a dashboard, not a page.
  Writing the runbook entry is the forcing function: an alert whose
  runbook says "investigate" is not actionable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What about a low-traffic service where ratios are noisy?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Add a minimum-volume guard to the expression, or you page on three failed health checks at 4am when the ratio hits 100%. For genuinely low-traffic services, longer windows and an absolute-count condition alongside the ratio work better — and be honest that an SLO on a service with a hundred requests a day is mostly ceremony.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How many pages per week is healthy?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Fewer than two per person. Above that, people start acknowledging without reading, and the next real page is missed. If you are above it, the fix is usually deleting alerts rather than fixing systems — most teams have several alerts that have never once led to an action.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S77
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Rolling replaces instances in batches. Cheapest — no duplicate environment — and it means both versions serve simultaneously, so the API must be backward compatible and any schema change must work for both. Rollback is another rolling deploy, so it takes as long as the deploy did.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      blue/green stands up a full parallel environment and switches at once. The advantage is genuinely instant rollback; the costs are double infrastructure during the window and the fact that stateful things do not switch cleanly — in-flight requests, sessions, and above all the shared database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      canary deployment is the only one that limits blast radius: a bad deploy affects 5% of users for five minutes rather than everyone immediately. Define the abort criteria numerically before the deploy, because a human watching a dashboard at 2am is not a control.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Three strategies, and what makes rollback real
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ROLLING     replace in batches
  cheapest; BOTH VERSIONS SERVE AT ONCE
  -> the API must be backward compatible
  rollback = another rolling deploy (as slow as the deploy)

BLUE/GREEN  full parallel environment, switch at once
  instant rollback (switch back)
  double infrastructure during the window
  in-flight requests, sessions and the DATABASE do not switch

CANARY      5% of traffic -> watch -> proceed or abort
  the ONLY one that limits blast radius
  define abort criteria NUMERICALLY, in advance:
    5xx rate > 0.5% for 2 min | p99 > 800ms | DLQ depth > 0
  bake time computed from REQUEST RATE, not a round number
  (5% for 5 minutes on a low-traffic service is a handful of requests
   and proves nothing)

*** THE HALF THAT ACTUALLY DECIDES WHETHER ROLLBACK WORKS ***
  if the deploy ran ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN, rolling back the code does
  NOT roll back the data - and the old version now queries a column that
  no longer exists.
  -> every schema change must be EXPAND-CONTRACT (next topic)
  -> without it, your rollback plan is a database restore. Hours.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Which would you choose for a payments API?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Canary with automatic rollback on alarm, plus expand-contract migrations. The blast radius limit is what matters when a bad deploy has financial consequences, and the automation matters because the decision to abort should not depend on someone noticing. Blue/green is tempting for the instant rollback and does not help if the schema has moved.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What about feature flags instead?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      They are complementary and arguably more powerful: deploy the code dark, then enable behaviour per user or percentage with no deploy at all, and roll back in seconds by flipping the flag. Use both — canary for the infrastructure change, flags for the behaviour change. The cost is flag debt, so give every flag an owner and a removal date.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S78
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A feature flag separates deploy from release. The code ships dark, and you turn it on for a percentage, a cohort, or one internal team — which makes the risky moment a configuration change you can reverse in seconds rather than a deployment.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A kill switch is the same mechanism aimed at an incident: disable an expensive feature, a failing integration, or a non-essential code path to shed load and restore the core service. It must not require a deploy, and it must be exercised regularly — a switch nobody has flipped since it was written is an untested code path.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The cost is flag debt. Every flag doubles the paths through your code, and a codebase with two hundred stale flags is untestable — the combinations are no longer enumerable. Give every flag an owner and a removal date, and treat removal as part of the work rather than as cleanup.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Types, and the debt
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        RELEASE FLAG      short-lived. Ship dark, ramp up, then DELETE.
                  lifetime: days to weeks

OPERATIONAL /     long-lived. Disable a feature under load, or when a
KILL SWITCH       dependency fails. Kept indefinitely, on purpose.

PERMISSION FLAG   long-lived by nature (entitlements, plans, beta access)

EXPERIMENT FLAG   A/B tests, with an analysis end date

THE DEBT
  200 stale flags = 2^200 code paths, none of them tested
  -> owner + removal date on every release flag
  -> a report of flags older than 90 days, reviewed
  -> removal is part of the feature, not cleanup afterwards

THE KILL SWITCH RULES
  1  a FLAG, never a deploy - it must work when CI is broken
  2  EXERCISED regularly, or it is untested code
  3  the fallback path must be visible to the user, not silent
  4  it must be usable by whoever is on call, without a code review

AND: flag evaluation must FAIL SAFE. If the flag service is unreachable,
the default must be the safe value - cached locally, not fetched on the
hot path.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Where should flags be evaluated?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Locally, from a cached ruleset refreshed in the background — never with a network call on the request path, or the flag service becomes a hard dependency of every request. And the default when the cache is empty must be the safe value, because a flag service outage should not change behaviour unpredictably.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do flags interact with schema changes?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        They pair well: the expand-contract migration makes both code versions work against the schema, and the flag controls which path is active. That gives you a reversible switch on top of a reversible schema, which is the combination that makes a risky change genuinely safe to attempt.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S79
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          expand-contract is the only migration pattern where rollback remains possible at every step, and that is what zero downtime actually requires. The failure people design around is downtime during the DDL; the failure that hurts is a deploy you cannot reverse.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Expand: add the new column as nullable, and deploy code that writes both and reads the old. Both versions now work against the schema, so rollback is free. Backfill in bounded batches, watching replication lag — never one enormous UPDATE, which holds locks, generates huge WAL and pushes replicas minutes behind.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Flip reads behind a flag, still writing both. Contract — drop the old column — only in a much later release, once you are certain you will not roll back. Collapsing contract into the first release is precisely what makes rollback impossible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Four releases, and the invariant
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          RELEASE 1 - EXPAND. Old code still works. Rollback is FREE.
  SET lock_timeout = '3s';                    -- do not queue behind a long read
  ALTER TABLE settlement ADD COLUMN currency_code char(3);  -- nullable: INSTANT
  app v2: writes BOTH, reads the OLD

RELEASE 1.5 - BACKFILL, bounded, watching lag
  UPDATE ... WHERE id >= lo AND id < hi AND currency_code IS NULL;  -- 5k rows
  COMMIT; check replica lag; pause if > 5s; sleep 50ms; repeat
  resumable from a checkpoint, and IDEMPOTENT (it WILL be interrupted)

RELEASE 2 - FLIP READS behind a flag. Old code STILL works.

RELEASE 3 - CONTRACT. Only once you will never roll back past release 2.
  ALTER TABLE settlement DROP COLUMN currency;

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ONLINE (PostgreSQL)
  ADD COLUMN nullable               instant, metadata only
  ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT const instant in PG 11+, FULL REWRITE before
  ADD CONSTRAINT                    NOT VALID, then VALIDATE separately
  CREATE INDEX                      CONCURRENTLY, or writes lock for the
                                    entire build
  DROP COLUMN                       instant

THE INVARIANT
  at EVERY point, version N-1 of the application works against the
  CURRENT schema. Rollback is therefore a CODE-ONLY operation.

AND: a migration WAITING for a lock QUEUES every query behind it.
One long-running read turns an "instant" DDL into a full outage.
-> SET lock_timeout and RETRY.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Where should migrations run in a deployment pipeline?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          As a separate step before the application rollout — a standalone job, not an init container running alongside replicas. With three replicas, three init containers race to run the same migration, which most tools serialise with an advisory lock and turn into a slow, confusing startup. One job, run once, failing loudly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What about renaming a column?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          There is no safe rename — it is expand-contract in disguise. Add the new column, dual-write, backfill, flip reads, drop the old. A direct RENAME breaks every running instance of the previous version instantly, which is exactly the irreversible change the pattern exists to avoid.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S80
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Capacity planning starts from the same estimation as any design: peak QPS, service time, and a target utilisation. Little's law gives concurrency, and the queueing curve says to size for around 70% at peak — because beyond that, latency rises hyperbolically rather than linearly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Autoscaling on CPU is the default and it is usually wrong for an IO-bound service. Such a service spends its time blocked on the database or a downstream call: under overload the thread pool fills, latency climbs, and CPU sits at 25% — so the policy never fires and the service degrades without scaling.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Scale on what actually saturates: in-flight requests, requests per second per instance, or best of all queue depth for a consumer, because that measures unprocessed work directly rather than a proxy for it. And remember that scaling takes minutes end to end, so for a spike you know the time of, pre-scale on a schedule.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The right signal, and the honest timing
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            SIZING
  peak QPS x service time = concurrency        (Little's law)
  6,000 QPS x 0.050s = 300 concurrent
  size for ~70% utilisation -> provision for ~430
  -> ~5 instances at 100 concurrent each

WHY CPU IS THE WRONG SIGNAL FOR AN IO-BOUND SERVICE
  overload: thread pool full, queue growing, p99 at 4s, users timing out
  CPU: 25%
  -> a 70% CPU target NEVER FIRES. Not misconfigured - measuring the
     wrong thing. The exhausted resource is CONCURRENCY.

SCALE ON SATURATION, best first
  queue depth / consumer lag    direct measure of unprocessed work
  in-flight requests            the thing running out
  requests/sec per instance     once you know an instance's capacity
  CPU                           only for genuinely CPU-bound work

END-TO-END SCALE-UP TIME - be honest about it
  policy reaction        15-30s
  node provisioning      60-180s
  image pull             10-40s
  JVM start + warmup     30-90s
  -----------------------------
  2-5 MINUTES

  -> for a spike you know the time of, PRE-SCALE on a schedule.
     Reactive autoscaling always lags; scheduled scaling is simply correct.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why does autoscaling oscillate?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Usually a scale-down window that is too short combined with a metric that falls as soon as capacity is added — you scale up, the metric drops, you scale down, it rises. Lengthen the scale-down stabilisation to several minutes and cap the percentage change per period. Oscillation also signals a metric that is a consequence of instance count rather than an independent measure of demand.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How much headroom should a cluster carry?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Name it in three parts rather than quoting one number: enough to lose one availability zone (roughly a third across three), enough for rolling-update surge, and enough to cover autoscaler lag. That typically lands around 55–65% steady-state utilisation — and presenting it as arithmetic rather than a number is what wins the cost conversation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S81
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Incident response has a shape worth knowing: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve, review. The important discipline is that mitigate comes before resolve — restore service first, understand it afterwards. Rolling back is usually the fastest mitigation and it eliminates a variable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Roles matter more than people expect. Someone runs the incident, someone communicates, someone investigates — and they should be different people, because the person debugging cannot also be updating stakeholders every fifteen minutes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A blameless postmortem assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew, and asks what made the failure possible. That is not politeness — it is the only way to get accurate information, because a review that assigns blame reliably produces people who omit details. Ask why was this easy to do rather than why did you do it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The review that produces change
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              SHAPE OF AN INCIDENT
  DETECT     alerting, or a user - and "how did we find out" is itself
             a finding. If a customer told you, your MTTD is the problem.
  TRIAGE     severity, roles: incident lead / comms / investigator
  MITIGATE   restore service. ROLL BACK FIRST if a deploy is implicated -
             it is fast, safe, and removes a variable.
  RESOLVE    the actual fix, afterwards, calmly
  REVIEW     blameless, within a few days

A POSTMORTEM THAT PRODUCES CHANGE
  timeline with timestamps, including WHAT PEOPLE BELIEVED at each point
  impact in USER terms, not error counts
  contributing factors, plural - never a single "root cause"
  what went WELL (so you keep doing it)
  ACTIONS with an OWNER and a DATE, tracked like tickets

QUESTIONS THAT WORK
  "what made this easy to do?"        not "who did it?"
  "what would have caught it sooner?"
  "what did we believe that was wrong?"
  "how did we find out?"              <- the detection finding

ERROR BUDGET POLICY, agreed IN ADVANCE
  budget remaining  -> ship features, take risks
  budget exhausted  -> freeze, spend the sprint on reliability
  negotiating this mid-incident is how error budgets become decorative.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why avoid the term 'root cause'?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because complex failures rarely have one. There is a chain: a missing alert, an unclear runbook, a config that defaulted badly, a review that did not catch it. Singular language makes people stop at the first plausible answer and miss the contributing factors — which are usually the cheaper things to fix.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What makes actions from a postmortem actually happen?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              An owner, a date, and tracking in the same system as normal work. Actions in a document nobody revisits are the norm, and they are why the same incident recurs. A useful discipline is reviewing the previous postmortem's actions at the start of the next one — it makes the gap visible.
