                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S82
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                chaos engineering is running controlled experiments against a real system. The feature that separates it from causing an outage is the stop condition — an alarm that aborts the experiment automatically if users are affected. Without one you are not experimenting, you are hoping.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The order matters. Start with a single instance kill and assert zero client errors. If that fails you have a graceful shutdown or draining problem, and every subsequent experiment is meaningless until it passes. It is also the most commonly failed test.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Then escalate: force a database failover and measure how long the application takes to recover — the gap between the database recovered and we recovered is the single most valuable number these exercises produce, and it is usually far worse than assumed because of DNS caching and stale connection pools.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What to inject, in order
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                RULES
  announced | business hours | a STOP CONDITION | a written HYPOTHESIS
  per step, so the experiment can FAIL rather than be a demonstration

1  KILL ONE INSTANCE            H: zero client errors
   fails? -> graceful shutdown / connection draining problem.
   Everything after this is meaningless until it passes.

2  FORCE A DATABASE FAILOVER    H: application recovers within 120s
   THE MOST VALUABLE NUMBER: the gap between "the database recovered"
   and "WE recovered". Usually far worse than assumed:
     cached DNS resolution + a pool holding sockets to a dead instance
     -> a 90-second failover becomes a ten-minute outage

3  INJECT 200ms DOWNSTREAM LATENCY
   H: the circuit breaker opens BEFORE the caller times out
   looking for a badly NESTED timeout budget

4  THROTTLE A DEPENDENCY        H: retries back off with jitter and a cap
   unjittered retries turn a brief throttle into a sustained one

5  EVACUATE AN AVAILABILITY ZONE
   did topology spread ACTUALLY spread you? is n-1 capacity real?

ALWAYS START WITH A HYPOTHESIS YOU EXPECT TO HOLD.
  The purpose is EVIDENCE that the system behaves as designed.
  An experiment you expect to fail is not an experiment - fix the
  known problem first.

A REAL INCIDENT DURING A GAME DAY IS A SUCCESS: you found a genuine
failure under controlled conditions with the right people watching.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How do you get permission to do this in production?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Start small and show results. The single-instance kill is nearly risk-free with a stop condition and either proves resilience or finds a real bug cheaply. Present the measured numbers — we recover from an instance loss in four seconds with zero errors builds far more confidence than an argument. Escalate as trust accumulates.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Which experiments should recur rather than run once?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Anything protecting a property that can regress silently: the instance kill (graceful shutdown breaks whenever someone edits a deployment), the database failover (pool and driver settings drift), and the zone evacuation. Run them on a schedule and treat a newly failing experiment exactly like a failing test — because that is what it is.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S83
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The honest position: start with a monolith, and specifically a modular monolith with enforced internal boundaries. Microservices solve an organisational problem — many teams deploying independently — and they cost you distributed transactions, network failure, and operational surface you did not previously have.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A modular monolith gets you most of the architectural benefit: clear boundaries, separate schemas per module, no cross-module database access, communication through defined interfaces. And you keep transactions, joins, one deployment and one place to debug.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  When you do split, use the strangler fig: route one capability at a time to a new service while the monolith keeps serving everything else, until nothing is left. A big-bang rewrite of a working system is the single most reliable way to spend two years and ship nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The path, and the tell for each direction
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  MONOLITH -> MODULAR MONOLITH -> SELECTIVE EXTRACTION

MODULAR MONOLITH - do this first, it is cheap
  separate schema per module; NO cross-module table access
  communication through interfaces, not shared tables
  enforce it: ArchUnit tests, or Java modules, or separate Gradle modules
  -> you get boundaries WITHOUT the network

EXTRACT A SERVICE WHEN ONE IS TRUE
  a different scaling profile   (video transcoding vs the API)
  a different team owns it and deploy contention is real
  a different technology is genuinely required
  a compliance boundary demands isolation
  the module is stable and its interface has not changed in months

DO NOT EXTRACT BECAUSE
  "microservices are best practice"
  the codebase feels large
  you want to try a new language

STRANGLER FIG
  put a facade in front, route ONE capability to the new service,
  verify, repeat. The monolith shrinks. Rollback is a routing change.

THE HONEST COSTS OF A SPLIT
  no distributed transactions -> sagas and compensation
  every call can fail, be slow, or arrive twice
  debugging needs distributed tracing you must now build
  N deploy pipelines, N on-call rotations, N sets of dashboards
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What are the three signs a split was wrong?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  You cannot deploy the two services independently — a change always requires both. They share a database. And a single user action fans out into a long synchronous chain across them. Any one means the boundary is in the wrong place, and the honest answer is often to merge them back rather than to add more machinery.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Is 'distributed monolith' a real thing?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Yes, and it is the worst outcome: services that must be deployed together, share a database, and call each other synchronously in long chains. You have taken on every cost of distribution and kept every constraint of the monolith. It usually comes from splitting along technical layers rather than business capabilities.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S84
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A bounded context is a boundary within which terms have one consistent meaning. Customer in billing (a payment method and an address) is not customer in support (a ticket history) or in shipping (a delivery address). Forcing one shared model across all three produces an object with forty fields that nobody owns.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    That is why bounded contexts are the strongest guide to service boundaries: the boundary goes where the language changes. If two teams use the same word differently, that is a seam.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    An aggregate is the unit of change and the boundary of a transaction: one root entity is the only entry point, invariants hold inside it, and you modify one aggregate per transaction. Getting aggregates right is what makes keep the transaction local achievable rather than aspirational.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Contexts, aggregates and the transaction boundary
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    THE SAME WORD, THREE MEANINGS
  BILLING    Customer = payment methods, billing address, tax status
  SUPPORT    Customer = tickets, satisfaction, contact history
  SHIPPING   Customer = delivery addresses, preferences

  A single shared Customer with 40 fields is owned by nobody and
  changed by everyone. The boundary goes WHERE THE LANGUAGE CHANGES.

AGGREGATE - the unit of change
  Order (root) -> OrderLine, ShippingAddress
    external code holds a reference to the ORDER, never to an OrderLine
    invariants (total = sum of lines) hold INSIDE the aggregate
    ONE aggregate per transaction

  -> if two things must change atomically, they belong in ONE aggregate
  -> if they can be eventually consistent, they are SEPARATE aggregates
     and you connect them with an event

  This is the design decision that determines whether you need
  distributed transactions. Get it right and you do not.

UBIQUITOUS LANGUAGE
  the code uses the words the domain experts use. If they say
  "settlement" and the class is called TransactionBatch, every
  conversation costs a translation - and translations lose things.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How do you find bounded contexts in an existing system?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Listen for the same word meaning different things, and for the places where a change always requires two teams to agree. Event storming — putting domain events on a wall in time order — surfaces them quickly, because clusters of events with shared vocabulary reveal themselves visually. It is also a fast way to find where nobody knows who owns something.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What is a context map?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A description of how bounded contexts relate: shared kernel, customer-supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer. The useful one is the anti-corruption layer — a translation shim so a legacy or third-party model does not leak into yours. Naming it signals you have integrated with something you did not control.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S85
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Boundaries follow business capabilities, not technical layers. A Payments service that owns its data and logic is a boundary; a Data Access Service called by everyone is a layer masquerading as a service, and it makes every feature require two deployments.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The practical test: could this team ship a feature without coordinating with another team? If almost every change touches two services, the boundary is in the wrong place — you have split something that should be together.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      And the second test: what data must change atomically? If two services must both update for a single business operation to be correct, either they should be one service, or that operation genuinely tolerates eventual consistency. Those are the only two answers.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The three signs a split was wrong
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      1  YOU CANNOT DEPLOY THEM INDEPENDENTLY
     every change requires both, released together
     -> the boundary is in the wrong place

2  THEY SHARE A DATABASE
     then they are one service with extra network hops.
     Shared tables mean you cannot change a schema without coordinating,
     which is exactly what the split was meant to avoid.

3  A SINGLE USER ACTION FANS OUT INTO A LONG SYNCHRONOUS CHAIN
     A -> B -> C -> D, all blocking
     availability multiplies (4 x 99.9% = 99.6%)
     latency adds
     -> either merge, or make the chain asynchronous

GOOD BOUNDARY                    BAD BOUNDARY
Payments, Inventory, Shipping    DataAccessService, ValidationService
(business capabilities)          (technical layers)
owns its data AND its logic      owns data OR logic, never both
a team can ship without          every feature touches three services
  coordinating

THE QUESTIONS THAT DECIDE IT
  "could this team ship a feature alone?"
  "what must change ATOMICALLY?"  -> that is one aggregate, one service
  "who gets paged when this breaks?" -> if the answer is "it depends",
                                        ownership is unclear
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      How big should a service be?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Big enough to own a business capability end to end, small enough for one team to hold in their head. One team is the better constraint than any line count — and if a team owns six tiny services that always change together, that is one service badly split, not six well-factored ones.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What if you get the boundary wrong?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Merge them back. That is a normal, healthy outcome and it is far cheaper than living with a bad split. The reason people resist is that merging feels like admitting failure — but boundaries are hypotheses, and the whole argument for a modular monolith first is that moving a boundary inside one deployable is nearly free.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S86
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Synchronous calls are simple to reason about and they couple availability: your service is only as available as the product of everything it calls, and latency adds up the chain. Asynchronous messaging decouples both — the producer does not wait and does not care whether the consumer is up.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The decision rule is: does the caller need the result to respond? If yes, synchronous. If it is a side effect — send a notification, update a projection, reindex, emit an audit record — make it asynchronous, and your latency and availability both improve immediately.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The chatty chain is the anti-pattern to name: A calls B calls C calls D, all synchronous. Latency adds, availability multiplies, and a slowdown anywhere propagates everywhere. Fix by collapsing the chain, fanning out in parallel, or making the tail asynchronous.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The chain, and how to fix it
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SYNCHRONOUS CHAIN
  A -> B -> C -> D
  latency      50 + 80 + 120 + 90 = 340ms, and the p99s compound
  availability 0.999^4 = 99.6%  (35 hours/year)
  a slowdown in D backs up through C, B and A

FIX 1 - PARALLELISE what is independent
  A calls B, C, D concurrently -> latency = max(80,120,90) = 120ms
  availability is unchanged, but the latency problem is solved

FIX 2 - MAKE THE TAIL ASYNCHRONOUS
  A -> B (sync, needed for the response)
  A -> queue -> C, D (async side effects)
  -> latency 130ms, and C and D being down does not fail the request

FIX 3 - COLLAPSE
  if A always calls B and cannot function without it, they may be
  one service that was split badly

THE RULE
  "does the caller need this to respond?"
    yes -> synchronous
    no  -> event or queue

  side effects that people wrongly make synchronous:
  notifications, audit logs, search indexing, analytics, cache warming,
  webhook delivery, recommendation updates
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Is asynchronous always better?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        No — it costs you a lot: eventual consistency, harder debugging, message ordering concerns, idempotency requirements, and a queue to operate. For a call whose result you need to respond, synchronous is simpler and correct. The mistake is making side effects synchronous, not making genuine dependencies synchronous.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you make a synchronous chain resilient without redesigning it?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Timeouts that nest, a circuit breaker per dependency with a defined fallback, and bulkheads so one slow dependency cannot consume the whole thread pool. That converts a hard dependency into a soft one, which raises your availability ceiling above the product of the chain — the only way that arithmetic works in your favour.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S87
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Event notification is a thin message: order 123 changed. Consumers call back for detail. It keeps the event small and recreates coupling — every consumer must call the producer, and they all do it at once, at the moment it published.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          event-carried state transfer puts the data in the event. Consumers need no callback, they can build local read models, and the producer sees no load spike. The cost is a larger event and a schema that is now a public contract you must evolve carefully.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The practical guidance: carry the fields consumers actually need, not the entire aggregate. A thin event forces a load spike and coupling; a fat event that dumps your internal model leaks your schema into a contract. Design the event shape deliberately, versioned, as an API in its own right.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Three event shapes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          EVENT NOTIFICATION       { "type":"OrderPlaced", "orderId":"123" }
  + tiny, and the schema barely changes
  - every consumer CALLS BACK -> coupling recreated, and a load spike
    on the producer at the exact moment it published

EVENT-CARRIED STATE      { "type":"OrderPlaced", "orderId":"123",
                           "customerId":"c-9", "totalMinor":4250,
                           "currency":"GBP", "lines":[...] }
  + no callback; consumers build local read models; producer sees no spike
  - larger; the schema is a PUBLIC CONTRACT now
  -> the usual right answer

EVENT SOURCING           the event log IS the source of truth
  a different thing entirely - see the next topic

DESIGN THE EVENT AS AN API
  version it | add fields additively | NEVER remove or repurpose one
  include an eventId (the consumer's idempotency key)
  include the aggregate version, so consumers can detect gaps and order
  do NOT dump your internal model - that leaks your schema into a contract

  { "eventId":"...", "type":"OrderPlaced", "version":"1.2",
    "occurredAt":"...", "aggregateId":"123", "aggregateVersion":7,
    "data": { ... } }
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you evolve an event schema safely?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Additive changes only: new optional fields, never removing or repurposing an existing one. Consumers must ignore unknown fields. When a breaking change is genuinely needed, publish both versions in parallel until every consumer has migrated — which requires knowing who your consumers are, and that is an argument for a schema registry.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What if an event is too large?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Publish a reference plus the commonly-needed fields, and let consumers fetch the rest — the claim-check pattern, where the payload goes to object storage and the event carries a pointer. That keeps the broker efficient while avoiding the load spike of a purely thin event, and it is the standard answer for events carrying documents or media.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CQRS separates the write model from the read model, so each can be shaped for its job — a normalised transactional model for writes, denormalised projections for reads. It does not require event sourcing, and conflating them is the most common misunderstanding.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            event sourcing makes the event log the source of truth: you store every credit and debit and derive the balance, rather than storing the balance. That gives you a complete audit history, temporal queries (what was this on 3 March), and the ability to build a new read model retroactively over all history.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Be precise about the three real costs, because that is what an interviewer is checking. Schema evolution forever — every event ever written must remain readable by every future version. Projection rebuild cost grows with history, so snapshots become mandatory. And no ad-hoc queries over current state unless a projection exists for it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            When it earns its cost
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CQRS alone - no event sourcing required
  writes -> normalised model
  reads  -> denormalised projections, updated async
  + each optimised independently; read scaling is trivial
  - eventual consistency between them, and the UI must handle it

EVENT SOURCING
  events for account ACC-123:
    { seq:1, AccountOpened,     2024-01-04 }
    { seq:2, FundsCredited,     +250000    }
    { seq:3, FeeCharged,          -1250    }
    { seq:4, SettlementPaidOut, -200000    }
  balance(t) = fold(events where at <= t)   <- temporal query, FREE
  audit trail = the log itself              <- not a separate table

THE THREE COSTS - state these
  1  SCHEMA EVOLUTION FOREVER. Every event ever written must stay
     readable. Upcasting v1 -> v2 -> v3 is permanent work.
  2  PROJECTION REBUILD grows with history -> snapshots are mandatory
       { accountId, upToSeq: 48210, balanceMinor: 48750 }
  3  NO AD-HOC SQL over current state unless a projection exists.
     Every new question may need a new projection.

WHERE IT IS RIGHT
  the history IS the product: a ledger, a balance, a dispute trail
  -> you were going to build an append-only audit anyway

WHERE IT IS NOT
  everything else. Applying it uniformly is the mistake.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you fix a bug that wrote incorrect events?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            You do not edit the log — that destroys the property you adopted it for. Write compensating events that correct the effect, exactly as a ledger writes reversing entries, and rebuild the projections. If the events are genuinely malformed rather than merely wrong, version the event type and upcast the bad ones on read.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Can you use CQRS without eventual consistency?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Yes, if the read model is updated in the same transaction as the write — a materialised view, or a projection table written alongside. You lose independent scaling of the read side but keep strong consistency. That middle ground is underused and is often the right answer when the UI cannot tolerate reading its own write late.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S89
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Once events cross team boundaries the schema is a public contract, and a schema registry enforces that mechanically rather than by convention — a producer literally cannot publish a schema that breaks the compatibility rule.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Backward compatible means new consumers can read old data — you may add optional fields and remove fields. Forward compatible means old consumers can read new data — you may add optional fields but not remove them. Full is both, and it is what you want when producers and consumers deploy independently in any order.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The practical rules follow: add fields as optional with defaults, never remove or repurpose a field, never change a type, and never reuse a field name for a different meaning. When a genuinely breaking change is needed, publish a new version alongside and retire the old only when every consumer has moved — which means knowing who they are.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Compatibility, and the rules that follow
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              BACKWARD   new consumer reads OLD data
  -> you may ADD optional fields, and REMOVE fields
  -> upgrade CONSUMERS first

FORWARD    old consumer reads NEW data
  -> you may ADD optional fields, but NOT remove
  -> upgrade PRODUCERS first

FULL       both. Deploy order does not matter.
  -> what you want when teams deploy independently

THE RULES
  add fields as OPTIONAL with a default          safe
  remove a field                                 breaks forward compat
  rename a field                                 = remove + add. BREAKING.
  change a type (int -> string)                  BREAKING
  reuse a name for a new meaning                 the worst one - it does
                                                 not error, it silently
                                                 misinterprets

A BREAKING CHANGE, done properly
  publish v2 ALONGSIDE v1
  consumers migrate at their own pace
  retire v1 only when every consumer has moved
  -> which requires KNOWING your consumers. The registry tells you.

AND: consumers MUST ignore unknown fields. A consumer that rejects
an unrecognised field makes every additive change breaking.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Avro and Protobuf are compact, strongly typed, and have well-defined evolution rules — good for high-volume internal streams. JSON Schema is more readable and easier to debug, at the cost of size. The important decision is not the format but that compatibility is enforced in CI rather than reviewed by humans.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What if a consumer needs a breaking change immediately?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Publish both versions in parallel and let them migrate — that is the whole point of the pattern. If the producer cannot afford to maintain two, the honest conversation is that the consumer's requirement is imposing a cost on the producer, and someone has to own that. Silently breaking consumers to avoid the conversation is how event-driven architectures lose trust.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S90
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Service discovery answers where is service B right now. Client-side discovery means the client queries a registry and picks an instance; server-side means it calls a stable address and something else routes. DNS-based discovery is the common middle ground and is what most orchestrators give you.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Configuration management is the related problem: values that differ per environment, and secrets that must not be in the image. The rules are one image promoted unchanged across environments, configuration injected at runtime, and secrets from a real secret store rather than environment variables baked at build time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A service mesh moves cross-cutting network concerns out of application code: mutual TLS between every service without touching a single codebase, retries and circuit breaking as configuration, traffic splitting for canaries, and consistent telemetry from both sides of every call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What a mesh gives you, and what it costs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                WITHOUT A MESH                    WITH A MESH
name resolution + L4 balancing    + mTLS everywhere, certs rotated,
  (DNS + the orchestrator)          ZERO application changes
retry/timeout/CB in each          + the same policy across every language
  language's own library
canary by replica-count ratio     + traffic split by weight or header
instrument each service           + golden signals for every service PAIR
per-connection balancing          + PER-REQUEST balancing
  (gRPC and keep-alive SKEW)        (fixes the gRPC skew properly)

THE COST - state it honestly
  ~50-100 MB and some CPU per pod for a sidecar (x 500 pods = real capacity)
  two extra hops per call, low single-digit ms
  a control plane to operate and upgrade
  debugging is HARDER before it is easier: app? sidecar? policy? control plane?

THE DECISION RULE
  need mTLS everywhere / uniform policy across many languages -> mesh
  need canaries only            -> progressive delivery tooling
  need tracing and metrics only -> OpenTelemetry, far cheaper
  fewer than ~15 services, one language -> a resilience library

  sidecar-free modes (eBPF dataplanes, ambient) remove most of the
  per-pod overhead and are worth naming as the current alternative.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Would you adopt a mesh for observability alone?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                No — OpenTelemetry gives you traces and metrics at a fraction of the operational cost, with an agent that needs no code change. A mesh earns its keep when you need mTLS everywhere or uniform traffic policy across many services and languages. Adopting one for dashboards is paying a large recurring cost for something available cheaply.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How does configuration reach a service safely?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                One image, promoted unchanged; configuration injected at runtime from the environment or a mounted file; secrets from a secret manager via a workload identity, never baked in and never in environment variables set at build time. And configuration changes should trigger a visible rollout rather than silently mutating a running fleet — hashing the config into the deployment is the usual trick.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S91
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The Richardson Maturity Model is a useful vocabulary and most production APIs sit at level 2 — resources, correct verbs, correct status codes — which is the pragmatic sweet spot. Level 3 hypermedia is rarely worth it outside genuinely long-lived public APIs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Model resources, not actions. POST /orders/123/cancel is a common and defensible compromise for an operation that is not a CRUD verb; a whole API of /doThing endpoints is level 0 with JSON, and you lose caching, idempotency semantics and meaningful status codes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  For versioning: URI versioning (/v1/orders) is ugly and unambiguous and by far the easiest to operate — it is visible in logs, routable, and cacheable. Header-based versioning is purer and harder to debug. The more important discipline is avoiding breaking changes at all, so most versions are never needed.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Verbs, status codes, versioning
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  RESOURCES, NOT ACTIONS
  GET    /orders?status=pending&page=...    list
  POST   /orders                            create  -> 201 + Location
  GET    /orders/123                        read
  PATCH  /orders/123                        partial update
  DELETE /orders/123                        -> 204
  POST   /orders/123/cancel                 a defensible compromise for a
                                            non-CRUD operation

IDEMPOTENCY OF VERBS - a real contract, not trivia
  GET, PUT, DELETE   idempotent -> safe for a client to retry
  POST               NOT idempotent -> needs an Idempotency-Key header

STATUS CODES THAT CARRY MEANING
  200 / 201 + Location / 202 Accepted (async) / 204
  400 malformed | 401 unauthenticated | 403 unauthorised
  404 | 409 conflict | 412 precondition failed | 422 semantically invalid
  429 + Retry-After | 503 + Retry-After

VERSIONING
  /v1/orders          visible in logs, routable, cacheable. Use this.
  Accept: v=1         purer, harder to debug and to route
  BEST: avoid breaking changes - add optional fields, never remove one.
        Most APIs need far fewer versions than they create.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  When would you version at all?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  When a change cannot be made additively — removing a field, changing a type, changing the meaning of a value. Everything else should be an additive change with clients ignoring what they do not recognise. A new version is a migration cost for every consumer, so the bar should be high.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Why does 202 Accepted matter?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Because it is the honest response for work that will not complete within the request. Returning 200 for something still in progress forces clients to guess, and holding the connection open converts your capacity problem into their timeout. A 202 with a status URL is a contract that says accepted, not finished, and it is what makes an async API legible.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S92
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Pagination should default to keyset rather than offset for anything that grows: constant cost per page, and stable under concurrent inserts. Return an opaque cursor the client passes back, and cap the page size server-side so a client cannot request a million rows.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Partial updates: PATCH with a merge document is the pragmatic choice, and the trap is distinguishing field absent from field set to null. JSON Merge Patch treats null as delete; if you need both meanings, use JSON Patch or a distinct sentinel — and document which you chose.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Errors deserve a consistent machine-readable shape, and RFC 7807 gives you one for free. A stable type URI is the field that matters: clients switch on it, so it must not change even when the human-readable message does.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Cursor, patch and error contracts
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    PAGINATION - keyset by default
  GET /orders?limit=20
  { "data": [...],
    "next": "eyJjcmVhdGVkQXQiOiIyMDI2LTA4LTMwVDEwOjAwOjAwWiIsImlkIjo5MX0" }
  GET /orders?limit=20&cursor=eyJj...

  cursor is OPAQUE (base64 of the sort key + filters + direction)
  -> you can change the encoding later
  -> sign it, and a client cannot craft one that scans arbitrary ranges
  cap limit server-side. Always.

PARTIAL UPDATE
  PATCH /orders/123
  { "note": null }
    JSON Merge Patch: null means DELETE the field
    if you need "set to null" AND "leave alone", use JSON Patch:
      [{ "op":"replace", "path":"/note", "value":null }]
  Document which you implement. Ambiguity here causes real data loss.

ERRORS - RFC 7807
  HTTP/1.1 422
  Content-Type: application/problem+json
  { "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
    "title": "Insufficient funds",
    "status": 422,
    "detail": "Balance 4250 is less than the requested 10000",
    "instance": "/orders/123",
    "balanceMinor": 4250 }            <- extension members are allowed

  the TYPE URI is the stable, machine-readable part.
  Clients switch on it - so it must not change when the wording does.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Should errors include a request id?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Yes — an extension member carrying the trace id, so a user can quote it in a support ticket and you can find the exact request. It costs one field and it turns it failed this morning into a one-second lookup. Return it on success too, in a header.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How do you handle validation errors with many fields?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    An extension member holding an array of per-field problems, each with a field pointer and its own type URI. One 422 with a list beats returning the first error and making the user resubmit repeatedly — and the pointer format should be JSON Pointer so nested fields are addressable.
