                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S93
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Any write endpoint a client might retry needs an idempotency key, because a timeout is precisely the case where the client cannot tell whether the first attempt succeeded. Without one, the only safe behaviours are to give up or to double-charge.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The contract: the client generates a key per logical operation and sends it as a header. The server claims it with an atomic conditional write before doing the work, and a repeat of the same key returns the original response rather than a conflict — otherwise a retrying client still cannot distinguish success from failure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two details that make it correct. Store the response so the repeat can return it. And bound the record with a TTL, which also bounds the guarantee — state the deduplication window explicitly, because a retry after it expires will be processed again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The full contract
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      CLIENT
  POST /payments
  Idempotency-Key: 7f3a-4b21-...        one key per LOGICAL operation
                                         (regenerated only for a new payment,
                                          reused for every retry of this one)

SERVER
  1  claim atomically, BEFORE the work
       INSERT INTO idempotency (key, request_hash, status)
       VALUES (?, ?, 'IN_PROGRESS')     -- UNIQUE constraint on key
     duplicate key -> go to 4

  2  do the work

  3  store the response body and status against the key

  4  on a repeat: return the STORED response, same status code
     -> a retrying client sees success, not a conflict

EDGE CASES THAT MATTER
  same key, DIFFERENT request body  -> 422. The client has a bug, and
                                       silently returning the old response
                                       would hide it. Compare a hash.
  concurrent duplicate, still       -> 409 with Retry-After, or wait
    IN_PROGRESS                        briefly and return the result
  TTL                               -> 24h to 30 days. This BOUNDS THE
                                       GUARANTEE - state the window.

WHERE IT IS NOT NEEDED
  naturally idempotent operations: PUT that sets an absolute value,
  DELETE. If you can express the write as "make the world look like
  this" rather than "apply this change", you get it for free.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Who generates the key?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The client, because only it knows which retries belong to the same logical operation. A server-generated key cannot work — the client would have to receive it first, which is exactly the round trip that failed. A UUID per user action, reused across every retry of that action, is the standard.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What if the client sends the same key for a genuinely different request?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Reject with 422 after comparing a hash of the request body. Returning the old response would silently discard a real payment, which is far worse than an error. The hash comparison is cheap and it catches the common bug of a client reusing a key across operations.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S94
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        gRPC wins for internal service-to-service traffic: a binary format that is much smaller and faster to parse than JSON, generated clients in every language, streaming, and deadline propagation built into the protocol. It costs you human-readable traffic, browser support without a proxy, and per-connection load balancing problems.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        GraphQL wins where clients have diverse needs — a mobile app on a slow connection fetching three screens in one call, without you building a BFF per client. It costs you caching (every query is a POST with a different body), and it hands query complexity to the client, which is a real availability risk.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        REST remains the right default for public APIs: cacheable, debuggable with curl, universally understood, and it works with every proxy and gateway. The strongest answer names the workload rather than the technology — internal high-volume, diverse clients, or public — and picks accordingly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Choosing, and what each costs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        REST      public APIs, cacheable, debuggable, universally understood
  cost: over-fetching and under-fetching; N+1 across resources

gRPC      internal service-to-service, high volume
  + binary, small, fast to parse; generated clients; streaming
  + DEADLINES propagate in the protocol
  cost: not human-readable; needs a proxy for browsers;
        PER-CONNECTION load balancing SKEWS badly (one HTTP/2 connection
        multiplexes everything, so a client pins to one backend)
        -> needs client-side balancing or an L7 proxy

GraphQL   diverse clients, one round trip, no BFF per client
  cost: HTTP CACHING IS LOST (POST, different body every time)
        N+1 IN RESOLVERS -> needs DataLoader batching
        the CLIENT controls query cost -> depth and complexity limits are
        mandatory, or a crafted query takes the service down
        authorisation must be per FIELD, not per endpoint

THE HONEST ANSWER
  internal, high volume, one org        -> gRPC
  public, cacheable, third parties      -> REST
  many clients with diverging needs     -> GraphQL, or REST + a BFF
  and most real estates use two of them
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What is the biggest operational surprise with gRPC?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Load balancing. A single HTTP/2 connection multiplexes every request, so a connection-level balancer pins a client to one backend and traffic skews badly — adding replicas does not help. You need client-side load balancing against a headless service, or an L7 proxy that balances per request. It catches people moving from REST.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you stop a GraphQL query from taking your service down?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Query depth limits, a complexity budget scored per field, persisted queries (clients send a hash of a pre-approved query rather than arbitrary text), and per-client rate limiting weighted by cost. Without those, a client can request a deeply nested expansion that fans out into millions of resolver calls.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S95
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Sessions keep state server-side: revocation is instant, and every request needs a lookup. JWT carries signed claims: no lookup, scales infinitely, and revocation is hard because the token is valid until it expires.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The standard compromise resolves that: a short-lived access token (5–15 minutes) that needs no lookup, plus a long-lived refresh token whose validity is checked against a store. You get a cheap request path and revocation that takes effect within one access-token lifetime.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          For authorisation: RBAC assigns permissions to roles and roles to users — simple, and it explodes combinatorially when rules depend on context. ABAC evaluates attributes of user, resource, action and environment, which expresses a manager may approve expenses in their own department under £5,000 without inventing a role per department and threshold.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The token compromise, and RBAC vs ABAC
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          SESSION            server-side state
  + instant revocation, small requests
  - a lookup per request; a shared store on the hot path

JWT                signed claims, no lookup
  + stateless, scales infinitely
  - REVOCATION IS HARD; every request carries it; key rotation must be
    planned (JWKS); the payload is READABLE - signed, not encrypted,
    so never put secrets in it

THE HYBRID - what most real systems do
  access token   5-15 min, JWT, NO lookup           -> cheap requests
  refresh token  long-lived, CHECKED against a store -> revocation works
                                                        within one lifetime

AUTHORISATION
  RBAC   user -> role -> permissions
         simple, auditable; EXPLODES when rules are contextual
         ("manager_of_dept_7_under_5000" is a smell)
  ABAC   decide from attributes:
         subject.dept == resource.dept
           AND subject.role == 'manager'
           AND resource.amount < 5000
         expressive; harder to audit ("who can do X?" needs evaluation)

  practical: RBAC for coarse access, ABAC/policy for fine-grained rules.

AND: AUTHORISATION BELONGS IN THE SERVICE.
  the gateway checks the token is VALID; only the service knows whether
  THIS user may see THIS record.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Where should the JWT be stored in a browser?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          An httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie — not localStorage, which is readable by any script and therefore one XSS away from token theft. The cookie needs CSRF protection (SameSite plus a token for state-changing requests), which is a well-understood trade against a vulnerability class that is not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A denylist of revoked token ids checked on each request — which reintroduces the lookup you were avoiding, though only for the denylist rather than the full session. In practice, short access-token lifetimes plus refresh-token revocation is the usual answer, and you accept a bounded window. For immediate global revocation, rotate the signing key.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            JWKS is what makes key rotation practical: the issuer publishes its public keys at a well-known endpoint, each with a key id, and the token header names which key signed it. Verifiers fetch and cache the set, so a new key is picked up automatically.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Rotation is therefore an overlap, not a switch: publish the new key alongside the old, start signing with the new one, and only remove the old after every outstanding token signed with it has expired. Removing it immediately invalidates every token in flight.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The blast radius of a compromised signing key is total — anyone holding it can mint tokens for any user. That is why the private key lives in a KMS or HSM and is never in application memory, why rotation should be routine rather than exceptional, and why short token lifetimes matter as a containment measure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Rotation, and blast radius
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            JWKS
  GET /.well-known/jwks.json
  { "keys": [ { "kid":"2026-08", "kty":"RSA", "n":"...", "use":"sig" },
              { "kid":"2026-05", "kty":"RSA", "n":"...", "use":"sig" } ] }
  token header: { "alg":"RS256", "kid":"2026-08" }
  -> verifier picks the key by kid; caches the set; refetches on an
     unknown kid (with rate limiting, or an attacker forces refetches)

ROTATION IS AN OVERLAP, NOT A SWITCH
  1  publish the new key alongside the old (verifiers now accept both)
  2  wait for caches to refresh
  3  START SIGNING with the new key
  4  wait for every token signed with the old to EXPIRE
  5  remove the old key
  -> skipping step 4 invalidates every token in flight

BLAST RADIUS OF A COMPROMISED SIGNING KEY
  TOTAL. Anyone holding it mints tokens for ANY user, and your systems
  accept them. It is indistinguishable from legitimate traffic.
  -> private key in a KMS/HSM, never in application memory
  -> rotation ROUTINE, so an emergency rotation is a rehearsed path
  -> short token lifetimes, so revoking the key contains it quickly
  -> alg pinned server-side: NEVER trust the token's own alg header
     (the "alg: none" and RS256->HS256 confusion attacks)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What is the alg confusion attack?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A verifier that trusts the token's own alg header can be tricked: set alg: none and drop the signature, or set HS256 and sign with the public RSA key as the HMAC secret, which the server then verifies successfully. The fix is to pin the expected algorithm server-side and ignore the header's claim. Most modern libraries do this, and it is worth verifying.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How often should you rotate signing keys?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Routinely — quarterly is common — precisely so the path is exercised. A key that has never been rotated means an emergency rotation will be the first attempt, under pressure, with unknown consumers holding cached key sets. The cadence matters less than the fact that it is a normal operation rather than an incident.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S97
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Secrets must not live in images, in environment variables set at build time, or in a repository. They live in a secret manager and are fetched at runtime through a workload identity — so nothing long-lived exists to leak, and rotation happens outside the application.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              For data at rest, envelope encryption is the standard pattern: the KMS issues a data key in plaintext and encrypted form, you encrypt locally with the plaintext key and discard it, and store the encrypted key alongside the ciphertext. Large payloads never transit the KMS, so cost scales with operations rather than volume.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The control that matters is the key policy: it is the root of trust for the key, so revoking access there makes every ciphertext undecryptable immediately — a real revocation rather than a request. And multi-region keys must exist before a cross-region copy is made, or your DR region decrypts nothing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Envelope encryption, and the operational traps
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              ENCRYPT
  GenerateDataKey -> plaintext key + ENCRYPTED key
  encrypt your data LOCALLY with the plaintext key
  SCRUB the plaintext from memory
  store the ENCRYPTED key beside the ciphertext

DECRYPT
  send the encrypted key back -> plaintext -> decrypt locally

WHY
  large payloads never transit the KMS -> cost scales with OPERATIONS
  the master key never leaves the HSM -> its material cannot be exfiltrated
  revoking the KEY POLICY makes every ciphertext undecryptable
    -> a REAL control, not a theoretical one

IN TRANSIT
  TLS 1.2 minimum, managed certificates, HSTS
  mutual TLS for partner integrations and, via a mesh, service-to-service

SECRETS
  a secret manager + workload identity. Never in an image, never in a
  build-time environment variable, never in git (history is permanent).
  rotation must be CONSUMED: a pool holding credentials from startup
  keeps the old password until connections recycle -> bound maxLifetime.

TRAPS
  KMS request QUOTAS - a high-volume service calling Decrypt per request
    will throttle -> data key caching, bounded by age and use count
  MULTI-REGION KEYS must exist BEFORE the cross-region copy is made
  ENCRYPTION CONTEXT - bind purpose/tenant to the ciphertext; decryption
    fails unless it matches, and it appears in audit logs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What is the most common real-world secret leak?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Not cryptography — it is an exposed diagnostic endpoint printing the whole configuration, or a secret committed to git and rotated but never purged from history, or a log line that includes a request body. The controls that matter most are keeping the management endpoint off any public path and scanning both commits and logs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Does encryption at rest protect against a compromised application?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              No, and it is worth being precise. It protects against offline access — a stolen disk, a leaked backup, a decommissioned drive. An application with valid credentials decrypts transparently, so a compromised service reads everything it is authorised to read. The control for that is least privilege and audit, not encryption.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S98
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Multi-tenancy has three shapes. Silo gives each tenant its own infrastructure — strongest isolation, simplest compliance story, and it does not scale operationally past a few dozen tenants. Pool shares everything with a tenant id on every row — cheapest and most efficient, and one bug leaks data across tenants.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Bridge is the middle ground and what most SaaS ends up running: shared compute, separate schemas or databases per tenant. Reasonable isolation, one deployment, and per-tenant backup and restore becomes possible — which is often the requirement that forces you off pool.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The failure mode in a pooled model is the noisy neighbour: one large tenant consuming disproportionate resources and degrading everyone. The defences are per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and for genuinely large tenants, promoting them to their own silo — a hybrid that most mature SaaS platforms run.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Three models, and enforcing isolation
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                SILO    infrastructure per tenant
  + strongest isolation; simple compliance; per-tenant scaling and restore
  - cost per tenant; N deployments to upgrade; does not scale past dozens

BRIDGE  shared compute, separate schema or database per tenant
  + good isolation; ONE deployment; per-tenant backup and restore
  - schema migrations across N schemas; connection pool pressure
  -> where most SaaS lands

POOL    everything shared, tenant_id on every row
  + cheapest, most efficient, trivial to add a tenant
  - ONE MISSING WHERE CLAUSE IS A CROSS-TENANT BREACH
  - noisy neighbours; per-tenant restore is very hard

ENFORCING POOL ISOLATION - do not rely on developers remembering
  Row-Level Security in the database:
    CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
      USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);
  -> the database enforces it even if a query forgets the clause
  plus: tenant id from the AUTHENTICATED CONTEXT, never from a request
        parameter; a test per table asserting cross-tenant reads return
        nothing.

NOISY NEIGHBOUR
  per-tenant rate limits and quotas
  per-tenant metrics, so you can SEE which one is the problem
  promote large tenants to a silo -> the hybrid most mature SaaS runs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How do you handle a tenant that outgrows the pool?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Migrate them to their own silo or bridge instance. That is why the tenant id should be pervasive from day one — it makes extraction a data migration rather than a redesign. Plan for the hybrid rather than treating it as a failure of the model; it is the normal end state.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What is the single most important control in a pooled model?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Enforcing the tenant filter below the application — row-level security in the database, or a mandatory scope in the data access layer that queries cannot bypass. Relying on every developer to remember a WHERE clause is a control that fails silently and catastrophically, and the failure is a data breach rather than a bug.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S99
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Threat modelling is a structured version of what could go wrong, and STRIDE gives you the prompts. Draw the data flow, mark the trust boundaries, and walk each boundary asking the six questions. Most of the value comes from drawing the boundaries at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Designing for audit is a separate requirement and it is easier to build in than to retrofit. The record needs who, what, when, from where, and the before-and-after state — and it must be in a store the audited system cannot modify, or it is not evidence.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  For compliance, the recurring engineering requirements are the ones worth naming: append-only records for anything financial, data retention and deletion that reaches every derived copy, encryption with documented key management, and the ability to prove a control was in place continuously rather than today.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  STRIDE, and what an auditor asks
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  STRIDE at each trust boundary
  Spoofing            can someone pretend to be another user or service?
                      -> authn, mTLS, signed requests
  Tampering           can data be modified in transit or at rest?
                      -> TLS, integrity checks, append-only records
  Repudiation         can someone deny they did it?
                      -> audit log they cannot alter
  Information         can data leak?
    disclosure        -> authz per record, encryption, log scrubbing
  Denial of service   can they exhaust a resource?
                      -> rate limits, quotas, bulkheads
  Elevation of        can a user become an admin, or a service exceed
    privilege         its scope? -> least privilege, no ambient authority

AN AUDIT RECORD THAT IS EVIDENCE
  who (authenticated identity, not a display name)
  what (action + resource id)
  when (server time, monotonic)
  from where (source address, client id, request/trace id)
  BEFORE and AFTER state for a change
  -> written to a store the audited system CANNOT modify or delete
     (separate account, append-only, object-lock)

THE THREE QUESTIONS AN AUDITOR ACTUALLY ASKS
  1  show me how this specific decision was made
  2  show me that a user could not see data they were not entitled to
  3  show me the control was in place CONTINUOUSLY, not just today
  -> design for these three and the rest is paperwork.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  When should threat modelling happen?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  At design time, on the data flow diagram, before code exists — that is when changing a boundary is free. Repeat it when the architecture changes materially or a new trust boundary appears (a new third-party integration, a new client type). Doing it once at launch and never again is the common failure.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What makes an audit log trustworthy?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That the system being audited cannot alter it. Same-account, same-database audit tables are convenient and prove little — a compromised application can rewrite them. Writing to a separate account with append-only and object-lock semantics is what turns a log into evidence, and it is the detail auditors actually probe.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S100
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The interesting part is not shortening — it is that this is a read-heavy key-value problem at roughly 100:1, so the whole design is caching and the write path is almost trivial.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Generate the short code from a counter encoded in base62, not from a hash of the URL. A counter is collision-free by construction; a hash needs collision handling, and truncating it to seven characters makes collisions likely enough to matter. Distribute the counter with ranges handed out per instance, so no coordination happens per request.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Redirect with 301 or 302, and that choice is a real trade: 301 is cached by browsers so subsequent visits never reach you (fast, cheap, and you lose analytics), 302 is not (you see every click, and you pay for it). Most shorteners use 302 for exactly that reason.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The skeleton
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    SCALE      100M new links/month, 100:1 read:write
  writes  ~40/s        trivial
  reads   ~4,000/s     the actual problem
  storage 100M x 500B x 5 years = ~300 GB    one machine, or lightly sharded

KEY GENERATION
  counter -> base62      collision-free, 7 chars = 3.5 trillion
  each instance takes a RANGE (1M ids) from a central allocator
    -> no coordination per request; gaps on restart are harmless
  NOT hash(url) truncated -> collisions need handling, and the check
    is a read on the write path
  custom aliases -> a separate uniqueness check

READ PATH - this is the whole system
  CDN / edge cache  ->  Redis  ->  database
  hit rate is very high: link popularity is heavily skewed
  cache the NEGATIVE too (unknown codes), or scanners penetrate to the DB

301 vs 302
  301 permanent  browser caches -> later visits never reach you
                 fast and cheap, and you LOSE analytics and the ability
                 to change or disable the link
  302 found      you see every click; you pay for every click
  -> most shorteners use 302 deliberately

ANALYTICS: never synchronous. Fire an event to a queue and redirect.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How would you handle a link that goes viral?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    It is a hot key, and the cache tier is where it lands. Local in-process caching in front of Redis absorbs it, and a CDN in front absorbs more. Because links are immutable, caching is safe and TTLs can be long — the failure mode is the opposite one, a scanner enumerating codes that do not exist, which negative caching handles.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Why not use a hash of the URL?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Because you want short codes, and truncating a hash to seven characters makes collisions likely enough to need a check-and-retry on every write — a read on the write path. It is also not idempotent in the way people expect: the same URL submitted by two users usually should produce two codes, since they may have different owners, expiry and analytics.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S101
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The core tension is that limiting must be accurate across instances while adding almost no latency. A per-instance counter is fast and wrong — ten instances each allowing 100 requests per minute permits 1,000.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The standard answer is a centralised counter in Redis with the whole check-and-decrement in a Lua script, so it is atomic in one round trip. Token bucket is usually the right algorithm because it permits short bursts while bounding the sustained rate, which is what an API client actually needs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      For extreme scale, relax exactness: each instance takes a lease of tokens from the central bucket and spends them locally, refreshing when low. That trades a small overshoot for removing Redis from the hot path — and being able to name that trade is what distinguishes the answer.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Centralised, then relaxed
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      REQUIREMENT   100 req/min per API key, across N instances, +<1ms latency

NAIVE         per-instance counter
  10 instances x 100 = 1,000 allowed. Wrong, and it varies with autoscaling.

CENTRALISED   Redis + Lua, atomic in ONE round trip
-- token bucket
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call("hget", KEYS[1], "t") or ARGV[1])
local last   = tonumber(redis.call("hget", KEYS[1], "ts") or ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(ARGV[1], tokens + (ARGV[3] - last) * ARGV[2])
if tokens < 1 then return 0 end
redis.call("hset", KEYS[1], "t", tokens - 1, "ts", ARGV[3])
redis.call("expire", KEYS[1], 120)
return 1

  ~0.3ms in the same AZ. Redis is now on the hot path -> if it is down,
  FAIL OPEN (allow) rather than rejecting all traffic.

AT EXTREME SCALE   local lease
  each instance leases 10 tokens, spends locally, refetches when low
  -> Redis off the hot path
  -> slight OVERSHOOT possible. State that trade.

SHARD THE HOT KEY
  one enormous client saturates one Redis slot
  -> key#0..key#9, each with limit/10, client hashes to one

RESPOND PROPERLY
  429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-Remaining / -Reset
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      What happens if Redis goes down?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Fail open — allow traffic — because rejecting everything converts a rate-limiter outage into a total outage. Combine with a coarse local limit as a backstop so you are not completely unprotected. For a limiter enforcing a paid quota rather than protecting capacity, the business may prefer fail closed, and that is a decision to surface rather than assume.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Sliding window or token bucket?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Token bucket for APIs, because clients legitimately burst — ten requests at once then idle — and a sliding window rejects that even though the sustained rate is fine. Sliding window counter is better when the requirement is literally no more than N per minute, such as a contractual quota.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        1↗

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S102
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The design decision that shapes everything: metadata in a database, content in object storage. Pastes are large, immutable blobs — putting them in a relational database bloats backups, destroys restore times, and consumes expensive storage for something with no query semantics.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        So the database holds the id, owner, expiry, visibility and a storage key; object storage holds the content. Reads go through a CDN for public pastes, and private ones are served with a short-lived presigned URL so your service never proxies bytes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Expiry is the operationally interesting part: object storage lifecycle rules delete content automatically without you running a sweeper, and a separate job reconciles metadata. Getting deletion to actually happen across both stores is where these designs usually leak.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Metadata and blob split
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SCALE   1M pastes/day, avg 10 KB, 100:1 read:write
  storage 10 GB/day -> ~3.6 TB/year   (object storage, not a database)
  reads   ~1,200/s   -> CDN absorbs almost all of it

SPLIT
  DATABASE   id (base62), owner, created_at, expires_at, visibility,
             syntax, size, storage_key, view_count
             -> small rows, indexed, cheap to back up
  OBJECT     the content itself
  STORAGE    -> cheap, unlimited, durable; lifecycle rules handle expiry

READ
  public   CDN -> object storage directly. Your service is not involved.
  private  service checks authz -> returns a SHORT-LIVED presigned URL
           -> bytes never touch your instances

WRITE
  validate size -> presigned PUT (large) or direct (small)
  -> insert metadata AFTER the object exists, or you have dangling rows

EXPIRY - where these designs leak
  S3 lifecycle rule deletes CONTENT automatically (no sweeper to run)
  a reconciliation job removes orphaned METADATA
  -> and the reverse: metadata deleted but content left is a data
     retention violation. Test both directions.

SYNTAX HIGHLIGHTING: client-side. Never render untrusted content
server-side, and serve it from a SEPARATE ORIGIN so a stored XSS
cannot reach your session cookies.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why not store content in the database?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Blobs bloat backups and restore times, consume expensive storage, and get loaded into memory by ORMs that were not expecting a megabyte. Object storage is an order of magnitude cheaper, durable across zones, and serves bytes directly to clients without your service in the path. The rule generalises: never put large immutable blobs in a relational database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you handle abuse?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Rate limit by IP and account, cap paste size, scan for credentials and known-malicious content on ingest, and serve user content from a separate origin so stored XSS cannot reach your cookies. Also make deletion and takedown a first-class operation with an audit trail, because you will need it.
