                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S103
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The whole design is one trade: fan-out on write versus fan-out on read. Writing to every follower's feed makes reads a single fast lookup and makes a post by someone with 50 million followers a 50-million-row write.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Fan-out on read is the opposite — writes are trivial, and every read merges posts from everyone you follow, which is slow and does not cache well.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The answer interviewers are looking for is the hybrid: fan out on write for normal accounts, and for celebrities above a follower threshold, do not fan out at all — merge their posts in at read time. Most users' feeds are precomputed; the handful of celebrity accounts are merged from a small, hot, well-cached set.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The hybrid, and why
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          FAN-OUT ON WRITE          push into every follower's feed
  + read = ONE lookup, fast, cacheable
  - a celebrity post = 50M writes; a write amplification of 50M:1
  - wasted work for inactive followers

FAN-OUT ON READ           merge at query time
  + writes trivial
  - reads merge N sources, slow, poor cache hit rate

*** HYBRID - the expected answer ***
  followers < 10,000   -> fan out on write into a per-user feed
  followers > 10,000   -> DO NOT fan out. Merge at read time.
  reading a feed = precomputed timeline + merge(celebrities you follow)
  -> celebrity posts are a SMALL, HOT set: perfectly cached

MORE REFINEMENTS
  only fan out to ACTIVE users (logged in within 30 days);
    inactive users' feeds are built lazily on next login
  cap the stored feed at ~1,000 entries; older pages fall back to a query
  feed entries store POST IDS, not content -> hydrate from a cache,
    so an edited or deleted post is correct everywhere

SCALE
  500M DAU, 2 posts/day avg -> 1B posts/day -> ~12,000 writes/s
  reads 10x -> 120,000/s -> this is a caching problem
  feed store: Redis sorted set per user, or a wide-column store
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          What ordering do you use?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Start with reverse chronological because it is simple and explicable, then say that real systems rank — engagement prediction, recency decay, diversity. The design implication of ranking is that the feed cannot be a simple precomputed list: you fetch a candidate set and score it at read time, which pushes you toward the hybrid regardless of follower counts.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you handle a deleted post?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Store post ids in the feed, not content, so hydration naturally skips deleted posts — you filter at read time and backfill the page to keep it full. Removing the id from millions of precomputed feeds is not viable, which is exactly why storing ids rather than content is the right call.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S104
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Chat is a connection management problem more than a messaging one. WebSocket connections are long-lived and stateful, so the hard questions are: which server holds a given user's connection, what happens when that server restarts, and how does a message reach a user connected elsewhere.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The answer is a session registry — a mapping from user to the gateway holding their connection — and a pub/sub layer between gateways. A message arrives at gateway A, looks up the recipient, and publishes to the channel that gateway B is subscribed to.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Delivery receipts drive the storage model: sent, delivered, read are three separate state transitions, each of which is a write and a push. That multiplies your write volume by roughly three, which is worth saying out loud during estimation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Connections, routing and ordering
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            CONNECTIONS
  WebSocket to a GATEWAY tier (stateful, sticky by connection)
  session registry in Redis:  user:123 -> gateway-7   (with a TTL + heartbeat)
  gateway restart -> clients reconnect with backoff + jitter
    -> a mass reconnect is a thundering herd. Stagger it.

ROUTING A MESSAGE
  arrives at gateway A -> persist -> look up recipient's gateway
  -> publish to that gateway's channel -> gateway B pushes over the socket
  recipient offline -> queue for delivery + a push notification

STORAGE
  partition by CONVERSATION id, sort by message id
  -> one conversation is one partition: ordered, and one read serves history
  message id: a time-sortable id (Snowflake-style), NOT a random UUID
  -> gives ordering AND pagination for free

ORDERING - the trap
  clients are on unreliable networks; timestamps are client clocks.
  ORDER BY the SERVER-ASSIGNED id within a conversation.
  Client-side, reconcile optimistic local messages by a client-supplied
  temporary id.

RECEIPTS multiply writes
  sent -> delivered -> read: three transitions per message per recipient
  -> in a group of 50, one message is ~150 state writes
  -> batch them; do not write one row per receipt per message

PRESENCE
  heartbeat -> Redis key with a short TTL; absence = offline
  fan out presence changes ONLY to people who are watching that user
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you scale WebSocket connections?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Horizontally, with the connection count per gateway as the sizing constraint — tens of thousands per instance depending on memory per connection. The gateway tier is stateful, so deploys must drain connections gradually rather than dropping them all, and clients need reconnect with jitter or a rolling deploy becomes a self-inflicted thundering herd.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What about message ordering across devices?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Order by the server-assigned id within a conversation, and have each device track the last id it has seen so it can request the gap on reconnect. Never rely on client timestamps — device clocks are wrong and users travel across time zones. This is also why the id should be time-sortable rather than random.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S105
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The shape is a fan-out pipeline with per-channel adapters, and the interesting parts are all reliability: deduplication, retries with different characteristics per channel, and respecting user preferences and quiet hours.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Each channel has genuinely different properties. Push is cheap, fast and unreliable (tokens expire silently). SMS is expensive, has strict rate limits per carrier, and is regulated. Email is cheap and has deliverability and reputation concerns that no other channel has.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Deduplication is the requirement people miss. The same logical event can arrive twice from an at-least-once upstream, and sending a duplicate SMS costs money and trust. A deduplication key per (user, event, channel) with a window is the mechanism.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pipeline and per-channel reality
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              PIPELINE
  event -> notification service
        -> resolve TEMPLATE + user PREFERENCES + locale
        -> decide channels (and honour quiet hours, per user timezone)
        -> DEDUPE  key = hash(userId, eventId, channel), TTL 24h
        -> per-channel QUEUE (separate, so SMS backlog does not block push)
        -> adapter -> provider
        -> record delivery status; handle async webhooks

PER-CHANNEL REALITY
  PUSH   cheap, fast; tokens EXPIRE SILENTLY -> prune on failure
         batch to the provider; per-device, not per-user
  SMS    EXPENSIVE, carrier rate limits, regulated (opt-in, quiet hours,
         STOP handling). A duplicate costs real money.
  EMAIL  cheap; DELIVERABILITY is the whole problem - SPF, DKIM, DMARC,
         bounce and complaint handling, reputation. A shared IP that
         someone else abused affects you.

PRIORITY - one queue per priority, not one queue
  transactional (password reset, payment)  -> immediate, never batched
  digest / marketing                        -> batched, deferrable, shed first

RETRIES DIFFER BY CHANNEL
  push  retry aggressively - it is free
  SMS   retry ONCE - each attempt costs money
  email retry over hours; a soft bounce is transient, a hard bounce is
        permanent and the address must be suppressed

TEMPLATE VERSIONING: render at SEND time from a versioned template, and
record which version was sent - you will be asked what a user received.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you avoid notification fatigue?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Aggregation and rate limiting per user, not just per channel: collapse five people liked your post into one notification, cap the number per hour, and respect quiet hours in the user's timezone. It is a product requirement with a real design consequence — it means notifications are buffered and batched rather than sent immediately.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              What is the hardest part operationally?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Deliverability for email, because it depends on reputation you build slowly and can lose quickly. Practically: authenticate properly, process bounces and complaints immediately, suppress hard bounces permanently, separate transactional and marketing traffic onto different IPs or subdomains, and monitor complaint rates as a first-class metric.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S106
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Autocomplete is a read-only, latency-critical problem: under 100ms including the network, on every keystroke. That budget rules out querying a database per keystroke and pushes everything toward precomputation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The classic structure is a trie with the top-k completions precomputed and stored at each node. Then a lookup is a walk down the prefix and a read of a ready-made list — no ranking at request time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Serve it from memory, and refresh the structure offline from query logs on a schedule. That separation is the key design point: the write path (aggregating what people searched for) is a batch job running hourly, and the read path never touches it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Precompute, serve from memory
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                BUDGET   <100ms end to end, on EVERY keystroke
  -> no database query per keystroke
  -> debounce client-side (~150ms) and cancel in-flight requests

STRUCTURE   trie with TOP-K STORED AT EACH NODE
  node "car" -> ["cars","careers","car insurance","carpet","cartoon"]
  lookup = walk the prefix + return the stored list. No ranking at request time.

  memory: a few million terms fits in a few GB -> serve from RAM
  alternative: a sorted key-value store, key = prefix, value = the list
               (simpler to operate, slightly less flexible)

BUILD PIPELINE - offline, hourly
  query logs -> aggregate counts (with time decay, so trends surface)
             -> filter: profanity, PII, spam, single-user queries
             -> compute top-k per prefix
             -> build the structure -> ship to serving nodes
  -> the read path NEVER touches this

SERVING
  many stateless replicas, each with the full structure in memory
  shard by first character only if it does not fit
  CDN in front for the most common prefixes

PERSONALISATION
  blend a small per-user history list with the global list at read time
  -> keep it cheap; it is a merge, not a re-rank

TYPO TOLERANCE: edit distance is expensive. Precompute common
misspellings into the trie instead, from the logs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                How do you handle trending queries?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Time-decayed counts in the aggregation, plus a much faster path for genuine spikes — a separate short-window count merged into the results, refreshed every few minutes. A breaking news term should surface in minutes, not in the next hourly build, and a separate hot-list is cheaper than rebuilding everything.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why not use a search engine for this?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                You can, and it is a reasonable pragmatic answer — Elasticsearch has completion suggesters backed by a finite state transducer. The reason to describe the trie is that it shows you understand what precomputation buys: the latency budget is met by doing the ranking offline, and any implementation that ranks per keystroke will struggle.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S107
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A crawler is a distributed BFS with politeness constraints, and the politeness is what makes it interesting: you must fetch billions of pages while never hitting one domain hard enough to be a problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That forces the frontier to be partitioned by domain, not by URL. All URLs for one host go to one queue with its own rate limit, so no two workers can hit the same site simultaneously. Partitioning by URL hash would spread one domain across every worker and defeat the whole constraint.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Deduplication is the other core problem, at two levels: URL-level (normalise, then check membership — a Bloom filter for scale) and content-level (a fingerprint such as simhash, so near-duplicate pages across mirrors are detected).
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Frontier, politeness, dedup
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  SCALE   1B pages/month -> ~400 pages/s sustained
  storage: 1B x 100 KB = 100 TB raw -> object storage, compressed

FRONTIER - partitioned BY DOMAIN, never by URL
  each domain gets a queue + its own rate limit + a next-fetch time
  a worker takes a DOMAIN, not a URL
  -> guarantees no two workers hit one site at once
  priority: PageRank-ish score, freshness, depth

POLITENESS
  robots.txt: fetch, CACHE (hours), honour Disallow and Crawl-delay
  default to conservative (1 req/s per domain) without an explicit delay
  identify yourself in User-Agent with a contact URL
  back off hard on 429 and 5xx - a site that is struggling is not a bug

DEDUPLICATION - two levels
  URL     normalise (lowercase host, strip fragments, sort query params,
          remove tracking params) -> Bloom filter of seen URLs
          (false positives skip a page - acceptable at this scale)
  CONTENT simhash / minhash fingerprint -> near-duplicate detection
          across mirrors and syndicated copies

TRAPS
  infinite spaces: calendars, session ids in URLs, faceted navigation
  -> depth limits, per-domain page caps, URL pattern detection
  redirect loops -> cap the chain
  enormous files -> cap the download size

RECRAWL: adaptive. A news homepage hourly, a static page monthly.
Track change frequency per URL and schedule accordingly.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  How do you decide what to crawl next?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A priority score combining estimated importance (inbound links), freshness need (observed change frequency), and depth from a seed. The frontier is effectively a priority queue per domain, and the interesting constraint is that politeness caps throughput per domain — so breadth across many domains is what gives you volume, not depth on any one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  What about JavaScript-rendered pages?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  They need a headless browser, which is one to two orders of magnitude more expensive per page than an HTTP fetch. So you classify: fetch cheaply first, detect that the content is thin or renders client-side, and queue only those for a rendering pool. Rendering everything is the naive choice that makes the crawler unaffordable.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S108
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The design centres on chunking and deduplication. Files are split into chunks, each hashed, and only chunks the server does not already have are uploaded — so re-uploading a 1GB file after editing a few bytes transfers kilobytes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Use content-defined chunking rather than fixed-size blocks. With fixed blocks, inserting one byte at the start shifts every subsequent boundary and every chunk hash changes. Content-defined boundaries mean only the chunks around the edit change.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Sync conflicts are the part to get right, and the answer is not automatic merging. Keep both versions — file (conflicted copy from another device) — because silently losing a user's edit is far worse than showing them two files. Use a version vector per file to detect genuine concurrency rather than a timestamp.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Chunks, metadata and conflicts
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    SPLIT
  METADATA (database)  file id, path, owner, version, chunk list, size,
                       permissions, device sync state
  CHUNKS (object       content-addressed by hash. Deduplicated GLOBALLY -
   storage)            one copy of a chunk shared by every user who has it

UPLOAD
  client chunks the file (content-defined, ~4 MB average)
  hashes each chunk
  asks the server WHICH hashes it already has
  uploads ONLY the missing ones (presigned URLs, parallel)
  commits new metadata pointing at the full chunk list
  -> editing 10 bytes of a 1 GB file transfers ~one chunk

SYNC
  long poll / WebSocket for change notifications
  client pulls the metadata delta, then fetches only missing chunks
  a per-device cursor tracks what it has seen

CONFLICTS - do NOT auto-merge
  version vector per file detects CONCURRENT edits (not a timestamp -
  device clocks are wrong)
  concurrent -> keep BOTH:
     report.docx  +  report (conflicted copy from another device).docx
  losing a user's edit silently is far worse than showing two files

DELETES: tombstone, not immediate removal - a delete must propagate,
and a device that was offline must not resurrect the file.

CHUNK GC: reference-counted; delete a chunk only when no file references
it. Do it lazily and carefully - a bug here destroys other users' data.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How does global deduplication interact with encryption?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Badly, and it is a real trade. Client-side encryption with per-user keys means identical files produce different ciphertext, so cross-user deduplication is impossible. Convergent encryption (key derived from the content hash) restores deduplication but leaks whether you hold a known file. Most consumer services choose server-side encryption and cross-user dedup; privacy-focused ones choose the opposite.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What is the hardest part in practice?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The client, not the server. Detecting local changes reliably across operating systems, handling partial writes from applications that save by writing a temp file and renaming, dealing with files locked by another process, and reconciling state after a crash mid-sync. The distributed systems part is well understood; the filesystem edge cases are endless.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S109
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Streaming is two systems: an offline transcoding pipeline and an online delivery path, and they have nothing in common operationally. The pipeline is batch, bursty and CPU-bound; delivery is a CDN problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      adaptive bitrate is the core delivery idea: encode each video at several resolutions and bitrates, split every rendition into 2–10 second segments, and publish a manifest. The player measures its own throughput and switches rendition between segments, so a bandwidth drop degrades quality rather than buffering.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Transcoding is embarrassingly parallel: split the source into chunks, transcode them independently across a fleet (spot instances suit this perfectly), then assemble. That turns a two-hour job into minutes and makes the cost proportional to work rather than to wall-clock time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Pipeline and delivery
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      UPLOAD -> PIPELINE (offline, batch, spot-friendly)
  presigned multipart upload to object storage
  -> event -> queue -> orchestration (a state machine, not a chain)
  -> SPLIT the source into chunks
  -> transcode chunks in PARALLEL across a fleet   <- embarrassingly parallel
       renditions: 240p 360p 480p 720p 1080p 4K
       codecs: H.264 (compatibility) + AV1/HEVC (efficiency)
  -> package into segments (HLS/DASH), generate the manifest
  -> thumbnails, subtitles, an audio-only rendition
  -> publish

  checkpoint per chunk -> a spot interruption costs ONE chunk

DELIVERY (online)
  player fetches the MANIFEST -> then segments from the CDN
  ABR: the player measures throughput and switches rendition between
       segments -> a bandwidth drop degrades QUALITY, not playback
  >95% of bytes served from the CDN edge; the origin is barely touched

STORAGE
  one source + ~6 renditions = several x the original.
  lifecycle: keep popular renditions hot, tier cold ones; consider
  transcoding rare renditions ON DEMAND rather than storing them.

DRM / access control
  signed segment URLs with short expiry, or token-authenticated CDN
  -> a leaked manifest must not grant permanent access
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Why segment rather than stream a single file?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Because segments make adaptive bitrate possible — the player can choose a different rendition for the next segment without restarting. They are also plain HTTP objects, so every CDN caches them with no special protocol. That combination is why HLS and DASH won over purpose-built streaming protocols.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      How do you make the pipeline cost-effective?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Spot instances with per-chunk checkpointing, since transcoding is interruptible; transcode lazily for rare renditions rather than eagerly for all; and prioritise by predicted popularity so a creator's audience is not waiting while an unwatched video transcodes. Also encode newer codecs only for content popular enough to repay the CPU.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S110
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The core problem is geospatial indexing under constant writes: drivers update their position every few seconds, and riders need nearby drivers in milliseconds. A B-tree on latitude and longitude cannot answer within 2km efficiently, because it is a two-dimensional query.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        geohash solves it by reducing two dimensions to one: nearby points share a prefix, so a proximity query becomes a prefix scan. Uber's H3 uses hexagons instead, which avoids the awkward property that square cells have inconsistent neighbour distances.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep driver locations in memory, not in a durable database — they are ephemeral, high-write, and losing them is a brief inconvenience rather than a correctness problem. Redis geospatial commands or an in-process index sharded by region are both reasonable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Index, match, and the contention
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SCALE   1M active drivers, position every 4s -> 250,000 writes/s
  -> these are EPHEMERAL. Do not put them in a durable database.
  -> Redis GEO, or an in-memory index sharded by region

INDEXING
  geohash: lat/lng -> "gcpvj0" ; a shared prefix = proximity
  -> "drivers near me" = a prefix range scan
  EDGE CASE: two nearby points can straddle a cell boundary and share
  no prefix -> always query the cell AND its 8 neighbours
  H3 (hexagons) avoids the inconsistent-neighbour-distance problem

MATCHING - the interesting part
  candidate drivers = nearby cells, filtered by availability
  rank by ETA (road network), not straight-line distance
  -> OFFER to one driver with a short timeout, then the next
  -> a naive "broadcast to all nearby" causes a race and a bad experience

CONTENTION
  one driver must not be assigned to two riders.
  -> atomic claim: conditional update on driver state
     (available -> offered -> assigned). CAS, not read-then-write.
  surge pricing = demand/supply per cell, computed on a short window

TRIP STATE is durable and belongs in a real database - it is money.
Driver POSITION is not.

WRITE OPTIMISATION
  most position updates change nothing useful. Only propagate a move
  beyond a threshold, or every Nth update -> cuts write volume hugely.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why rank by ETA rather than distance?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Because a driver 500m away across a river with no bridge is further, in the only sense that matters, than one 2km away on a direct road. Straight-line distance is a cheap candidate filter; the actual ranking needs a routing engine. Saying that distinction out loud shows you have thought about the domain rather than only the index.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        How do you prevent double-assignment?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        An atomic state transition on the driver record — a conditional update from available to offered that fails if someone else won. Never read-then-write. The same conditional-write primitive that gives you idempotency elsewhere solves assignment contention here, which is worth noting as a recurring pattern.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S111
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Ticket booking is a contention problem, not a scale one. Ten thousand people pressing buy for the same seat in the same second is a small number of requests and a very hard correctness requirement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The mechanism is a hold: reserve the seat for a short window (5–10 minutes) while the user pays, with the hold expiring automatically. That turns a long user-facing checkout into a short database transaction, which is what makes the contention manageable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Expiry must be automatic and lazy, not a sweeper you rely on. Store an expires_at and treat any hold past it as available at read time, with a background job cleaning up. A design where seats leak because a cleanup job failed is a design that sells out with empty seats.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Holds, atomic claims, and the queue
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          THE SHAPE
  seat states: AVAILABLE -> HELD (expires_at) -> SOLD
  hold window 5-10 minutes, long enough to pay

ATOMIC CLAIM - the whole correctness story
  UPDATE seats
  SET status='HELD', held_by=:user, expires_at=now()+interval '10 minutes'
  WHERE seat_id=:id
    AND (status='AVAILABLE'
         OR (status='HELD' AND expires_at < now()));   -- lazy expiry
  -- 1 row updated -> you have it.  0 rows -> someone else won.

  no SELECT first. No lock held across the payment. No sweeper required
  for correctness - expiry is evaluated at read time.

PAYMENT
  hold -> take payment -> confirm SOLD
  payment fails or times out -> the hold simply EXPIRES. No compensation
  needed, which is why holds are better than "reserve then undo".

FOR A HIGH-DEMAND ON-SALE
  a VIRTUAL WAITING ROOM in front: admit N users per second into the
  purchase flow, everyone else waits with a position.
  -> converts a thundering herd into a controlled rate
  -> and it is honest: the user sees a queue rather than a failure

SEAT SELECTION UX
  show availability from a cache, but ALWAYS re-validate on claim.
  A user seeing a seat that is gone is acceptable; a user paying for
  a seat someone else has is not.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Why not lock the seat row for the whole checkout?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Because checkout takes minutes and involves a network call to a payment provider. Holding a database lock across that pins a connection, blocks other transactions, and risks the lock outliving the process. The hold pattern converts a minutes-long business operation into a millisecond database transaction plus a timestamp.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you handle the seat map for a 60,000-seat stadium?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Do not send 60,000 rows to a browser. Send aggregate availability per section, and fetch seat-level detail only for the section the user is viewing. Cache the aggregate with a short TTL and accept staleness there, since the claim is re-validated atomically anyway.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S112
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            A job scheduler has two distinct problems: when to run (time-based dispatch, including delayed and recurring jobs) and exactly-once execution across a fleet where any worker may crash mid-job.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            For delayed jobs, a sorted set by execution time is the standard structure: poll for entries whose time has arrived. It is simple, it scales, and it handles both delayed and recurring jobs with one mechanism.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Execution safety comes from a lease, not a lock: a worker claims a job with a visibility timeout and must heartbeat to extend it. A crashed worker simply stops heartbeating and the job becomes claimable again — no failure detection needed, and no risk of a job being stuck forever because a lock holder died.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Dispatch, lease, and the pitfalls
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            STORAGE
  Redis sorted set: score = execute_at (epoch ms), member = job id
  ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 now LIMIT 0 100   -> due jobs
  or a database table with an index on (status, execute_at)

  at very large scale, shard by time bucket to avoid one hot key

CLAIM - a LEASE, not a lock
  UPDATE jobs SET status='RUNNING', worker=:me,
                  lease_expires=now()+interval '60 seconds', attempt=attempt+1
  WHERE id=:id AND (status='PENDING'
                    OR (status='RUNNING' AND lease_expires < now()));
  worker HEARTBEATS to extend the lease while working
  crash -> lease expires -> another worker claims it. No detection needed.

EXACTLY-ONCE EFFECT
  at-least-once execution is guaranteed; duplicates are not.
  -> the JOB HANDLER must be idempotent. This is the contract.

RECURRING JOBS
  after success, schedule the next occurrence.
  concurrency policy: FORBID overlap by default (a run that overruns its
  schedule must not stack), and a missed-run policy so a scheduler
  outage does not produce a burst of catch-up executions.

RETRIES: exponential backoff with jitter, a max attempt count, then a
dead-letter state with an alert.

THE ALERT PEOPLE FORGET
  alert on ABSENCE - a job that has not run when it should have.
  A failure produces an error you can see; a job that never fires
  produces silence.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How do you guarantee a job runs exactly once?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            You do not — you guarantee at-least-once and make the handler idempotent. A worker can complete the work and crash before marking it done, which is indistinguishable from crashing before starting. Claim before the work, make the effect idempotent, and reconcile. Promising exactly-once execution is a claim nobody can implement.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            How would you support millions of delayed jobs?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Shard the sorted set by time bucket (one key per minute), so no single key is hot and expired buckets can be dropped wholesale. Poll only the current and previous bucket. For very long delays, a two-tier approach — coarse buckets promoted into fine ones as they approach — keeps the working set small.
