                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S113
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A metrics backend is a time-series database problem, and the defining constraint is cardinality: the number of distinct series, which is the product of every label's distinct values. Storage and query cost scale with series count far more than with data point volume.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The write path is append-only and extremely high volume, which suits columnar storage with delta-of-delta encoding on timestamps and XOR compression on values — real systems achieve better than 10x compression, often much more, because consecutive samples are similar.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Downsampling is what makes long retention affordable: keep raw data for days, five-minute aggregates for weeks, hourly for years. A dashboard showing a year does not need per-second resolution, and storing it is pure cost.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Cardinality, compression, retention
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              CARDINALITY IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM
  series = product of distinct label values
  http_requests{endpoint, status, region}  = 10 x 5 x 3 = 150     fine
  + user_id (500k)                         = 75,000,000           fatal
  -> the backend dies, and you lose observability during the incident
  -> ENFORCE bounded labels; high cardinality belongs in traces/logs

WRITE PATH
  ingest -> shard by SERIES (hash of the label set) -> per-series append
  in-memory head block -> flushed to immutable blocks on disk
  columnar layout: timestamps and values stored separately
    delta-of-delta on timestamps (regular intervals compress to ~1 bit)
    XOR compression on float values
  -> >10x compression is normal

READ PATH
  query = select series by label matchers -> read blocks -> aggregate
  inverted index from label -> series id makes matching fast
  a query touching millions of series is slow no matter what you do
  -> RECORDING RULES precompute expensive dashboard queries

RETENTION - downsample
  raw (15s)   15 days
  5m rollup   90 days
  1h rollup   2 years
  -> a year-long dashboard does not need per-second points

HIGH AVAILABILITY
  two independent ingesters receiving the same data (simplest), or a
  clustered store with replication. Metrics are usually TOLERANT of a
  small gap - do not over-engineer this.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why is high cardinality worse than high volume?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because volume compresses and cardinality does not. Ten million points in one series is a few kilobytes after delta-of-delta encoding; one point in each of ten million series is ten million index entries, ten million series headers, and a query that must touch all of them. The cost is per-series, not per-point.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Push or pull for collection?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Pull (scraping) gives you a natural health signal — a target that stops responding is visibly down — and centralised control of the interval. Push suits short-lived jobs that may not exist when a scrape happens, and clients behind a firewall. Most systems use pull with a push gateway for batch jobs, which is a reasonable answer to give.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • S114
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Log aggregation is a high-volume write, low-volume read problem with a fundamental tension: full-text search over everything is expensive, and you rarely know in advance which fields you will need.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The architecture is agent → buffer → index → object storage. The buffer is essential, not optional: log volume spikes exactly when things go wrong, which is exactly when you least want the pipeline to drop data or push back on the applications producing it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The cost lever that matters is tiering: index recent logs for fast search, and archive older ones to object storage queryable more slowly. Indexing everything for a year costs more than the systems producing the logs — and almost all searches are for the last few days.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Pipeline, tiering, and cost
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                PIPELINE
  app -> stdout (structured JSON, ONE line per event)
      -> node agent (Fluent Bit / Vector) tails, enriches, batches
      -> BUFFER (Kafka)      <- ESSENTIAL. Volume spikes exactly when
                                things break. Without it you drop data
                                or push back on production.
      -> indexer -> hot index (searchable)
      -> ALSO -> object storage (cheap, queryable slowly)

TIERING - the cost lever
  hot   7 days    indexed, full-text search, fast          expensive
  warm  30 days   indexed, fewer replicas, slower hardware
  cold  1 year+   object storage + Athena/Presto           very cheap
  -> almost every search is for the last few days

DROP AT THE AGENT, not after ingestion
  you pay for ingestion as well as storage.
  filter DEBUG at the shipper; sample high-volume noisy events.

INDEX DESIGN
  time-based indices (one per day) -> deletion is dropping an index,
  which is instant. Deleting rows from one giant index is not.
  index only the FIELDS YOU SEARCH ON; store the rest unindexed.

STRUCTURED LOGGING IS THE ENABLER
  {"ts":..., "level":"ERROR", "trace_id":"4bf9...", "merchant_id":"...",
   "event":"settlement_failed", "error_code":"PARTNER_TIMEOUT"}
  -> filter by field, not regex over prose
  -> and trace_id links a log line to the full distributed trace

RETENTION IS ALSO A COMPLIANCE CONTROL: logs contain personal data,
so short retention is data minimisation, not just cost saving.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                What do you do when log volume exceeds what you can afford to index?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sample aggressively and deliberately: index 100% of errors and warnings, and a small percentage of info-level events, keeping everything in cheap object storage regardless. That preserves your ability to investigate while cutting index cost by an order of magnitude. Blanket-dropping by level loses the successful requests that provide context for the failures.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why buffer with a log rather than write directly to the index?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Because the index is the slowest, most failure-prone part, and log volume spikes precisely during an incident. A durable buffer decouples production from indexing — the indexer can fall behind and catch up, be restarted, or be replaced entirely, and you can replay into a new index without touching the applications.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • S115
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Ad click counting is a write-heavy aggregation problem where exactness matters commercially — advertisers are billed on these numbers — and where the raw volume makes per-click database writes impossible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The shape is a streaming pipeline: clicks land on a log, workers aggregate into time windows, and results are written to a store that serves both dashboards and billing. Aggregation happens in the stream, not in the database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The hard parts are deduplication (the same click arriving twice from an at-least-once pipeline must not be billed twice) and late events (a mobile client offline for an hour submits clicks that belong to a window you already closed). Both need explicit answers, and watermarking with a grace period is the standard one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Streaming aggregation with correctness
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  SCALE   1M clicks/s peak
  per-click database writes: impossible
  -> aggregate in the STREAM

PIPELINE
  click -> lightweight collector (validate, enrich, emit) -> Kafka
        -> stream processor: windowed aggregation by (ad, campaign, minute)
        -> emit window results -> serving store (fast reads)
        -> raw events -> object storage (for reprocessing and audit)

DEDUPLICATION
  each click carries a client-generated id
  dedupe within a window using a Bloom filter or a key-value store with TTL
  -> a false positive drops a real click; a false negative bills twice
  -> for BILLING, prefer exact dedup on a bounded window over a Bloom filter

LATE EVENTS - the part people miss
  a mobile client offline for an hour submits clicks for a CLOSED window
  -> WATERMARK: the window closes at T + grace (say 10 minutes)
  -> events later than the grace period go to a LATE stream, reconciled
     in a nightly batch that CORRECTS the totals
  -> and the correction must be auditable, because it changes an invoice

LAMBDA-ish ARCHITECTURE, honestly
  streaming path  -> fast, approximate, for dashboards
  batch path      -> nightly, exact, from the raw log, for BILLING
  -> the batch result is authoritative. State this explicitly - it is
     the honest way to have both speed and correctness.

FRAUD: bot filtering before counting - it changes what is billable,
so it belongs in the pipeline, not in a report afterwards.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Why keep both a streaming and a batch path?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Because they optimise different things and the requirements genuinely differ. Dashboards need numbers within seconds and tolerate small errors; billing needs exactness and tolerates a day's delay. Rather than compromising both, run both and declare the batch result authoritative — which also gives you a reprocessing path when a bug is found.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  How do you handle a bug discovered a week later?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Reprocess from the raw event log in object storage, which is why you keep it. That is the main argument for storing raw events rather than only aggregates: aggregates cannot be recomputed differently, and a change to fraud rules or attribution logic means recomputing history. Store raw, derive everything else.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • S116
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The serving path is a two-stage funnel: cheap candidate generation narrows millions of items to a few hundred, then expensive ranking scores those precisely. Trying to rank everything is the naive design and it cannot meet a latency budget.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Candidate generation is usually approximate nearest neighbour over embeddings, plus simple retrieval strategies merged together — recently viewed, popular in your region, from creators you follow. Diversity of sources at this stage matters more than the sophistication of any one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The architectural point is that models are trained offline and features are precomputed. The serving path does a vector lookup, a feature fetch from a low-latency store, and one model inference — nothing that touches a training pipeline. Confusing the two is what makes recommendation systems slow.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Two stages, and the feature store
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    BUDGET  <100ms for the whole path

STAGE 1 - CANDIDATE GENERATION   millions -> ~500
  ANN over item embeddings (HNSW), keyed by a user embedding
  + merge several cheap sources:
      recently viewed / similar to recent
      popular in region and segment
      from followed creators
      editorial or business rules
  -> diversity of SOURCES matters more than sophistication here
  ~10ms

STAGE 2 - RANKING                ~500 -> 20
  a model scoring (user, item, context) features
  one batched inference over 500 candidates
  ~30-50ms

STAGE 3 - RE-RANK / POLICY       business rules
  diversity (not five items from one creator), freshness, dedup against
  what was shown recently, hard filters (region, age, availability)

FEATURE STORE - the piece that makes it possible
  OFFLINE  batch-computed features for training (must match serving!)
  ONLINE   low-latency store (Redis/DynamoDB) for the same features
  -> TRAINING/SERVING SKEW is the classic bug: features computed
     differently in the two paths, so the model performs worse in
     production than in evaluation, and nothing looks broken.

FALLBACK: if the model or the ANN index is unavailable, serve popular
items. A recommendation surface must never be empty.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    What is training/serving skew?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Computing a feature differently in training and serving — a batch job using a full day's data while the online path uses a rolling hour, or a subtly different definition of recent. The model then sees inputs it was not trained on, performs worse, and nothing errors. A shared feature definition used by both paths is the structural fix.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    How do you evaluate a change?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Offline metrics first (does the new model rank held-out clicks better), then an online A/B test on real traffic, because offline metrics predict online performance imperfectly. Guard the test with business metrics, not just click-through — a model that maximises clicks can degrade retention, which is the classic recommender failure.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • S117
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A distributed cache is a partitioned in-memory key-value store, and the two decisions that define it are how keys map to nodes and what happens when the membership changes.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes, so adding or removing a node moves roughly 1/N of keys rather than nearly all of them. Plain modulo hashing remaps almost everything on a resize, which for a cache means a total miss storm against the database.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The critical design question is what happens when the cache is unavailable. If the database cannot survive a full miss storm, the cache is load-bearing rather than an optimisation — and that must be an explicit decision with a mitigation, not something you discover during an incident.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Partitioning, replication, and the load-bearing question
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      PARTITIONING
  consistent hashing + virtual nodes (150-300 positions per physical node)
  -> adding a node moves ~1/N of keys, not ~all
  -> removing one spreads its keys across MANY successors, not one

CLIENT-SIDE vs PROXY
  client-side (memcached style)  no extra hop; every client needs the
                                 ring and must agree on it
  proxy (Twemproxy, Envoy)       one hop; simpler clients; a component
                                 to operate and scale

REPLICATION - decide deliberately
  none      simplest; a node loss means those keys miss. Often FINE.
  replicas  survive a node loss; you now have consistency questions
            about a CACHE, which is usually not worth it

EVICTION: allkeys-lru + a TTL. Never `noeviction` on a cache - a full
instance starts REJECTING WRITES, which surfaces as application errors.

HOT KEYS: one key can saturate one node however you hash.
  -> local in-process cache in front (short TTL)
  -> or replicate that key: key#0..key#9

*** THE QUESTION THAT MATTERS ***
  can the database survive a 0% hit rate?
    yes -> the cache is an optimisation. Good.
    no  -> the cache is LOAD-BEARING. It is a single point of failure.
           -> mitigate: request coalescing, rate-limit cache-miss traffic
              to the database, warm gradually after a restart, and
              NEVER restart the whole tier at once.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Should a cache be replicated?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Usually not — it adds consistency problems to something that is by definition disposable, and losing a node should just mean those keys miss. Replicate when a full miss for that key set would overwhelm the origin, which is really a signal that the cache is load-bearing and the origin needs attention.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      How do you warm a cache after a restart?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Gradually, and with the origin protected. Bring nodes back one at a time, use request coalescing so a thousand concurrent misses for one key produce one origin query, and rate-limit miss traffic to the database. Restarting the whole tier at once and letting it fill naturally is how a cache restart becomes a database outage.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • S118
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The requirements pull against each other: unique across many machines, roughly sortable by time so it works as a database key, compact, and generated without coordination per request.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A Snowflake id satisfies all four: 41 bits of millisecond timestamp, 10 bits of machine id, 12 bits of sequence within a millisecond. That gives 4,096 ids per machine per millisecond, fits in a 64-bit integer, and sorts by time.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A random UUIDv4 is simpler and has a real cost as a primary key: random values scatter B-tree inserts across the whole index, causing page splits and poor cache locality. UUIDv7 fixes this by putting a timestamp in the high bits — which is worth naming, because it is the modern answer to why not just use a UUID.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The options, and what each costs
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        SNOWFLAKE (64-bit)
  [ 1 unused | 41 timestamp ms | 10 machine id | 12 sequence ]
  4,096 ids per machine per ms; ~69 years from the epoch
  + compact, TIME-SORTABLE, no coordination per id
  - needs unique machine ids (from ZooKeeper, or the orchestrator)
  - CLOCK SKEW: if the clock goes backwards, WAIT rather than emit a
    duplicate. This is the failure case to name.

UUIDv4 (128-bit, random)
  + zero coordination, trivially available everywhere
  - RANDOM -> scatters B-tree inserts, page splits, poor cache locality
  - twice the storage, and worse as a foreign key everywhere

UUIDv7 (128-bit, time-ordered)
  [ 48-bit timestamp ms | random ]
  + sortable, no coordination, standard
  - still 128 bits
  -> the modern default when you do not need 64-bit compactness

DATABASE SEQUENCE
  + simple, gapless-ish, sortable
  - a round trip per id (or batch allocation), and a single point of
    coordination. Fine at moderate scale; a bottleneck at high write rates.

TICKET SERVER WITH RANGES
  each instance takes a block of 100,000 ids and serves locally
  -> no per-id coordination, gaps on restart (harmless)
  -> the pragmatic middle ground

AND: do not leak business meaning. A sequential public id tells
competitors your order volume.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What happens if the clock moves backwards?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Snowflake must refuse to emit ids until the clock catches up, because emitting with an earlier timestamp risks a duplicate. That means a brief stall rather than a correctness failure, and it must be handled explicitly — a naive implementation that just uses the current time will produce duplicates after an NTP correction.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Why does a random primary key hurt so much?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Because a B-tree index insert at a random position touches a random page, which is likely not in cache and causes a split. Sequential inserts append to the rightmost page, which is always hot. On a large table the difference in insert throughput is substantial, and it also fragments the index over time.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • S119
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A ledger is not a balances table — it is an append-only log of double-entry entries. Every transaction writes balanced debits and credits, the sum of all entries is always zero, and the balance of an account is derived by summing its entries.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          That structure is what makes errors detectable: if the global sum is not zero, something is wrong and you can find it. A mutable balances table can drift silently, and there is no way to prove what happened.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Immutability is schema and permissions, not a database choice: grant the application INSERT only, and express corrections as reversing entries rather than updates. Then what was the balance on 3 March is answerable by construction, which is exactly what an auditor asks.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The model, and the balance question
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          SCHEMA
  CREATE TABLE ledger_entry (
    id            bigserial primary key,
    transaction_id uuid    not null,       -- groups the balanced entries
    account_id    bigint   not null,
    direction     char(1)  not null,       -- 'D' debit, 'C' credit
    amount_minor  bigint   not null CHECK (amount_minor > 0),
    currency      char(3)  not null,
    created_at    timestamptz not null default now(),
    idempotency_key text UNIQUE            -- retries are safe
  );
  REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON ledger_entry FROM app_role;   -- INSERT ONLY

INVARIANTS
  per transaction:  SUM(debits) = SUM(credits)          -- enforce in a tx
  globally:         SUM(signed amounts) = 0             -- a reconciliation check
  never mix currencies in one transaction without an explicit FX pair

CORRECTIONS ARE NEW ENTRIES, never updates
  a mistake is fixed by a REVERSING transaction that references the
  original. The history shows both, which is the point.

BALANCE - the design decision
  derived: SUM over entries. Always correct. Slow as history grows.
  -> SNAPSHOT: a balance row per account per day (or per N entries),
     with the current balance = snapshot + entries since.
     the snapshot is a CACHE, rebuildable from the log.
  -> and a nightly job that recomputes from scratch and ALERTS on
     any divergence. That job is your correctness canary.

MONEY IS AN INTEGER IN MINOR UNITS. Never a float. Never.
Currency travels with every amount.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Where does concurrency bite?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          On a hot account — a merchant settlement account receiving thousands of entries a second. Since entries are append-only there is no update contention on the log itself, which is a real advantage. Contention appears on the snapshot row, so update it asynchronously or shard it, rather than serialising every write behind one row.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          How do you handle a balance check before a debit?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Read the balance and write conditionally in one transaction — a check-then-act at Read Committed is a write skew waiting to happen. Either lock the account row, use Serializable and retry, or express the constraint so the database enforces it. This is exactly the write-skew scenario from the isolation topic, in its most expensive form.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • S120
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Integrating with a payment gateway is fundamentally about not knowing whether a request succeeded. A timeout means the charge may or may not have happened, and both retrying blindly and giving up are wrong.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            So the design has three parts: an idempotency key on every request so a retry is safe, a local record written before the call so you always know an attempt was made, and a reconciliation process that compares your records with the provider's and resolves anything unknown.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Reconciliation is not a nice-to-have — it is the mechanism that makes the system correct. Webhooks are unreliable and can arrive out of order or twice; a daily settlement file from the provider is authoritative, and the difference between it and your ledger is the thing you must drive to zero.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Write first, retry safely, reconcile always
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            THE FLOW
  1  write a local PaymentAttempt (PENDING) with our idempotency key
     -> BEFORE the network call. If we crash now, we know we tried.
  2  POST to the gateway with Idempotency-Key
  3  outcomes:
       200 success        -> mark SUCCEEDED, write ledger entries
       4xx declined       -> mark DECLINED (terminal)
       TIMEOUT / 5xx      -> STATUS UNKNOWN. Do NOT retry blindly.
                             -> retry with the SAME key (safe), or
                             -> QUERY the gateway for that key
                             -> or leave for reconciliation

WEBHOOKS - unreliable by nature
  may arrive twice, out of order, or never
  -> verify the signature
  -> dedupe on the provider's event id
  -> handle out-of-order via a status precedence (never move SUCCEEDED
     back to PENDING)
  -> they are an OPTIMISATION. Reconciliation is the correctness mechanism.

RECONCILIATION - the part that makes it correct
  daily: fetch the provider's settlement file
  three-way compare: our attempts | our ledger | their file
    in theirs, not ours    -> a charge we do not know about. INVESTIGATE.
    in ours, not theirs    -> a PENDING that never completed. Resolve.
    amount mismatch        -> fees, FX, or a partial capture
  -> drive the exception count to zero, every day
  -> the count of unreconciled items is a first-class business metric

NEVER let the customer's request depend on the webhook arriving.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            What do you do with a payment stuck in UNKNOWN?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Query the provider for that idempotency key, which is what it is for — most gateways let you look up by it. If that is unavailable, leave it pending and let reconciliation resolve it against the settlement file, with a bounded window after which it is escalated. Never guess, and never let a stuck attempt block the user indefinitely — tell them it is processing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Why is the local record written before the call?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Because a crash between sending the request and recording it leaves you with a charge you have no record of — the worst outcome, since you cannot even reconcile what you do not know you attempted. Writing first means every attempt is discoverable, and an orphaned PENDING is a known unknown rather than an invisible one.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • S121
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Fraud detection has a split latency budget: an inline decision must return in tens of milliseconds because a payment is waiting on it, while a slower asynchronous path can do heavier analysis and act after the fact. Trying to do everything inline is the mistake.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The inline path evaluates rules and a model over precomputed features — counts and aggregates maintained by a streaming job, not computed by querying the transaction table at request time. Card used in 3 countries in the last hour must be a counter lookup, not a scan.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Name the tradeoff explicitly: false positives cost real customers. Blocking a legitimate transaction is a visible failure with a support call attached, so most systems have three outcomes rather than two — approve, review, decline — and tune the thresholds with the business, not alone.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two paths, and the feature problem
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              INLINE (<50ms, blocking the payment)
  fetch precomputed features from a low-latency store
      velocity: txns in last 1m / 1h / 24h, per card / device / ip
      novelty: first time at this merchant? new device? new country?
      amount vs this customer's own distribution
  -> rules (hard blocks: sanctioned entity, known-bad device)
  -> model score
  -> APPROVE | REVIEW | DECLINE
  FAIL OPEN or FAIL CLOSED? A business decision, per amount band.
     small amount + scorer down -> approve, catch it async
     large amount + scorer down -> hold for review

ASYNC (seconds to minutes)
  the full event stream -> graph features (shared devices, shared
  addresses across accounts), heavier models, cross-account patterns
  -> can still reverse: hold the payout, freeze the account, flag for review
  -> most real fraud RINGS are only visible here, not per-transaction

FEATURES - the actual engineering problem
  a streaming job maintains counters in a KV store, keyed by
  card/device/ip/account, with sliding windows.
  MUST be identical in definition to what the model trained on.
  -> training/serving skew here means silently degraded detection

FEEDBACK LOOP
  confirmed fraud + chargebacks (which arrive WEEKS later) become labels
  -> label delay is the hard part: you retrain on data whose ground truth
     you only learn after the fact, and fraud patterns shift faster than that

METRICS: not "accuracy" - fraud is ~0.1% of traffic, so predicting
"never fraud" is 99.9% accurate and useless.
  -> precision/recall, $ blocked vs $ lost, and FALSE POSITIVE RATE
     tracked as a customer-experience metric.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Why not just query the transaction table for velocity?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Because it is a scan under a hard latency budget, on the write-hot table, in the payment path — it will not hold at volume and it couples fraud checks to the transaction store's health. Streaming counters make it an O(1) lookup, at the cost of maintaining a pipeline and accepting a small lag.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              How do you handle the label delay?
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Accept that confirmed labels arrive weeks late via chargebacks, and supplement them with faster signals — manual review outcomes, customer disputes, rule hits. Retrain on a schedule that reflects the label lag, and monitor score distribution drift rather than waiting for accuracy metrics that cannot be computed yet.
