                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L24
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      A class that takes its collaborators through the constructor needs no factory, no singleton accessor, and no service locator. Construction moves to one place at startup (the composition root), where the wiring is explicit and readable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      This is why modern codebases have far fewer creational patterns than the GoF catalogue suggests. Say this in an interview when singleton comes up — it shows you know the pattern's purpose rather than just its shape.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      DI replaces the creational patterns
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      // WITH creational patterns everywhere
class OrderService {
    void place(Order o) {
        Logger log        = Logger.getInstance();               // Singleton
        Repo repo         = RepoFactory.create("mysql");        // Factory
        Mailer m          = ServiceLocator.get(Mailer.class);   // Locator
        // three hidden dependencies; untestable without global setup
    }
}

// WITH constructor injection
class OrderService {
    private final Logger log;
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final Mailer mailer;

    OrderService(Logger log, OrderRepository repo, Mailer mailer) {
        this.log = log; this.repo = repo; this.mailer = mailer;
    }
    // Every dependency is visible in the signature.
    // The test passes fakes. No framework required.
}

// COMPOSITION ROOT - the one place that knows concrete types
var service = new OrderService(
    new Slf4jLogger(),
    new MySqlOrderRepository(dataSource),
    new SesMailer(sesClient));

// A long constructor is now a DESIGN SIGNAL: too many dependencies
// means the class has too many responsibilities.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A constructor must be named after its class, so two constructors differing only by meaning have to differ by parameter types. A static factory can be called Duration.ofSeconds and Duration.ofMillis — same signature, different meaning, both readable.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The ability to return a subtype is what lets List.of() return a different implementation for zero, one, or many elements without the caller knowing or caring.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Names, caching, subtypes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        // Constructors cannot express intent
new Duration(60);        // 60 what?

// Static factories can
Duration.ofSeconds(60);
Duration.ofMinutes(1);   // same param type, different meaning - impossible
                         // with constructors

// 2. Not required to create a new instance
public static Boolean valueOf(boolean b) {
    return b ? Boolean.TRUE : Boolean.FALSE;    // cached, never allocates
}

// 3. Can return a SUBTYPE the caller does not know about
public static <E> List<E> of(E... elements) {
    return switch (elements.length) {
        case 0  -> ImmutableCollections.EMPTY_LIST;   // three different
        case 1  -> new List12<>(elements[0]);         // implementations,
        default -> new ListN<>(elements);             // one API
    };
}

// CONVENTIONAL NAMES
//   of / valueOf   an instance for these values
//   from           type conversion
//   getInstance    possibly cached
//   newInstance    guaranteed new
//   create         guaranteed new

// COST: a class with only private constructors cannot be subclassed.
// Often a feature, occasionally a limitation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • L26
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Object adapter holds an instance of the adaptee and delegates; class adapter inherits from it. Object adapter is nearly always right — it works with final classes, can adapt subclasses, and does not inherit the adaptee's whole surface.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The strategic value is that Adapter is where you put the ugliness. Third-party exceptions, odd null conventions and unit mismatches get translated once, at the boundary, so your domain never learns the vendor's vocabulary.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Object adapter at a boundary
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          // Your domain owns this interface
interface PaymentProcessor {
    PaymentResult charge(Money amount, CardToken token);
}

// The vendor's SDK, which you cannot change
class StripeSdk {
    StripeCharge createCharge(int amountInCents, String currency, String src)
        throws StripeException { ... }
}

// The adapter: translates types, units, AND exceptions
class StripeAdapter implements PaymentProcessor {
    private final StripeSdk stripe;

    public PaymentResult charge(Money amount, CardToken token) {
        try {
            StripeCharge c = stripe.createCharge(
                (int) amount.minorUnits(),          // unit translation
                amount.currency().code(),
                token.value());
            return PaymentResult.success(c.getId());
        } catch (StripeCardException e) {
            return PaymentResult.declined(e.getDeclineCode());   // vendor
        } catch (StripeException e) {                            // exception
            throw new PaymentUnavailable(e);                     // translated
        }
    }
}
// Swapping to Adyen = one new adapter. The domain does not change.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • L27
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The key structural detail is that the decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and holds a reference to it. That is what lets decorators nest arbitrarily and why the caller cannot tell how many layers there are.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Java's I/O streams are the canonical example, and so is every HTTP middleware chain you have written. The cost is debugging: a stack trace through five decorators is hard to read, and the order of wrapping matters.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Stacking behaviour at runtime
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            interface DataSource { void write(String s); String read(); }

class FileDataSource implements DataSource { /* the real one */ }

abstract class Decorator implements DataSource {
    protected final DataSource wrapped;              // SAME interface
    Decorator(DataSource wrapped) { this.wrapped = wrapped; }
}

class Encrypted extends Decorator {
    Encrypted(DataSource d) { super(d); }
    public void write(String s) { wrapped.write(encrypt(s)); }
    public String read()        { return decrypt(wrapped.read()); }
}
class Compressed extends Decorator {
    Compressed(DataSource d) { super(d); }
    public void write(String s) { wrapped.write(zip(s)); }
    public String read()        { return unzip(wrapped.read()); }
}

// Any combination, chosen at runtime
DataSource ds = new Encrypted(new Compressed(new FileDataSource("f.txt")));
ds.write("secret");         // compress, then encrypt, then write

// ORDER MATTERS: compress-then-encrypt is right;
// encrypt-then-compress compresses random bytes and achieves nothing.

// Java's own I/O is exactly this:
new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f)));

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • L28
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Structurally Decorator and Proxy are near-identical — both implement the target interface and hold a reference to it. The distinction is what they do: a decorator's job is to add to the result, a proxy's job is to decide whether and when to call at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The other practical difference is who creates the wrapped object. A decorator is handed one; a proxy usually creates or manages the lifetime of its subject, which is what makes lazy loading possible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Telling them apart
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              // DECORATOR - adds behaviour, is GIVEN the object, stacks freely
new Compressed(new Encrypted(realSource))
   → intent: the result is different (compressed, encrypted)

// PROXY - controls access, usually CREATES/owns the subject, rarely stacks
class LazyImage implements Image {
    private final String path;
    private RealImage real;                  // not loaded yet
    public void display() {
        if (real == null) real = new RealImage(path);   // proxy DECIDES when
        real.display();
    }
}
   → intent: the result is the same, the access is controlled

// INHERITANCE - compile-time, permanent, one combination only
class CompressedEncryptedFileSource extends FileSource { ... }
   → intent: a new type

QUICK TEST
  "Can I add and remove this at runtime, in any order?"  -> Decorator
  "Am I deciding whether the real call happens at all?"  -> Proxy
  "Is this a genuinely new type forever?"                -> Inheritance

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                A facade does not hide the subsystem — advanced callers can still reach past it. It provides the common path, so the ninety percent case is one call, and the ten percent case is still possible.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The risk is the facade growing into a God object as every new use case adds a method. When it exceeds roughly a dozen methods, split it by use case rather than continuing to add.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                One call instead of six
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                // WITHOUT: every caller must know the correct sequence
VideoFile file          = new VideoFile(path);
Codec source            = CodecFactory.extract(file);
Codec dest              = format.equals("mp4") ? new Mp4Codec() : new OggCodec();
VideoBuffer buffer      = BitrateReader.read(file, source);
VideoBuffer converted   = BitrateReader.convert(buffer, dest);
File result             = new AudioMixer().fix(converted);
// six classes, one correct order, repeated at every call site

// WITH a facade
class VideoConverter {
    public File convert(String path, String format) {
        // exactly the six lines above, written ONCE
    }
}
new VideoConverter().convert("clip.ogg", "mp4");

// The subsystem stays public. A caller needing custom bitrate handling
// can still use BitrateReader directly - the facade is a shortcut,
// not a wall.

// SMELL: a facade with 30 methods is no longer a facade. Split it:
//   VideoConverter, VideoThumbnailer, VideoMetadataReader

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • L30
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Virtual proxies defer expensive creation until first use. Protection proxies check permissions before delegating. Remote proxies make a network call look like a local one — every RPC stub is this. Caching proxies memoise results.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Proxies are everywhere in frameworks: Hibernate's lazy collections, Spring's @Transactional, every mocking library. They are usually generated at runtime rather than hand-written, which is worth mentioning.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The four kinds
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  interface Image { void display(); }

// VIRTUAL - defer expensive work until actually needed
class LazyImage implements Image {
    private final String path;
    private RealImage real;
    public void display() {
        if (real == null) real = new RealImage(path);   // 5MB load, deferred
        real.display();
    }
}

// PROTECTION - authorise before delegating
class SecureDocument implements Document {
    private final Document doc; private final User user;
    public String read() {
        if (!user.canRead(doc)) throw new AccessDenied();
        return doc.read();
    }
}

// CACHING - memoise
class CachedApi implements Api {
    private final Api api;
    private final Map<String, Response> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public Response get(String k) { return cache.computeIfAbsent(k, api::get); }
}

// REMOTE - local call, network underneath. Every gRPC/REST stub.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • L31
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The design decision is where the child-management methods live. Putting add() and remove() on the shared interface makes the client uniform but forces leaves to implement methods that do not apply — an ISP violation the GoF book explicitly acknowledges as a trade-off.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Putting them only on the composite keeps each type honest, at the cost of the client sometimes needing to know which it has. For interviews, the safer answer is child methods on the composite only, and say why.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    A tree the client cannot tell apart
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    interface FileSystemNode {
    String name();
    long   size();                      // both leaves and composites have this
}

class FileLeaf implements FileSystemNode {
    private final long bytes;
    public long size() { return bytes; }
}

class Directory implements FileSystemNode {
    private final List<FileSystemNode> children = new ArrayList<>();

    public void add(FileSystemNode n)    { children.add(n); }     // composite
    public void remove(FileSystemNode n) { children.remove(n); }  // ONLY

    public long size() {                                // recursion is the point
        return children.stream().mapToLong(FileSystemNode::size).sum();
    }
}

// The client does not branch on type
long total = node.size();      // works for one file or a 10,000-node tree

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L32
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The classic setup: shapes (circle, square) and rendering (vector, raster). Inheritance gives you VectorCircle, RasterCircle, VectorSquare, RasterSquare — and adding a third shape or a third renderer multiplies again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Bridge separates the abstraction hierarchy from the implementation hierarchy and connects them with composition. Recognising it is mostly about noticing that a class name contains two adjectives.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two hierarchies, one reference
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      // WITHOUT bridge: m x n classes
class VectorCircle {}  class RasterCircle {}
class VectorSquare {}  class RasterSquare {}
// add a Triangle -> 2 more.  add SvgRenderer -> 3 more.  m x n.

// WITH bridge: m + n classes
interface Renderer {                          // IMPLEMENTATION axis
    void renderCircle(double x, double y, double r);
    void renderRect(double x, double y, double w, double h);
}
class VectorRenderer implements Renderer { ... }
class RasterRenderer implements Renderer { ... }

abstract class Shape {                        // ABSTRACTION axis
    protected final Renderer renderer;        // the BRIDGE
    Shape(Renderer renderer) { this.renderer = renderer; }
    abstract void draw();
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double x, y, r;
    void draw() { renderer.renderCircle(x, y, r); }
}
class Square extends Shape { ... }

new Circle(new RasterRenderer(), 0, 0, 5);    // any combination
// 3 shapes + 3 renderers = 6 classes, not 9.

// THE TELL: a class name with two adjectives (BufferedEncryptedStream).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • L33
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A forest of a million trees does not need a million copies of the mesh and texture — it needs a million (x, y) pairs pointing at a handful of shared TreeType objects. Java's Integer.valueOf cache and string interning are flyweights you already use.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It only pays at genuinely large object counts, and it forces the shared part to be immutable, since it is visible to everyone. Reach for it when profiling shows memory pressure, not before.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Shared intrinsic, passed extrinsic
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        // INTRINSIC - shared, immutable, expensive
record TreeType(String name, Color color, Texture texture) {
    void draw(Canvas c, int x, int y) {  c.drawMesh(texture, x, y); }
}

class TreeTypeFactory {
    private static final Map<String, TreeType> CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static TreeType get(String name, Color color, Texture t) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(name + color, k -> new TreeType(name, color, t));
    }
}

// EXTRINSIC - unique per instance, tiny
record Tree(int x, int y, TreeType type) {      // holds a REFERENCE
    void draw(Canvas c) { type.draw(c, x, y); }
}

// 1,000,000 trees, 3 TreeType objects.
// Without: 1M x (mesh + texture) ≈ gigabytes
// With:    1M x (2 ints + pointer) + 3 shared objects ≈ megabytes

// YOU ALREADY USE THESE
Integer.valueOf(100)   // cached -128..127; == works, which surprises people
"hello".intern()       // string pool

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • L34
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The rules are mechanical: all fields final, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs on the way in and mutable fields on the way out, and the class final so a subclass cannot add mutability.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The cost is allocation — every modification produces a new object. In practice this is almost always the right trade, and Java records make it nearly free to write.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Making it actually immutable
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          public final class Period {                       // final: no mutable subclass
    private final Date start;                     // final fields
    private final Date end;
    private final List<String> tags;

    public Period(Date start, Date end, List<String> tags) {
        // DEFENSIVE COPY IN - the caller still holds their Date
        this.start = new Date(start.getTime());
        this.end   = new Date(end.getTime());
        this.tags  = List.copyOf(tags);
        if (this.start.after(this.end))            // validate AFTER copying,
            throw new IllegalArgumentException();  // or you check a value the
    }                                              // caller can still change

    // DEFENSIVE COPY OUT - or the caller mutates your internals
    public Date start() { return new Date(start.getTime()); }
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }    // already unmodifiable

    // "Modification" returns a new instance
    public Period withEnd(Date newEnd) { return new Period(start, newEnd, tags); }
}

// Records do most of this for you - but NOT the defensive copies:
record Period(LocalDate start, LocalDate end) {   // LocalDate is immutable ✓
    Period { if (start.isAfter(end)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • L35
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Delegation is the mechanism — an object forwarding a call to another object it holds. Wrapper is the shape — an object with the same interface as the thing it holds, which is what Decorator and Proxy both are. Mixin is a way to share implementation without inheritance, which Java approximates with default methods on interfaces.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The useful distinction in review: delegation without a matching interface is just composition. It becomes a wrapper only when the outer type is substitutable for the inner one.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Precise vocabulary
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            // DELEGATION - forwarding, no shared interface required
class Car {
    private final Engine engine;
    void start() { engine.ignite(); }     // delegating, not wrapping
}

// WRAPPER - same interface as what it holds (Decorator/Proxy are both this)
class LoggingList<E> implements List<E> {
    private final List<E> inner;
    public boolean add(E e) { log(e); return inner.add(e); }
    // substitutable for the thing it wraps
}

// MIXIN - shared behaviour without a base class (default methods)
interface Auditable {
    Instant createdAt();
    default Duration age() {              // implementation, no state
        return Duration.between(createdAt(), Instant.now());
    }
}
class Order implements Auditable, Comparable<Order> { ... }   // multiple mixins

// Java has no true mixins (no state in interfaces). Scala traits and
// Kotlin's delegation (`by`) come closer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Done whenYou can spot a growing if/else chain, a hard-coded algorithm, or a notification problem and convert it to the right behavioural pattern on the spot.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • L36
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Each branch becomes a class implementing a common interface; the context holds one and delegates. Adding a case becomes adding a class, which is Open/Closed delivered along the algorithm axis.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              In modern Java a strategy is often just a lambda or a method reference — Comparator is the standard library's most-used Strategy. Do not build an interface hierarchy when a functional interface will do.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Killing the if/else chain
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              // BEFORE: every new method edits this file
class Checkout {
    Money fee(String method, Money amount) {
        if (method.equals("card"))   return amount.percent(2.5);
        if (method.equals("upi"))    return Money.ZERO;
        if (method.equals("wallet")) return amount.percent(1.0);
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(method);
    }
}

// AFTER: a new method is a new class
interface FeePolicy { Money fee(Money amount); }

class CardFee   implements FeePolicy { public Money fee(Money a){ return a.percent(2.5);} }
class UpiFee    implements FeePolicy { public Money fee(Money a){ return Money.ZERO; } }
class WalletFee implements FeePolicy { public Money fee(Money a){ return a.percent(1.0);} }

class Checkout {
    private final FeePolicy policy;                 // injected
    Checkout(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; }
    Money fee(Money amount) { return policy.fee(amount); }   // no branching
}

// Often a lambda is enough - do not over-build
Map<String, FeePolicy> policies = Map.of(
    "card", a -> a.percent(2.5),
    "upi",  a -> Money.ZERO);

// The standard library's Strategy you use daily:
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::total).reversed());
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Follow-ups they will ask
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              “Strategy vs simply passing a lambda?”
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              They are the same pattern. Use a named interface when the strategy has multiple methods, needs state, or the name itself documents the domain concept. Use a lambda when it is one function.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • L37
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies them on change. The listener must be able to detach, and something must actually call detach — in UI code that is usually a lifecycle hook, and forgetting it is the lapsed listener problem.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Two further sharp edges: notification order is not guaranteed and should not be relied on, and a listener that throws can prevent later listeners from being notified unless you isolate each call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Subject, observers, and the leak
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                interface OrderListener { void onPlaced(Order o); }

class OrderService {
    private final List<OrderListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    //                                            ^ safe iteration while
    //                                              a listener unsubscribes

    public void subscribe(OrderListener l)   { listeners.add(l); }
    public void unsubscribe(OrderListener l) { listeners.remove(l); }  // MUST exist

    private void notifyPlaced(Order o) {
        for (OrderListener l : listeners) {
            try { l.onPlaced(o); }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("listener failed", e); }
            //    ^ one bad listener must not block the rest
        }
    }
}

// THE LAPSED LISTENER LEAK
class OrderScreen {
    OrderScreen(OrderService svc) { svc.subscribe(this::refresh); }
    // screen closes... but the service still holds the reference.
    // The screen, its views and its data are never collected.
}
// FIX: unsubscribe in the lifecycle teardown, or hold WeakReferences.

// DO NOT rely on notification ORDER. If B must run after A, that is a
// dependency Observer cannot express - use an explicit pipeline.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • L38
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  That indirection is the trade. Pub-sub decouples completely, allows publishers and subscribers to be deployed separately, and supports persistence and replay. It also makes control flow untraceable — you cannot find the handlers by following references.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  In-process, Observer is usually right: it is traceable and synchronous. Reach for a broker when you genuinely need decoupling across process or team boundaries.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The broker in between
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  // OBSERVER - the subject KNOWS its listeners
class OrderService {
    private final List<OrderListener> listeners;      // direct references
    void place(Order o) { listeners.forEach(l -> l.onPlaced(o)); }
}
// + synchronous, traceable: "find usages" shows every handler
// + errors propagate to a place you can see
// - subject and listener share a type; both must be deployed together

// PUB-SUB - neither side knows the other
class OrderService {
    private final EventBus bus;
    void place(Order o) { bus.publish(new OrderPlaced(o.id())); }
}
// elsewhere, possibly another service entirely:
bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> mailer.sendConfirmation(e.orderId()));

// + total decoupling, async, can persist/replay, fan out to many consumers
// - "who handles OrderPlaced?" is not answerable from the IDE
// - error handling and ordering become YOUR problem
// - a typo in the event name fails silently

// IN-PROCESS: prefer Observer. It is traceable.
// ACROSS SERVICES: pub-sub, with a real broker (Kafka, SNS/SQS).

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • L39
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Once an action is an object, it has a lifetime independent of the call. You can put it on a queue for a worker, write it to an audit log, or push it on a stack so it can be reversed. None of that is possible with a plain method call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The GoF form has a receiver, but in practice the command often just closes over what it needs. Keep the interface to one execute() method plus undo() if you need it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    An action as an object
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    interface Command {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

class AddTextCommand implements Command {
    private final Document doc;
    private final String text;
    private int insertedAt;                       // state needed to reverse

    public void execute() {
        insertedAt = doc.cursor();
        doc.insert(insertedAt, text);
    }
    public void undo() {
        doc.delete(insertedAt, insertedAt + text.length());
    }
}

// The invoker knows NOTHING about what the command does
class Button {
    private final Command command;
    void click() { command.execute(); }
}

// Because it is an object, you get all of this for free:
queue.submit(command);                    // execute later, on a worker
auditLog.write(command.describe());       // record what was requested
history.push(command);                    // undo
retryPolicy.run(command::execute);        // retry safely if idempotent

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L40
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Each command must capture enough state at execute time to reverse itself — the position it inserted at, the value it overwrote. Capturing it at construction time is a common bug, because the document may change before execution.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      For commands that cannot be cleanly reversed, the alternative is Memento: snapshot the whole state before, restore it on undo. Simpler, and heavier in memory.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Two stacks, one rule
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      class History {
    private final Deque<Command> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Command> redoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void run(Command c) {
        c.execute();
        undoStack.push(c);
        redoStack.clear();          // THE RULE people forget:
    }                               // a new action invalidates the redo branch

    void undo() {
        if (undoStack.isEmpty()) return;
        Command c = undoStack.pop();
        c.undo();
        redoStack.push(c);
    }

    void redo() {
        if (redoStack.isEmpty()) return;
        Command c = redoStack.pop();
        c.execute();
        undoStack.push(c);
    }
}

// COMPOSITE COMMAND - one undo for a multi-step action
class MacroCommand implements Command {
    private final List<Command> steps;
    public void execute() { steps.forEach(Command::execute); }
    public void undo() {
        for (int i = steps.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) steps.get(i).undo();
        //  ^ REVERSE order, or you undo into an inconsistent state
    }
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • L41
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The giveaway is a class with a status enum and methods that all start by checking it. As states multiply, every method grows another branch, and the legal transitions are scattered across the file instead of stated in one place.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        With State, each class handles only its own transitions, and the set of classes is the state diagram. Adding a state stops touching existing code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Transitions owned by states
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        // BEFORE: every method branches on status
class Order {
    Status status;
    void ship() {
        if (status == DRAFT)     throw new IllegalStateException("not paid");
        if (status == CANCELLED) throw new IllegalStateException("cancelled");
        if (status == SHIPPED)   throw new IllegalStateException("already");
        status = SHIPPED;
    }
    void cancel() { /* the same four branches again */ }
}

// AFTER: each state knows its own legal moves
interface OrderState {
    default OrderState pay()    { throw new IllegalTransition(); }
    default OrderState ship()   { throw new IllegalTransition(); }
    default OrderState cancel() { throw new IllegalTransition(); }
}

class Draft implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay()    { return new Paid(); }
    public OrderState cancel() { return new Cancelled(); }
    // ship() inherits the default throw - illegal BY CONSTRUCTION
}
class Paid implements OrderState {
    public OrderState ship()   { return new Shipped(); }
    public OrderState cancel() { return new Refunding(); }
}
class Shipped implements OrderState { /* terminal */ }

class Order {
    private OrderState state = new Draft();
    void ship() { state = state.ship(); }        // no branching anywhere
}

// The class list IS the state diagram. That is the win.
