                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • L42
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          A second tell is whether the implementations know about each other. Strategies are independent and interchangeable; states return the next state, so they reference each other and form a graph.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Interviewers ask this specifically because the structures are identical. The answer is intent and transition ownership, not shape.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Same shape, opposite intent
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          // STRATEGY - the CLIENT chooses, strategies never know each other
new Checkout(new CardFee());          // caller decides
new Checkout(new UpiFee());           // swap freely, any time
// CardFee has no idea UpiFee exists.

// STATE - the OBJECT transitions itself, states reference each other
class Draft implements OrderState {
    public OrderState pay() { return new Paid(); }   // Draft KNOWS Paid
}
// The client calls order.pay(); it does not pick "Paid".

DIMENSION            STRATEGY              STATE
who chooses          the client            the object itself
implementations      independent           reference each other
changes during life  usually set once      changes constantly
represents           an algorithm          a lifecycle position
adding one           independent class     must wire transitions in

// If your "strategies" return other strategies, you have written State.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • L43
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The base class owns the algorithm's order — which is exactly the part you do not want subclasses changing — and calls abstract or overridable hooks at the varying points. Mark the template method final so the sequence cannot be broken.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The trade-off against Strategy: Template Method is compile-time and inheritance-based, Strategy is runtime and composition-based. Template Method wins when there are many small variation points; Strategy wins when there is one and you want to swap it live.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Fixed order, variable steps
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            abstract class DataImporter {

    public final void run(Path file) {          // FINAL: order is not negotiable
        var raw       = read(file);             // hook
        var records   = parse(raw);             // hook
        validate(records);                      // shared
        var saved     = save(records);          // hook
        afterImport(saved);                     // optional hook
    }

    protected abstract String read(Path f);
    protected abstract List<Record> parse(String raw);
    protected abstract int save(List<Record> rs);

    private void validate(List<Record> rs) { /* shared by all importers */ }
    protected void afterImport(int count) { }   // HOOK: default does nothing
}

class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    protected List<Record> parse(String raw) { /* CSV */ }
    protected void afterImport(int c) { metrics.increment("csv", c); }
}
class JsonImporter extends DataImporter { /* only parse differs */ }

// The Hollywood principle: "don't call us, we'll call you."
// Subclasses never invoke the algorithm; the base class invokes them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            My notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • L44
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Each handler decides: handle it, pass it on, or both. The sender does not know which handler will respond, and handlers can be reordered or inserted without touching each other.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Two decisions define your variant: whether a handler may stop the chain, and whether handlers can act on the way back up. HTTP middleware usually allows both, which is why it can wrap timing and error handling around everything downstream.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              A handler chain
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              abstract class Handler {
    private Handler next;
    Handler linkTo(Handler next) { this.next = next; return next; }

    public final void handle(Request r) {
        if (process(r)) {                    // true = handled, stop here
            return;
        }
        if (next != null) next.handle(r);
    }
    protected abstract boolean process(Request r);
}

class AuthHandler extends Handler {
    protected boolean process(Request r) {
        if (!r.hasValidToken()) { r.reject(401); return true; }   // STOPS
        return false;                                             // continue
    }
}
class RateLimitHandler extends Handler { ... }
class RouteHandler extends Handler { ... }

// Wire it - order is the configuration
Handler chain = new AuthHandler();
chain.linkTo(new RateLimitHandler()).linkTo(new RouteHandler());
chain.handle(request);

// MIDDLEWARE VARIANT - acts on the way back up too
Response handle(Request r, Chain next) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    Response resp = next.proceed(r);            // everything downstream
    metrics.record(System.nanoTime() - start);  // runs AFTER
    return resp;
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • L45
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The value is that the traversal logic lives with the collection that understands its own structure, while the client writes the same loop regardless. It also permits multiple independent traversals at once, each with its own position.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The detail worth knowing is fail-fast behaviour: modifying a collection while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException, which is a deliberate design choice to surface a bug rather than produce silent corruption.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Implementing one
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                class BinaryTree<T> implements Iterable<T> {
    private Node<T> root;

    public Iterator<T> iterator() {          // in-order, lazily
        return new Iterator<>() {
            private final Deque<Node<T>> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
            private Node<T> current = root;

            public boolean hasNext() { return current != null || !stack.isEmpty(); }

            public T next() {
                while (current != null) { stack.push(current); current = current.left; }
                Node<T> node = stack.pop();
                current = node.right;
                return node.value;
            }
        };
    }
}

// The client never learns it is a tree
for (String s : tree) { ... }

// FAIL-FAST: deliberate, and worth explaining
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a","b"));
for (String s : list) list.remove(s);     // ConcurrentModificationException
// Correct removal during iteration:
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("a"));
// or use the iterator's own remove():
var it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) { if (cond(it.next())) it.remove(); }

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The canonical case is a dialog where changing one field enables, disables or clears others. Wiring those rules directly between widgets couples every widget to every other; a mediator holds the interaction rules in one readable place.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The risk is real: the mediator accumulates all the logic and becomes a God object. That is acceptable when the logic genuinely is the coordination — and a warning sign when it starts doing the components' work for them.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  n² wiring becomes n
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  // WITHOUT: every control knows the others
class LoginButton {
    private UsernameField user; private PasswordField pass;
    private ErrorLabel error;  private RememberCheckbox remember;
    // and each of those knows several others. n^2 references.
}

// WITH: everyone knows only the mediator
interface DialogMediator { void notify(Component sender, String event); }

class LoginDialog implements DialogMediator {
    private final UsernameField user;  private final PasswordField pass;
    private final LoginButton   login; private final ErrorLabel error;

    public void notify(Component sender, String event) {
        if (sender == user && event.equals("changed")) {
            login.setEnabled(user.isValid() && pass.isFilled());
            error.clear();
        }
        if (sender == login && event.equals("clicked")) {
            if (!authenticate()) error.show("Invalid credentials");
        }
    }
    // ALL interaction rules, one place, readable top to bottom
}

class UsernameField extends Component {
    void onChange() { mediator.notify(this, "changed"); }   // knows only this
}

// MEDIATOR vs OBSERVER: mediator is about coordinating a known set of
// colleagues; observer is about broadcasting to unknown listeners.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  My notes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Saved links
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    1↗

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • L47
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The originator creates the memento and is the only thing that can read it. The caretaker holds mementos and hands them back, but must not be able to inspect or modify them — otherwise you have just made the private state public with extra steps.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    In Java this is usually done with a private nested class implementing a marker interface: the outside world sees the marker, only the originator sees the fields.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Snapshot without exposing state
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    class Editor {
    private String content;
    private int cursor;

    // Opaque to everyone except Editor
    public interface Snapshot { }                 // marker: no methods

    private class State implements Snapshot {     // PRIVATE nested class
        final String content = Editor.this.content;
        final int    cursor  = Editor.this.cursor;
    }

    public Snapshot save() { return new State(); }

    public void restore(Snapshot s) {
        State state = (State) s;                  // only Editor can read it
        this.content = state.content;
        this.cursor  = state.cursor;
    }
}

// The caretaker holds them blindly
class History {
    private final Deque<Editor.Snapshot> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void push(Editor.Snapshot s) { stack.push(s); }   // cannot inspect it
    Editor.Snapshot pop()        { return stack.pop(); }
}

// MEMENTO vs COMMAND for undo:
//   Command  - store the ACTION, reverse it. Memory-cheap, needs a
//              correct undo() per command.
//   Memento  - store the STATE, restore it. Always correct, uses more
//              memory. Right when actions are hard to reverse.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L48
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      It works by double dispatch: the element calls visitor.visit(this), so the concrete types of both element and visitor determine the method. That is what recovers the type information a single virtual call loses.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      The cost is severe and worth stating: adding a new element type forces you to edit the visitor interface and every implementation. Visitor is only correct when the type hierarchy is stable and the operations change — the exact opposite of most business code.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Double dispatch
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      interface Node { <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v); }

record NumberNode(double value)          implements Node {
    public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitNumber(this); }
}
record AddNode(Node left, Node right)    implements Node {
    public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); }
}

interface Visitor<R> {
    R visitNumber(NumberNode n);
    R visitAdd(AddNode n);
}

// A NEW OPERATION is a new class - no AST class is edited
class Evaluator implements Visitor<Double> {
    public Double visitNumber(NumberNode n) { return n.value(); }
    public Double visitAdd(AddNode n) {
        return n.left().accept(this) + n.right().accept(this);
    }
}
class Printer implements Visitor<String> { ... }   // and another, and another

// THE TRADE, stated plainly:
//   new OPERATION  -> one new visitor class          ✓ easy
//   new NODE TYPE  -> edit the interface and EVERY   ✗ brutal
//                     visitor implementation

// Use it when types are stable and operations grow: compilers, ASTs,
// document formats. Java's sealed interfaces + pattern matching are
// now often a better answer.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • L49
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Each grammar rule becomes a class implementing an interpret(context) method. Composite expressions hold sub-expressions, so evaluation is a recursive walk. It is Composite plus an operation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        It does not scale: a real language grammar produces dozens of classes and poor performance. For anything beyond a small DSL — a filter expression, a rules engine, a formula field — use a parser generator instead.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A grammar as classes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        interface Expression { boolean interpret(Map<String, Object> context); }

record Equals(String field, Object value) implements Expression {
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, Object> ctx) {
        return Objects.equals(ctx.get(field), value);
    }
}
record And(Expression left, Expression right) implements Expression {
    public boolean interpret(Map<String, Object> ctx) {
        return left.interpret(ctx) && right.interpret(ctx);   // recursion
    }
}
record Or(Expression left, Expression right)  implements Expression { ... }
record Not(Expression inner)                  implements Expression { ... }

// "country = IN AND (tier = gold OR spend > 10000)"
Expression rule = new And(
    new Equals("country", "IN"),
    new Or(new Equals("tier", "gold"),
           new GreaterThan("spend", 10_000)));

boolean matches = rule.interpret(customerAttributes);

// GOOD FOR: feature-flag rules, search filters, permission expressions,
//           small formula languages
// BAD FOR:  anything you would call a programming language. Use ANTLR.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • L50
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The right use is where doing nothing is a valid behaviour: a no-op logger, an empty collection, a guest user with no permissions. The caller's code gets simpler and there is no branch to forget.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The wrong use is where absence means something went wrong. Silently doing nothing turns a loud failure into a mystery. When absence is exceptional, use Optional or throw — those force the caller to decide.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Do-nothing instead of null
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          interface Logger { void log(String msg); }

class NullLogger implements Logger {
    static final Logger INSTANCE = new NullLogger();
    public void log(String msg) { }               // deliberately nothing
}

// BEFORE - the check is everywhere and one call site will forget it
if (logger != null) logger.log("started");

// AFTER - no check, no NPE possible
class Service {
    private final Logger logger;
    Service(Logger logger) {
        this.logger = logger != null ? logger : NullLogger.INSTANCE;
    }
    void start() { logger.log("started"); }       // always safe
}

// YOU ALREADY USE THESE
Collections.emptyList()        // iterate with no null check
Optional.empty()
DiscountPolicy.NONE            // a policy that discounts nothing

// WHEN NOT TO: absence is an ERROR, not a valid state
Account acct = repo.find(id);        // not found -> NullAccount?
acct.debit(500);                     // silently does nothing. Money "moves".
// -> return Optional<Account>, or throw AccountNotFound.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          • L51
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Setter injection allows an object to exist in a half-built state, so every method must tolerate a null collaborator. Field injection via reflection hides dependencies entirely and makes the class impossible to construct in a test without the framework.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Use constructor injection for required dependencies and setter injection only for genuinely optional ones. A constructor with eight parameters is not an argument against the technique — it is the technique telling you the class does too much.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Constructor injection, and why
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            // CONSTRUCTOR - required, visible, final, testable without a framework
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final PaymentGateway  payments;

    OrderService(OrderRepository repo, PaymentGateway payments) {
        this.repo     = Objects.requireNonNull(repo);
        this.payments = Objects.requireNonNull(payments);
    }
}
new OrderService(new FakeRepo(), new FakeGateway());     // trivial test

// SETTER - only for genuinely OPTIONAL collaborators
class OrderService {
    private MetricsCollector metrics = MetricsCollector.NOOP;   // sane default
    void setMetrics(MetricsCollector m) { this.metrics = m; }
}

// FIELD INJECTION - avoid
class OrderService {
    @Autowired private OrderRepository repo;    // not final; invisible;
    // cannot construct this in a test without reflection or a container
}

// THE DESIGN SIGNAL
// 8 constructor parameters is not a reason to switch to field injection.
// It is the class telling you it has 8 responsibilities.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            My notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • L52
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              IoC means the framework calls your code rather than your code calling the framework — the Hollywood principle. Template Method is IoC. A servlet is IoC. DI is IoC applied specifically to object construction.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The container's actual job is building the object graph in dependency order and managing lifetimes. That is genuinely useful at scale and pure overhead for a hundred-line program.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              IoC, DI, and the container
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              // NOT inverted - your code drives, and constructs what it needs
class Report {
    void run() {
        var db = new MySqlDatabase("localhost");   // decides the concrete type
        var data = db.query("...");
    }
}

// INVERTED - the caller decides; Report just declares what it needs
class Report {
    private final Database db;
    Report(Database db) { this.db = db; }
}

// THE COMPOSITION ROOT - the ONE place that knows concrete types.
// This is the whole "container" for a small application:
public static void main(String[] args) {
    var ds       = new HikariDataSource(config);
    var repo     = new MySqlOrderRepository(ds);
    var payments = new StripeAdapter(stripeSdk);
    var service  = new OrderService(repo, payments);
    new HttpServer(service).start();
}
// Explicit, greppable, no annotations, no reflection, no startup magic.

// A CONTAINER does this by reflection, and adds:
//   - lifetime scopes (singleton, per-request, per-thread)
//   - lazy construction
//   - graph resolution when there are hundreds of beans
// Worth it at scale. Not worth it at 20 classes.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • L53
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The difference is direction: with DI, dependencies are pushed in and are visible; with a locator, they are pulled from a global and are hidden. A class using a locator compiles fine and fails at runtime when the registry is not configured.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                It survives in places where DI is impractical — legacy code, plugin systems, static contexts. Name it as a deliberate compromise rather than a design choice.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Why DI wins
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                // SERVICE LOCATOR - the dependency is invisible
class OrderService {
    void place(Order o) {
        var repo = ServiceLocator.get(OrderRepository.class);    // hidden
        var pay  = ServiceLocator.get(PaymentGateway.class);     // hidden
        ...
    }
}
// Problems:
//   the constructor signature is a lie - it claims no dependencies
//   the test must configure a GLOBAL, and tests leak into each other
//   a missing registration fails at RUNTIME, not compile time
//   you cannot tell what this class needs without reading every method

// DEPENDENCY INJECTION - the dependency is part of the contract
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final PaymentGateway  payments;
    OrderService(OrderRepository repo, PaymentGateway payments) { ... }
}
//   signature is honest; test passes fakes; missing dep = compile error

// WHERE A LOCATOR IS STILL DEFENSIBLE
//   plugin systems loading unknown implementations at runtime
//   static contexts you cannot inject into (some legacy frameworks)
//   Java's own ServiceLoader / SPI mechanism

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • L54
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The interface belongs to the domain (that is DIP), and the SQL implementation belongs to infrastructure. That inversion is what makes the domain testable with an in-memory list and swappable to a different store.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  The common mistake is a repository that returns database rows or leaks query objects — then it is a DAO with a nicer name. A repository deals in domain aggregates, and its methods are named in domain language.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A collection, not a table
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  // DOMAIN owns the interface, in domain vocabulary
package domain;
public interface OrderRepository {
    Optional<Order> byId(OrderId id);
    List<Order> placedBy(CustomerId customer);
    List<Order> awaitingShipment();          // domain concept, not a WHERE clause
    void save(Order order);
}

// INFRASTRUCTURE implements it
package infra;
class JdbcOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    public List<Order> awaitingShipment() {
        var rows = jdbc.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='PAID' "
                            + "AND shipped_at IS NULL", MAPPER);
        return rows.stream().map(this::toDomain).toList();   // rows -> aggregates
    }
}

// TESTS use a real, working implementation with no database
class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final Map<OrderId, Order> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public Optional<Order> byId(OrderId id) { return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id)); }
    public void save(Order o) { store.put(o.id(), o); }
}

// SMELLS
//   findAll() returning 10M rows          -> no domain concept
//   methods returning ResultSet / Row     -> that is a DAO
//   query builders leaking to the caller  -> the abstraction failed

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    The repository saves; the unit of work decides when. It collects new, dirty and removed objects, then writes them in one transaction on commit — so the atomicity boundary matches the business operation rather than each individual save.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    In most applications a framework provides this: an ORM session, or a declarative transaction annotation. Knowing the pattern is how you explain what that annotation is actually doing.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    One transaction per business operation
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    // WITHOUT: three independent commits, no atomicity
void placeOrder(Cart cart) {
    orderRepo.save(order);        // committed
    inventoryRepo.save(stock);    // committed
    paymentRepo.save(payment);    // THROWS -> order and stock already written
}

// WITH a unit of work
class UnitOfWork implements AutoCloseable {
    private final List<Object> newObjects   = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<Object> dirtyObjects = new ArrayList<>();

    void registerNew(Object o)   { newObjects.add(o); }
    void registerDirty(Object o) { dirtyObjects.add(o); }

    void commit() {
        try (var tx = dataSource.begin()) {
            newObjects.forEach(o   -> mapperFor(o).insert(o));
            dirtyObjects.forEach(o -> mapperFor(o).update(o));
            tx.commit();                     // ALL or NOTHING
        }
    }
}

try (var uow = new UnitOfWork()) {
    var service = new OrderService(uow);
    service.placeOrder(cart);
    uow.commit();                            // one transaction
}

// YOU HAVE USED THIS ALREADY
//   @Transactional            - Spring's unit of work
//   EntityManager / Session   - JPA's, with dirty checking on flush

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L56
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Active Record couples every entity to the database schema and to a framework base class. That is a genuinely good trade for CRUD-heavy applications — Rails and Django built their success on it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Data Mapper wins when the domain model diverges from the schema, when domain logic is rich enough to want unit tests without a database, or when the same domain serves several storage backends.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Where persistence knowledge lives
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      // ACTIVE RECORD - the entity knows how to save itself
class Order extends ActiveRecord {
    Long id; String status; Money total;

    void save()   { db.execute("UPDATE orders SET ... WHERE id=?", id); }
    static Order find(Long id) { ... }
}
order.setStatus("PAID");
order.save();                          // convenient

// + fast to write, obvious, great for CRUD
// - entity coupled to the schema AND a base class
// - cannot unit test domain logic without a database
// - the entity has two responsibilities (SRP)

// DATA MAPPER - a separate object moves data between domain and storage
class Order {                          // pure domain: no DB knowledge at all
    private OrderStatus status;
    void markPaid() {
        if (status != DRAFT) throw new IllegalTransition();
        status = PAID;                 // testable with `new Order()`
    }
}
class OrderMapper {
    void save(Order o) { jdbc.execute("UPDATE orders SET ...", ...); }
    Order load(ResultSet rs) { ... }
}

// + domain is pure and unit-testable
// + schema and model can diverge
// - more classes, more mapping code

// PICK: Active Record for CRUD apps; Data Mapper when the domain has
// real rules worth testing in isolation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • L57
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        A controller should parse the request and delegate. A domain object should hold the rules. The service in between coordinates: start a transaction, load aggregates, call domain methods, save, publish events.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The failure mode is the anemic domain model — services holding all the logic and entities reduced to field bags. If your service reads a value out of an entity, computes something, and writes it back, that logic belongs on the entity.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Orchestration, not rules
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        // CONTROLLER - transport only
@PostMapping("/orders/{id}/pay")
ResponseEntity<?> pay(@PathVariable String id, @RequestBody PayRequest req) {
    var result = orderService.pay(new OrderId(id), req.toCommand());
    return ResponseEntity.ok(OrderDto.from(result));
}

// SERVICE - transaction, authorisation, orchestration. NO business rules.
class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    public Order pay(OrderId id, PayCommand cmd) {
        var order = orders.byId(id).orElseThrow(OrderNotFound::new);
        authz.require(currentUser(), CAN_PAY, order);

        var receipt = payments.charge(order.total(), cmd.token());  // external
        order.markPaid(receipt.reference());     // <- the RULE lives on Order

        orders.save(order);
        events.publish(new OrderPaid(order.id()));
        return order;
    }
}

// DOMAIN - the rules
class Order {
    void markPaid(String reference) {
        if (status != DRAFT) throw new IllegalTransition(status, PAID);
        if (total.isZero())  throw new CannotPayZero();
        this.status = PAID; this.paymentRef = reference;
    }
}

// ANEMIC SMELL: if the service does
//     if (order.getStatus() == DRAFT) order.setStatus(PAID);
// then Order is a struct and the rule is in the wrong place.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The domain model is shaped by business rules; the API response is shaped by what a client needs. Coupling them means every internal refactor risks an external contract, and every API convenience distorts the model.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          The cost is mapping code. Keep the mapping in one place per boundary and resist putting logic in it — a mapper that makes decisions is a service in disguise.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Keeping the wire out of the domain
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          // DOMAIN - shaped by rules
class Order {
    private OrderId id;
    private Money total;
    private OrderStatus status;
    private List<LineItem> items;
    private Customer customer;              // lazy-loaded relation
    private String internalRiskScore;       // must NEVER leave the system
}

// Serialising this entity directly:
//   - renaming a field breaks every client
//   - internalRiskScore leaks
//   - touching customer triggers a lazy load during serialisation
//   - the JSON shape is dictated by the ORM

// DTO - shaped by what the client needs
record OrderDto(String id, String status, long totalMinor,
                String currency, List<ItemDto> items) {

    static OrderDto from(Order o) {         // mapping in ONE place
        return new OrderDto(
            o.id().value(),
            o.status().name(),
            o.total().minorUnits(),
            o.total().currency().code(),
            o.items().stream().map(ItemDto::from).toList());
    }
}

// Now: rename a domain field freely - only the mapper changes.
// Add an API field - the domain does not move.
// Different clients get different DTOs from one model.
