                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Each rule implements isSatisfiedBy(candidate), and and, or and not combine them. The rule gets a name — EligibleForFreeShipping — which is far more communicative than an inline boolean expression.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            The advanced form also converts a specification to a query predicate, so the same rule can filter in memory or in SQL. That is where it earns its complexity.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Named, composable rules
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            interface Specification<T> {
    boolean isSatisfiedBy(T candidate);

    default Specification<T> and(Specification<T> other) {
        return c -> this.isSatisfiedBy(c) && other.isSatisfiedBy(c);
    }
    default Specification<T> or(Specification<T> other) {
        return c -> this.isSatisfiedBy(c) || other.isSatisfiedBy(c);
    }
    default Specification<T> not() { return c -> !this.isSatisfiedBy(c); }
}

record OrderOver(Money threshold) implements Specification<Order> {
    public boolean isSatisfiedBy(Order o) { return o.total().isGreaterThan(threshold); }
}
record ShipsTo(Country country) implements Specification<Order> {
    public boolean isSatisfiedBy(Order o) { return o.address().country().equals(country); }
}
record PlacedByPrimeMember() implements Specification<Order> { ... }

// The rule gets a NAME and lives in one place
Specification<Order> freeShipping =
    new OrderOver(Money.rupees(500))
        .and(new ShipsTo(INDIA))
        .or(new PlacedByPrimeMember());

if (freeShipping.isSatisfiedBy(order)) { ... }
orders.stream().filter(freeShipping::isSatisfiedBy).toList();

// Unit-testable in isolation, reusable in pricing, checkout and reporting
// - instead of the same condition written three slightly different ways.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The benefit is real: the order service stops importing the mailer, the analytics client and the loyalty service. The cost is that the call graph now lives in runtime registrations rather than in the source.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Use it for genuinely optional side effects — notifications, analytics, cache warming. Do not use it for steps the operation depends on, because a silently dropped event becomes a silently incomplete business process.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Decoupled, and untraceable
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              class EventBus {
    private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<?>>> handlers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    <E> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> handler) {
        handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).add(handler);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    <E> void publish(E event) {
        for (var h : handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of())) {
            try { ((Consumer<E>) h).accept(event); }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { log.error("handler failed", e); }
        }
    }
}

// Publisher knows nothing about consumers
class OrderService {
    void place(Order o) {
        orders.save(o);
        bus.publish(new OrderPlaced(o.id(), o.total()));
    }
}
// Registered somewhere else entirely
bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> mailer.sendConfirmation(e.orderId()));
bus.subscribe(OrderPlaced.class, e -> analytics.track("order", e.total()));

// THE COST, stated honestly
//   "What happens on OrderPlaced?" is not answerable from the IDE
//   a handler that throws is swallowed
//   ordering between handlers is undefined
//   a refactor can silently orphan a subscription

// RULE: events for OPTIONAL side effects. Direct calls for required steps.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              My notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Three states. Closed passes calls through and counts failures. Open rejects immediately without calling. After a cooldown it goes half-open and allows a trial call — success closes it, failure opens it again.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The point is protecting yourself, not the dependency. Every request waiting 30 seconds on a dead service is a thread you cannot use for healthy traffic, and that is how one failure becomes total.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Closed, open, half-open
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                class CircuitBreaker {
    enum State { CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN }

    private volatile State state = State.CLOSED;
    private final AtomicInteger failures = new AtomicInteger();
    private volatile Instant openedAt;

    private final int threshold = 5;
    private final Duration cooldown = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

    <T> T call(Supplier<T> action, Supplier<T> fallback) {
        if (state == State.OPEN) {
            if (Duration.between(openedAt, Instant.now()).compareTo(cooldown) > 0)
                state = State.HALF_OPEN;         // time to try one
            else
                return fallback.get();           // FAIL FAST - no call made
        }
        try {
            T result = action.get();
            onSuccess();
            return result;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            onFailure();
            return fallback.get();
        }
    }

    private void onSuccess() { failures.set(0); state = State.CLOSED; }

    private void onFailure() {
        if (state == State.HALF_OPEN || failures.incrementAndGet() >= threshold) {
            state = State.OPEN; openedAt = Instant.now();
        }
    }
}

// ALWAYS pair with a timeout. A breaker cannot trip on a call that
// never returns - "slow" must be counted as "failed".

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • L62
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Exponential backoff spreads retries out over time; jitter spreads them across clients. Both are needed. Cap the total attempts and the total elapsed time, or a retry storm outlives the outage that caused it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Only retry what is safe to repeat. A read is naturally idempotent; a payment is not, unless you send an idempotency key so the server can recognise the duplicate.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Backoff, jitter, and idempotency
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  <T> T withRetry(Supplier<T> action, int maxAttempts) {
    RuntimeException last = null;
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++) {
        try { return action.get(); }
        catch (RetryableException e) {
            last = e;
            long base   = (long) (100 * Math.pow(2, attempt));   // 100,200,400,800
            long capped = Math.min(base, 10_000);                // cap the wait
            long jitter = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(capped);
            sleep(jitter);                       // FULL jitter: 0..capped
        }
        catch (NonRetryableException e) { throw e; }   // 400s: never retry
    }
    throw last;
}

// WHAT IS SAFE TO RETRY
//   GET, PUT, DELETE          naturally idempotent
//   429, 503, timeouts        retryable
//   400, 401, 403, 404, 422   NEVER - the result will not change
//   POST                      only with an idempotency key

// IDEMPOTENCY KEY - makes an unsafe operation safe to repeat
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 7f3a-...          // client generates ONCE per logical op
// The server stores the key with the result. A repeat returns the
// original response instead of charging twice.

// AND: retries must be bounded at every layer. Three layers each
// retrying 3 times is 27 calls to a service that is already struggling.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Token bucket refills at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token; an empty bucket means rejection. Because unused tokens accumulate, an idle client can burst — which is usually what you want for user-facing APIs.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Leaky bucket drains at a constant rate regardless of arrivals, so output is perfectly smooth. Use it when the thing downstream cannot tolerate bursts at all.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Token bucket, thread-safe
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerSecond;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefillNanos;

    TokenBucket(long capacity, double refillPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerSecond = refillPerSecond;
        this.tokens = capacity;                  // start full: burst allowed
        this.lastRefillNanos = System.nanoTime();
    }

    synchronized boolean tryConsume(long n) {
        refill();
        if (tokens >= n) { tokens -= n; return true; }
        return false;                            // rate limited
    }

    private void refill() {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        double elapsed = (now - lastRefillNanos) / 1e9;
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillPerSecond);
        lastRefillNanos = now;                   // lazy refill: no timer thread
    }
}

// Per-user limiting
class RateLimiter {
    private final Map<UserId, TokenBucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    boolean allow(UserId u) {
        return buckets.computeIfAbsent(u, k -> new TokenBucket(10, 1.0))
                      .tryConsume(1);
    }
    // Production concern: evict idle buckets, or this map is a memory leak.
}

// TOKEN BUCKET: burst of 10, then 1/sec.        Good for user APIs.
// LEAKY BUCKET: exactly 1/sec, never more.      Good for a fragile
//                                               downstream dependency.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Producers put work on a queue, consumers take it off, and the queue handles all the coordination. BlockingQueue gives you the blocking and the thread safety, so you write no locks.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      With a bounded queue, a producer that outruns consumers blocks — which is backpressure, and it is a feature. It pushes the problem back to where it can be handled instead of silently accumulating.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Bounded queue, with backpressure
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      BlockingQueue<Task> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);   // BOUNDED

// Producer
class Producer implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            Task t = fetchWork();
            queue.put(t);              // BLOCKS when full -> backpressure
            // queue.offer(t, 5, SECONDS)  -> bounded wait, then shed load
        }
    }
}

// Consumer
class Consumer implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            try {
                Task t = queue.take();          // BLOCKS when empty
                process(t);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // restore the flag
                return;                                // and EXIT
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                log.error("task failed", e);           // do not kill the thread
            }
        }
    }
}

// POISON PILL - clean shutdown
private static final Task STOP = new Task();
for (int i = 0; i < consumers; i++) queue.put(STOP);
// each consumer sees STOP, re-inserts it if needed, and exits

// WHY BOUNDED MATTERS
//   unbounded + producer faster than consumer = OutOfMemoryError
//   Executors.newFixedThreadPool() uses an UNBOUNDED queue. That is
//   the default that takes services down.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        The distinction matters because a registry is a legitimate design element — a map of format names to parsers, of currencies to formatters. It becomes a service locator when arbitrary code reaches into it for its dependencies.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Keep registries narrow and typed. A registry of one specific kind of thing, injected into what needs it, is fine. A global Registry.get(Object.class) is a service locator with a different name.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Narrow and injected
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        // FINE: a typed registry of one kind of thing, INJECTED
class ParserRegistry {
    private final Map<String, Parser> parsers;

    ParserRegistry(Map<String, Parser> parsers) {          // built at startup
        this.parsers = Map.copyOf(parsers);
    }
    Parser forFormat(String format) {
        Parser p = parsers.get(format);
        if (p == null) throw new UnsupportedFormat(format);
        return p;
    }
}

class ImportService {
    private final ParserRegistry registry;                 // injected
    ImportService(ParserRegistry registry) { this.registry = registry; }
}

// NOT FINE: a global bag of everything, reached into from anywhere
class Registry {
    static final Map<Class<?>, Object> ALL = new HashMap<>();
    static <T> T get(Class<T> t) { return (T) ALL.get(t); }
}
// This is a Service Locator. Hidden dependencies, global mutable state,
// tests that leak into each other.

// SINGLETON vs REGISTRY
//   Singleton: one instance of ONE class, globally reachable
//   Registry:  a lookup of MANY instances, ideally injected

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Define a narrow interface, discover implementations at runtime, and treat every plugin as hostile: it will throw, hang, and be built against an older version of your interface. Isolate each call.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Java's ServiceLoader gives you discovery via a metadata file with no framework. Beyond that, decide explicitly on versioning and on whether a failing plugin degrades or fails the operation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Discovery and isolation
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          // 1. A NARROW interface - the extension point
public interface ExportFormat {
    String name();                       // "csv", "pdf"
    boolean supports(String mime);
    byte[] export(Report r) throws ExportException;
}

// 2. DISCOVERY - Java's built-in SPI, no framework
//    META-INF/services/com.example.ExportFormat
//      com.acme.CsvExport
//      com.acme.PdfExport
ServiceLoader<ExportFormat> loaded = ServiceLoader.load(ExportFormat.class);

// 3. ISOLATION - a plugin WILL misbehave
class PluginRegistry {
    private final Map<String, ExportFormat> plugins = new HashMap<>();

    void load() {
        for (ExportFormat p : ServiceLoader.load(ExportFormat.class)) {
            try { plugins.put(p.name(), p); }
            catch (Throwable t) {                       // Throwable, not Exception
                log.error("plugin {} failed to load", p.getClass(), t);
            }   // one bad plugin must not stop startup
        }
    }

    byte[] export(String format, Report r) {
        var p = plugins.get(format);
        if (p == null) throw new UnsupportedFormat(format);
        try { return p.export(r); }
        catch (Throwable t) { throw new ExportFailed(format, t); }
    }
}

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Push the toggle to the edge and make the two paths whole implementations behind one interface. Then the flag chooses a strategy once, at wiring time, instead of appearing in twenty methods.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Give every toggle an owner and a removal date. The real cost of feature flags is not the branch — it is the combinatorial explosion of untested states when twelve of them accumulate.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Toggle at the edge, not inline
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            // SCATTERED - the flag leaks into the domain and never leaves
class CheckoutService {
    void checkout(Cart c) {
        if (flags.isOn("new-pricing")) { ... } else { ... }
        if (flags.isOn("new-pricing")) { ... }        // again
        if (flags.isOn("new-tax") && flags.isOn("new-pricing")) { ... }
        // untestable combinations, and nobody dares delete it
    }
}

// AT THE EDGE - one decision, two complete implementations
interface PricingEngine { Money price(Cart c); }
class LegacyPricing implements PricingEngine { ... }
class NewPricing    implements PricingEngine { ... }

// The toggle is consulted ONCE, at wiring
PricingEngine engine = flags.isOn("new-pricing")
    ? new NewPricing(taxService)
    : new LegacyPricing(taxService);
var checkout = new CheckoutService(engine);

// Both paths are independently testable. Removing the flag deletes
// one class and one line.

// TOGGLE HYGIENE
//   every flag gets an owner and a REMOVAL DATE
//   release toggles are temporary; ops kill-switches are permanent
//   n flags = 2^n states; you test maybe 3 of them

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Done whenYou can state which fields are shared, what guards each one, and defend a design against two threads calling the same method at once.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            StudyJava concurrency - java.util.concurrent →Effective Java - item summaries →

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            • L68
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Write it down. For every mutable field ask whether more than one thread can reach it, and if so, name the lock or the mechanism that protects it. A field with no answer is a race condition waiting to be found in production.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              The three strategies in order of preference: make it immutable, confine it to one thread, or guard it with a lock. Reach for locks last, because they are the option that can deadlock.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Document the policy
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              // State the policy in the code, where it can be reviewed
class OrderCache {
    @GuardedBy("this")
    private final Map<OrderId, Order> cache = new HashMap<>();

    private final AtomicLong hits = new AtomicLong();     // thread-safe itself

    private final Instant createdAt = Instant.now();      // immutable: free

    synchronized Optional<Order> get(OrderId id) {
        var o = cache.get(id);
        if (o != null) hits.incrementAndGet();
        return Optional.ofNullable(o);
    }
}

// THE THREE STRATEGIES, in order of preference
// 1. IMMUTABLE       no shared mutable state -> nothing to protect
// 2. CONFINED        one thread owns it (thread-local, or an actor)
// 3. GUARDED         a lock, and every access takes the SAME lock

// THE MOST COMMON BUG: a thread-safe collection used non-atomically
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);        // TWO operations, racy
                                               // even on ConcurrentHashMap
map.putIfAbsent(k, v);                         // ONE atomic operation
map.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> expensive());    // atomic, computed once

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              • L69
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Sharing immutable objects across threads is always safe, so most concurrency problems disappear by construction rather than being solved. This is why functional-style designs scale more easily.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                The requirement is that the object is fully immutable, including the objects it references. A final field pointing at a mutable list is not immutable, and final on the reference does not help.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Free thread safety
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                // SAFE to share across any number of threads, no synchronization
public record Money(long minorUnits, Currency currency) {
    public Money plus(Money o) {
        return new Money(minorUnits + o.minorUnits, currency);   // NEW object
    }
}

// NOT immutable, despite every field being final
public final class Order {
    private final List<LineItem> items;         // final REFERENCE...
    public List<LineItem> items() { return items; }   // ...mutable CONTENTS
}
order.items().add(x);          // any thread can mutate it. Not safe.

// FIXED
public final class Order {
    private final List<LineItem> items;
    public Order(List<LineItem> items) { this.items = List.copyOf(items); }
    public List<LineItem> items() { return items; }   // unmodifiable
}

// SAFE PUBLICATION - final fields have a special JMM guarantee:
// if an object is only reachable through final fields set in the
// constructor, other threads cannot see it partially built.
// This is why immutable objects need no volatile.

// "MODIFYING" an immutable object shared between threads:
private final AtomicReference<Config> config = new AtomicReference<>(initial);
config.updateAndGet(c -> c.withTimeout(newTimeout));   // lock-free swap

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                • L70
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  A method-level synchronized locks the entire instance, so two unrelated fields contend with each other. Splitting into separate lock objects lets independent state proceed in parallel — at the cost of having to reason about lock ordering.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Never lock on something a caller can also lock: not this if the class is public, and never on a String literal or a boxed Integer, since those are shared across the JVM.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Lock granularity
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  // COARSE - one lock, everything serialises
class Stats {
    private long reads, writes;
    synchronized void read()  { reads++; }     // a reader blocks a writer
    synchronized void write() { writes++; }    // for no reason
}

// FINE - independent state, independent locks
class Stats {
    private final Object readLock  = new Object();
    private final Object writeLock = new Object();
    private long reads, writes;

    void read()  { synchronized (readLock)  { reads++; } }
    void write() { synchronized (writeLock) { writes++; } }
}

// BETTER for counters - no lock at all
class Stats {
    private final LongAdder reads = new LongAdder();    // beats AtomicLong
    void read() { reads.increment(); }                  // under contention
}

// NEVER LOCK ON THESE
synchronized (this) { }              // in a public class: callers can lock it too
synchronized ("lock") { }            // string literals are INTERNED and shared
synchronized (Integer.valueOf(1)) { } // boxed ints are cached and shared
// -> always: private final Object lock = new Object();

// AND: keep the critical section SHORT. Never do I/O inside a lock.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  • L71
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    It also supports multiple condition variables, interruptible acquisition, and optional fairness. The cost is that you must release it in a finally block — forgetting is a permanently held lock.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Fairness prevents starvation by serving threads in arrival order, and it is significantly slower. Leave it off unless you have measured actual starvation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    tryLock, conditions, and finally
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    class Account {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private long balance;

    void deposit(long amount) {
        lock.lock();
        try { balance += amount; }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }        // FINALLY, always. No exceptions.
    }

    // The capability synchronized does not have: giving up
    boolean transferTo(Account other, long amount) throws InterruptedException {
        if (!lock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)) return false;       // do not wait forever
        try {
            if (!other.lock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)) return false;
            try {
                if (balance < amount) return false;
                balance -= amount; other.balance += amount;
                return true;
            } finally { other.lock.unlock(); }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

// CONDITIONS - multiple wait sets on one lock
private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        while (isFull()) notFull.await();      // WHILE, never if - spurious wakeups
        queue.add(item);
        notEmpty.signal();                     // wake only waiting consumers
    } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

// FAIRNESS: new ReentrantLock(true) prevents starvation, costs throughput.
// Leave it false unless you have measured starvation.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    My notes

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    • L72
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      For short critical sections the extra bookkeeping costs more than it saves, and a plain lock or a concurrent collection is faster. Measure before choosing it.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      StampedLock adds optimistic reading: take a stamp, read without locking, then validate. If a writer intervened, fall back to a real read lock. It is faster and much easier to misuse — it is not reentrant.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Many readers, one writer
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      class Cache {
    private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();

    String get(String k) {
        rw.readLock().lock();                  // many readers concurrently
        try { return map.get(k); }
        finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
    }

    void put(String k, String v) {
        rw.writeLock().lock();                 // exclusive
        try { map.put(k, v); }
        finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }
}

// LOCK DOWNGRADE is legal: write -> read. UPGRADE is NOT (it deadlocks).
rw.writeLock().lock();
try {
    map.put(k, v);
    rw.readLock().lock();                      // acquire read BEFORE releasing
} finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }         // now downgraded

// StampedLock - optimistic reads, faster, NOT reentrant
long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
String value = map.get(k);                     // read with NO lock
if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {                     // did a writer intervene?
    stamp = sl.readLock();
    try { value = map.get(k); } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
}

// HONEST ADVICE: for a map, ConcurrentHashMap beats all of this.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      • L73
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        This is optimistic concurrency at the hardware level — a single CPU instruction. It avoids the context switches a lock causes, which is why atomics outperform locks under moderate contention.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Under heavy contention the retry loop starts wasting work, and LongAdder beats AtomicLong by striping across cells. Also know the ABA problem: a value changing from A to B and back looks unchanged to CAS.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Lock-free updates
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong();
counter.incrementAndGet();                     // CAS loop under the hood

// The loop, made explicit:
long current, next;
do {
    current = counter.get();
    next    = current + 1;
} while (!counter.compareAndSet(current, next));   // retry if someone else won

// Modern form - do this instead of writing the loop
counter.updateAndGet(v -> v + 1);
counter.accumulateAndGet(5, Long::sum);

// Lock-free update of a whole immutable object
AtomicReference<Config> ref = new AtomicReference<>(initial);
ref.updateAndGet(c -> c.withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30)));

// UNDER HIGH CONTENTION: LongAdder stripes across cells
LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();
adder.increment();                             // no shared hot cache line
adder.sum();                                   // slightly stale, much faster

// THE ABA PROBLEM
// Thread 1 reads A. Thread 2 changes A->B->A. Thread 1's CAS SUCCEEDS,
// but the world moved underneath it. Matters for lock-free data
// structures (a popped-and-pushed stack node).
// Fix: AtomicStampedReference - pair the value with a version counter.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        My notes
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Saved links

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        • L74
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          containsKey followed by put is two atomic operations with a race between them. The compound methods — putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge — exist precisely to close that gap.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Know the other collections too: CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy listener lists, BlockingQueue for producer-consumer, ConcurrentSkipListMap when you need a sorted concurrent map.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Atomic operations, not atomic sequences
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          // RACY even on ConcurrentHashMap - two operations, gap between them
if (!map.containsKey(key)) {
    map.put(key, expensiveToCompute());        // two threads both compute
}

// ATOMIC
map.putIfAbsent(key, value);                            // value already known
map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensiveToCompute());    // computed ONCE
map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);                        // atomic counter
map.compute(key, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);

// computeIfAbsent CAVEAT: the mapping function runs while holding a bin
// lock. Do not do I/O in it, and never modify the same map inside it -
// that deadlocks.

// CHOOSING A COLLECTION
ConcurrentHashMap       general concurrent map; weakly-consistent iteration
ConcurrentSkipListMap   sorted, concurrent, O(log n)
CopyOnWriteArrayList    read-heavy, rare writes (listener lists). Every
                        write copies the array - never for write-heavy use.
ArrayBlockingQueue      bounded producer-consumer  <- your default
LinkedBlockingQueue     optionally bounded; UNBOUNDED by default (danger)
ConcurrentLinkedQueue   unbounded, non-blocking

// size() on a concurrent collection is an ESTIMATE. Do not branch on it.
